titles.en: The Masterpiece I Could Never Draw

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Raiden Lin plays the cheerful, slightly useless Lin son so well that the Syndicate and the police both ignore him. In fact he draws the family's safe rooms, and knows the weak point of every building in the city. One night he's kneeling in the middle of an illegal race on the old shipyard road, drawing a warehouse, and a motorbike stops two metres from him.

Jinx gets off it to beat some sense into him. He looks up, smiles, and tells her that her intake manifold is beautiful. The next morning he's at her garage near the Docks with three coffees. She drinks all three.

She grew up in a chop shop under the flyover and swore she'd never be owned by anyone again, least of all the Lins. He'd like to marry her. He asks on a napkin, drawn to scale. She says not yet. He keeps asking.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Raiden is the Lin who talks. In every other book he's in the background, cheerful, drawing something, being an idiot on purpose. I wanted to know what he was like when he stopped pretending, and who would be the first person he did it for. It had to be someone who'd see through him at a hundred and ninety kilometres an hour.

This is the lightest book in the series so far, and the most kissing. They get together in chapter three and never really stop. The trouble isn't whether they'll fall in love. It's her father's shop, his father's name, and two people who were each hidden as children learning to stop hiding each other.

He's rich, and he spoils her: a building, a dyno, a lathe, a hill. She's paying half. She insisted.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a warm, funny romance, but it has some hard moments:

• A man hit by a van, with injuries and a night in hospital (Raiden Gets Hit by a Car)

• A child hidden in a freezer for eleven hours, and a ten-year-old crossing a border alone (Memes at 2 A.M., Ten, Walking Home Alone)

• A threat against a loved one, a knife and an armed crew (Her Father Calls After Five Years, The Men Who Own Her Father, She Builds Her Way Out, Raiden Stops Playing Dumb)

• A remembered attempted assault on a teenage girl, which she fought off; not shown on the page (Her Father Says Sorry, She Lets Him In)

• A friend coming back injured, and grief and fear (The Masterpiece He Could Never Draw)

• A workshop fire and smoke inhalation (The Fire at the Shop)

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
The black door — Jinx's first garage, near the Iron Docks, under an old sign that says TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS.
The shipyard road — Two kilometres of cracked concrete between the dead shipyard and the cranes. Illegal races at one in the morning.
Mrs. Tong's — The noodle place on the corner that only serves men off the container ships. The table by the fridge, back to the wall.
The Meridian — Raiden's glass tower in the Symmetrical Ward. Thirty-one floors. The desk man calls the pale green bike “the tram”.
The pale green bike — The one Jinx built him. Twenty kilometres an hour, lights like a train, a drawing board on the tank, a bell.
The steel room — Behind her tool wall. A light that comes on by itself, air, a line out, a warm lamp she added, and a tin of peaches.
The napkins — Thirty-one proposals, each drawn to scale, kept in his wallet where other people keep photographs.
Under the flyover — The Slums of the Industry, where the sun never gets in. Her father's shop, CAO MOTOR REPAIR.
The gap — Behind the scrap heap, between the wall and the pillar. On the archive drawings from 1974.
The triple — A 1973 two-stroke, three cylinders, a widowmaker. Seized for seven years. Ran at 5:40 a.m.
Oh-three-one-one — The day she left. The code to everything she owns.
JINX — The shop in the old chandler's warehouse three doors down, with a long low window anyone can see into. The sign she cut herself.
The stair — Behind the third shelf on the mezzanine. Two hours of fire board. Used once.
The driveway — One point two kilometres on the hill above the reservoir road. It is a racetrack.
The monkey — The passenger in a racing sidecar, who hangs off the side. Raiden says navigator.
Dyno — A rolling road that measures a bike's power at the back wheel.
Intake manifold — The pipes that carry air and fuel into the engine. Hers are all the same length, by hand.

chapters.title: Sketching in the Middle of a Race Track
chapters.desc: May 2021. An illegal race on the old shipyard road, a man kneeling on the tarmac drawing a warehouse, and a very angry mechanic who nearly kills him.
chapters.epigraph: “I didn’t hit him. Write that down. I want it on record that I didn’t hit him.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
The race on the old shipyard road started at one in the morning, because that was when the last security van went past the gates of the Iron Docks and didn’t come back.

Jinx wasn’t racing. She never raced. She tested.

There was a difference, and she’d explained it to enough men in leather jackets to be tired of it. A race was when you wanted to beat someone. A test was when you wanted to know something. Tonight she wanted to know if the new intake would hold its tune past nine thousand revs on a warm night with the sea air coming in off the basin, and the only straight in the city long enough to find out was two kilometres of cracked concrete between the dead shipyard and the cranes.

So she sat on her bike at the back of the line, under the last working streetlight, with her visor up, and listened.

The bike was black and low and long, and she’d built every part of it that mattered. The frame was hers. The swingarm was hers. The tank was a dented thing she’d found in a breaker’s yard and beaten out by hand over a week of evenings, and on it, in orange and white, a carp swam up toward a spark plug, the same carp that swam up the inside of her left forearm. The engine was a big old four from a bike nobody wanted any more, and she’d taken it to pieces on her kitchen table and put it back together better.

The intake was new. She’d made it on Tuesday.

Four runners, each the same length to the millimetre, curving down from the carburettors into the head like the fingers of a hand. She’d matched them to the ports with a file and a lamp and a great deal of swearing, because if one runner was even slightly longer than the others, that cylinder breathed differently, and the whole engine felt it, like a stone in a shoe.

It idled clean, but that meant nothing. Everything idled clean.

✦ ✦ ✦

Down the line, the first two bikes went.

She heard them before she saw them, the scream going up and up and then the doppler drop as they came past the old shipyard gates, and the crowd along the fence shouted, and somebody let off a firework that went sideways into the water. Twelve bikes tonight. Eight cars, earlier, which she hadn’t bothered to watch, because cars were bikes for cowards. A few hundred people along the fences with their phones out and beer in their hands and nobody looking at the road behind them.

Big Fok the starter waved her up.

She rolled forward to the line, a smear of white paint somebody had put down years ago that was now mostly gone. Next to her was a boy on a stolen-looking sports bike with a fairing that didn’t match the frame. He revved it at her. She didn’t look at him.

She put her visor down.

The world went small and dark and quiet, just her breathing and the engine and the two kilometres of road under the orange lights, and the cranes at the far end like giraffes against the sky.

Big Fok dropped his arm.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bike went.

Nought to a hundred in the time it took to think the number. The front wheel lifted a hand’s width and came down and she tucked in flat behind the screen and wound it on, and the revs climbed, six, seven, eight, and the note changed the way she’d hoped it would, hardened, came on clean and fierce with no flat spot at all, nine thousand, nine and a half, and the boy on the stolen bike was somewhere behind her in another life. The shipyard gates went past in a smear. The intake was holding. It was holding. She was going to have to buy herself a drink.

And then there was a man in the road.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was kneeling.

Afterwards, at three in the morning when she couldn’t sleep, that was what she kept coming back to. He was kneeling on the concrete in the middle of the road, just past the last of the shipyard gates, in the orange light, with his back half to her and a sketchbook on his knee.

Drawing.

She saw him at the speed you see things at a hundred and ninety kilometres an hour, which is to say she saw him whole, all at once, like a room lit by lightning. A white shirt. Black hair falling in his eyes. A pencil. His head tipped up, looking at the old warehouse on the left of the road, the big one with the arched roof, as if it was the only thing in the world.

She didn’t think. Thinking would have killed him.

Her hands did it. Front brake and back brake together, hard, harder than she’d ever used them, the front tyre squealing and the back of the bike coming round and wanting to go, her whole weight thrown back, the forks diving, the road coming up at her. She held it. She didn’t know how. The bike shook under her like an animal and slid and slowed, and the man got bigger in her visor, and still he didn’t move—

She stopped two metres from him.

She measured it later, with a tape, in daylight, because she couldn’t not. A shade over two metres from the black stripe of her front tyre to the place where his knee had been.

He looked round.

He looked at her, sitting there on a smoking bike in the middle of the road with her front wheel nearly in his lap, and he smiled. A wide, easy, delighted smile, as if she’d turned up early for a lunch they’d planned.

“Oh, hello,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got off the bike.

She didn’t remember putting the side stand down. She found out afterwards she hadn’t; the bike had fallen over on its side on the concrete and scraped the end of her new exhaust, which she would also never forgive him for. She pulled off her helmet and threw it at the road and walked up to him, and he stood up, still holding the sketchbook, and she grabbed him by the front of his white shirt with both fists and pulled him off balance so that his face was right in front of hers.

“Are you trying to die?” she said.

She’d meant to shout it. It came out low and shaking, which was worse.

“No,” he said. He seemed to think about it. “I don’t think so. Not tonight.”

“You’re kneeling in the middle of a race.”

“Is it a race? I thought it was more of a—” He waved the pencil at the fences, the crowd, the fireworks. “A gathering.”

“There are twelve bikes on this road.”

“Eleven now, I suppose.” He looked past her at her bike, lying on its side. “Is it all right? I’m so sorry. I’ll pay for it.”

She shook him. He was taller than her, just, and thinner, and he let her do it, which made her angrier.

“You’re a suicidal idiot,” she said. “You’re a suicidal idiot who’s going to get me killed. I could have hit you. I could have put you through that fence and gone through it after you and they’d have been scraping us both off the concrete with a shovel. What is wrong with you? What are you even doing?”

He held up the sketchbook between them, politely, as if it explained everything.

She looked at it. She couldn’t help it.

It was the warehouse. The one with the arched roof. He’d drawn it in a few minutes, in pencil, and it was beautiful. The long curve of the roof, the iron ribs, the rows of tall windows. And over it, faint, a spiral, starting tiny in one corner and opening out, and out, until it met the edge of the roof exactly.

“It’s the golden ratio,” he said. “The whole building. Somebody built it on purpose, in 1931, and then everyone forgot. Look. The windows are in it too. I’ve been trying to see it from the front for a year, but there’s always a lorry parked in the way, and tonight the road was empty.”

“The road was empty,” Jinx said, “because there’s a race on it.”

He looked at her, then. Properly. As if he’d only just noticed her.

His eyes moved over her face, and then down, past her shoulder, to her bike on the ground. The polite smile went. What came instead was bright and greedy, the look she knew she got herself when she opened up an engine and found the fault.

“Oh,” he said. “Oh, that’s beautiful.”

“What?”

“Your intake manifold.” He stepped round her, still with her fist in his shirt, so she had to turn with him. “Look at it. They’re all the same length. All four. And the curves are the same. Did you make that? You made that. Nobody sells one like that. That’s hand-made. It’s perfectly symmetrical. It looks like a hand. It looks like someone holding something they don’t want to drop.”

Jinx had nothing to say to that.

She stood there in the middle of the old shipyard road with her fist in a stranger’s shirt, and the bikes behind them had stopped coming, because somebody had seen, and the crowd along the fences had gone quiet in the way crowds go quiet when they think they might be about to see a fight. And she had been about to hit him. She knew she had. Her right hand had been ready for it. She had been raised in a chop shop under the flyover, with men who settled things with their hands, and she had been going to hit him.

And he’d looked at her bike and said it looked like someone holding something they didn’t want to drop.

Nobody had ever looked at anything she’d made like that. The men at her father’s shop hadn’t, or her father, or the collectors who paid her a fortune and talked about horsepower and resale value. None of them had seen what she was trying to do.

She let go of his shirt.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Get off the road,” she said.

“Yes,” he said. “Of course. Sorry.” He didn’t move. He was still looking at her. “I’m Raiden.”

“I don’t care.”

“What’s your name?”

She picked up her helmet. There was a new scrape down one side of it. She looked at that instead of him.

“Jinx.”

“That’s not a name,” said Raiden. “That’s a warning.”

“Yes,” said Jinx.

He laughed. It was a good laugh, loud and surprised, as if he hadn’t expected it either, and she felt the corner of her own mouth move and pressed it flat.

She went and picked up her bike. It was heavy; it always was, on its side. He came to help. She told him not to touch it, and he stopped with his hands up in the air, and watched her lift it, and his eyebrows went up, slightly, and stayed there.

The exhaust was scraped. The left mirror was gone. The intake was fine. She checked it twice, crouched on the concrete with her phone torch, running her thumb along each runner, and it was fine.

When she stood up, he was still there.

“Can I see you again?” he said.

She stared at him.

“Not like this,” he said quickly. “Not in a road. Somewhere with a chair. Tomorrow? I could come to you. Wherever you keep it.” He nodded at the bike. “I want to see the rest of it. I want to draw it properly. And I want to buy you dinner, to say sorry for the mirror, and because I’d like to. Mostly because I’d like to.”

She put her helmet on.

“Get off the road,” she said, through the visor.

She started the bike and turned it round. She rode back to the start line in second gear, with the whole crowd watching and nobody saying a word.

When she looked back, from the start line, he’d got off the road.

He was sitting on the fence by the shipyard gates, with his sketchbook on his knee, drawing.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found out the next morning what he’d been drawing.

He’d drawn her, or tried to. He hadn’t got her face. He’d drawn her bike, lying on its side on the concrete, with the front wheel still turning and the carp on the tank, and the intake, perfect, every runner exactly right. And her boots beside it. And her hand, hanging down by her side, with the fingers still curled the way they’d been in his shirt.

Underneath, in small neat capitals, he’d written: J’s bike, as it really is. R. 2021.

He brought it to her garage at ten in the morning, with three coffees.

chapters.title: “Nice Intake Manifold” Is Not a Pick-Up Line
chapters.desc: He turns up at her garage the next morning with a sketchbook and three coffees. She drinks all three. It worked anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “I brought three because I didn’t know how you took it. Now I know. You take all three.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
Her garage was near the Iron Docks, in a street of ship chandlers and rope shops where nobody asked anybody anything.

It was a narrow brick building with a black roll-up door, squeezed between a man who sold marine paint and a man who sold anchors, and above the door, in faded white letters, it still said TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS, because she’d never got round to painting over it and liked that it put people off. Two rooms upstairs. A kitchen that was really a hot plate and a sink. A bathroom with a shower that worked if you hit the pipe. And downstairs, the only part that mattered: the workshop, long and high and cool, with the benches down one side and the lathe at the back and bikes everywhere, on stands, on the floor, in pieces, hanging from the ceiling on chains.

On Sunday morning she had the roll-up door half open for the air, and she was lying on her creeper under a small red bike with her head by the sump, when a pair of clean brown shoes stopped beside her boots.

“Good morning,” said the man from the road.

She lay still under the bike.

“I’ve brought coffee,” he said. “Three. I didn’t know how you took it. So there’s black, and there’s one with milk, and there’s one with condensed milk, from the man on the corner, who says nobody under sixty drinks it but you might.”

Jinx pushed herself out on the creeper and looked up at him.

He was standing in the doorway with the sun behind him, holding a cardboard tray with three cups in it and a sketchbook under his arm. He was wearing a different white shirt, and grey trousers that had clearly cost more than her lathe, and he had a pencil behind his ear. He looked about twenty-three, pleased with himself, and wrong for the street in every way.

“How did you find me?” she said.

“I asked the man with the flag.”

“Big Fok doesn’t tell people where I live.”

“He didn’t,” said Raiden. “He told me you’d kill me if I came here. Then I asked the boy with the stolen fairing, and he told me the street, because he wanted me to die. Then I asked the woman who sells anchors, and she looked at me for ages and said the black door.” He held out the tray. “Coffee?”

✦ ✦ ✦

She drank the black one standing up, in about four swallows, because she’d been up since six and her head hurt.

Then she drank the one with milk, slower, sitting on an oil drum by the bench, while he walked round her workshop with his hands behind his back, as if it were a museum, not touching anything.

Then she looked at the third one.

“You can have it,” he said, without turning round. “I don’t drink coffee. It makes my hands shake. I’d be no use to anybody.”

“Then why did you buy three?”

“I told you. I didn’t know how you took it.” He’d stopped in front of the lathe. “Now I know. You take all three.”

She drank the condensed milk one. It was sweet and strong and exactly what her father used to drink at five in the morning under the flyover, She hadn’t had one in three years. She wasn’t going to tell him that.

“This is a Weiler,” he said, about the lathe.

“Yes.”

“It’s older than me.”

“It’s older than both of us.”

“It’s beautiful,” he said, and turned round. “Everything in here’s beautiful. Did you know that? Everything’s exactly where it should be. Even the mess. Especially the mess.” He looked up at the bikes hanging from the ceiling on their chains. “The light comes in from the door and goes all the way to the back. Someone designed this building to do that, for the rope makers, so they could see the twist in the line. And you’ve put your bench exactly where the light’s best at ten in the morning.”

“I put it there because that’s where the plug is.”

“Then the plug’s in the right place,” said Raiden, seriously, and sat down on an upturned crate across from her and opened his sketchbook. “I brought you something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the drawing.

He held it out to her across the gap between the crate and the oil drum, and she put down the empty cup and wiped her hands on her overalls, twice, and took it.

It was her bike, on its side, on the concrete, from last night. She hadn’t known he’d seen it like that. He’d only had a minute. But it was all there: the turning wheel, the scrape on the exhaust, the carp on the tank. And the intake, every runner, the curves, the little lip where she’d filed the mouth of the third one by hand because the casting had been rough.

And her boots. And her hand.

J’s bike, as it really is. R. 2021.

She looked at it.

“Is it wrong?” he said. “I only had a minute. I did the intake from memory, after. I might have got the—”

“It’s not wrong.”

“Oh,” he said. “Good.”

She didn’t give it back. She stood up and walked to the back wall, where she had a line of string strung between two nails, with clothes pegs on it, and her own drawings hanging off it, the bad ones she did in biro on the backs of invoices when she was working out a part. She took down an old one and pegged his up in its place.

When she turned round, he was watching her with his chin on his hand, and his smile was smaller than the one from last night. He looked as if he’d been given something.

“Have dinner with me,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

“No,” said Jinx.

She went back to the small red bike and lay down on the creeper and pushed herself under it.

There was a pause above her.

“That’s fine,” said Raiden’s voice. “I’ll wait.”

“For what?”

“For you to say yes.”

“I’m not going to say yes.”

“Then I’ll wait a long time,” he said, and she heard the crate creak as he sat back down. “It’s all right. I’m very good at waiting. I’ve got nothing on today. I’ll just sit here and draw your workshop, if you don’t mind. You won’t know I’m here.”

She knew he was there.

She knew he was there all morning. He didn’t talk much, which surprised her. He drew. Every so often she heard the pencil stop, and knew he was looking at her, and then it started again. Once he got up and walked round to see the bike from another side, and stood there for twenty minutes, and she nearly told him to go away and didn’t.

At twelve, the boy the small red bike belonged to came for it.

He was young and thin, with burn scars on both hands, shiny and pink, and a delivery bag from a flower shop on his shoulder. His name was Xiao Pan. He came every month, for a service she didn’t charge him for, because in February he had stood at her door and said Zhao Zhendong’s name, the way he’d been told to. She owed Zhao Zhendong a favour. So she’d built the boy a bike that his hands could manage: light controls, a thumb throttle, a clutch that pulled like a feather. He’d cried when he first rode it. She’d pretended not to see.

He stopped dead in the doorway when he saw the man on the crate.

Raiden looked up from his sketchbook.

“Oh,” he said. “Hello.”

Xiao Pan looked at Jinx with wide eyes, then at the bike. He took it and wheeled it out into the street without a word and rode away faster than she’d ever seen him go.

Jinx watched him go.

“Do you know him?” she said.

“No,” said Raiden. “I’ve never seen him in my life.”

She looked at him. He looked back at her, pleasant and blank.

He was lying. She didn’t know how she knew. She could always tell when an engine was lying to her, when it sounded fine and wasn’t, and this was the same thing: a sound that was fine and a feeling underneath it that wasn’t. But she didn’t know what he was lying about, and it was Sunday, and her head had stopped hurting, so she let it go.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came back at three with lunch.

He hadn’t asked if she wanted lunch. He just went out, without saying anything, and came back forty minutes later with two paper bags from the noodle place on the corner that only served men off the container ships, and which did not, as a rule, serve men in grey trousers.

“Mrs. Tong said you have the beef,” he said. “With extra greens, and you take the greens out and leave them on the side, and she doesn’t know why you order them.”

“She talks too much.”

“She does. I liked her.” He put a carton down on the bench beside her, on a clean rag, and took the lid off, and put chopsticks beside it, split, and the little packet of chilli oil, opened. He did it neatly and quickly, without fuss. He’d done it before. “She asked if I was your boyfriend.”

Jinx had the noodles halfway to her mouth.

“What did you say?”

“I said not yet,” said Raiden. “And she gave me extra beef.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At six he was still there.

She’d done two brake jobs and a carb rebuild and had argued on the phone with a collector who wanted his bike painted gold, and Raiden had filled half his sketchbook. He hadn’t said a word in an hour. He’d made her tea, once, from the kettle on the back shelf, without asking where anything was, and found the tea and the cups and the tin of biscuits she kept for customers, and put a cup beside her elbow just when she wanted it.

She looked at him, finally, across the workshop.

He was sitting on his crate in the long low light from the door, with his sleeves rolled up and pencil on his fingers, drawing the bikes on their chains, and his face was calm. The big smile from last night was gone. He looked like someone doing the thing he was good at, in a place he liked.

He wasn’t going to leave, she thought. And she didn’t want him to, which annoyed her more.

“Why are you still here?” she said.

He looked up.

“I told you,” he said. “I’m waiting for you to say yes. And you’re very interesting to watch. You talk to nobody and you don’t stop moving and every single thing you do, you do properly.” He turned the sketchbook round. It was her, from behind, bent over the carb with her shoulders up and the light on the back of her neck. Not her face. “I’ve been trying all day. I can’t get you. It’s driving me mad.”

She looked at the drawing. Then at him.

“You don’t know anything about me,” she said.

“Well, you nearly died last night so you wouldn’t kill a stranger,” said Raiden. “You took that bike off the road at a hundred and ninety and held it, and then you got off and checked the intake before you checked your own hands. You build bikes for boys with burnt hands and don’t charge them. And you take your coffee all three ways.” He shut the sketchbook. “I want to know the rest. I’ll go when you tell me to. Then I’ll come back tomorrow and ask again. So you might as well say yes now and save us both the bus fare.”

She didn’t say anything for a while.

Outside, a container ship sounded its horn in the basin, long and low. Somebody in the rope shop next door was pulling down their shutter.

“Thursday,” said Jinx.

He sat still.

“Really?”

“I’m busy until Thursday.”

“Thursday’s perfect. Thursday’s the best day of the week. Thursday’s—” He stopped himself. He stood up and put the sketchbook under his arm. He picked the empty coffee cups up off the floor and dropped them in the bin by the door. Then he stood in the doorway in the evening light, looking at her as if there was something else he wanted to say and he’d decided not to.

“I’ll pick you up at seven,” he said instead. “There’s a thing I have to go to. A party. It’ll be terrible. You can watch me be an idiot in public, and then I’ll take you somewhere good to eat, and you can tell me what’s wrong with everyone there.”

“I don’t go to parties.”

“You don’t have to talk to anyone. You can stand behind me and frighten them.”

That was so exactly what she’d have done that she nearly laughed.

“Seven,” she said.

He gave her the big smile, the one from the road.

Then he went out into the street. She heard him walk away toward the corner and stop at Mrs. Tong’s, heard Mrs. Tong say something, and heard him laugh, loud and happy, the whole length of the street.

Jinx stood in the middle of her workshop with grease to her elbows and listened to it until it was gone.

Then she went and looked at the drawing on the string for a while.

J’s bike, as it really is.

She’d find out later that his surname was Lin. That his father was the most frightening man in the Walled City. That he’d known exactly who Xiao Pan was, and who had sent him, and what that meant about her.

On Sunday, she didn’t know any of that. On Sunday he was just a man who’d brought her three coffees, and seen her intake, and stayed.

chapters.title: The Socialite Everyone Ignores
chapters.desc: A gallery opening forty floors up. He plays the fool so well that the whole room believes him. She watches him count the exits and knows he isn’t one.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody shoots the boy who can’t find his own coat.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
At five o’clock on Thursday a courier came to the black door with a box.

It was a big flat box, matte black, with a ribbon, and the courier held it out to her at arm’s length, as if it might go off, and asked her to sign. Jinx signed with a greasy thumb. She put the box on the bench and looked at it while she finished a wheel bearing. Then she washed her hands, twice, and opened it.

Inside, in black tissue paper, was a leather jacket.

It was nothing like hers. Hers was fifteen years old and had belonged to a man at her father’s shop who’d died, and it had a cigarette burn on the left cuff and a zip that only went up if you held your breath. This one was black and soft and heavy, with a high collar and silver zips, and when she held it up against herself in the reflection of the lathe guard it was exactly her size across the shoulders, which nothing ever was. She had to buy men’s jackets, because of her shoulders, and then the sleeves were too long.

The sleeves were the right length.

Underneath it, in the tissue, was a pair of black boots in her size, and a card, in small neat capitals:

You don’t have to wear these. I only wanted you to have something that fits. You can wear your own and look better than everyone there anyway. R.

She stood there holding the jacket for a while.

Then she put on her own jacket, the old one with the burn on the cuff, and the new boots.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at seven in a taxi.

She was waiting on the step with the roll-up door down behind her, and he got out of the taxi and stopped on the pavement and looked at her, from the boots up, slowly, all the way to her face. He was in a dark grey suit and a silver waistcoat with a pattern on it like the inside of a watch, and he looked like the kind of money that didn’t have to say so.

“You wore the boots,” he said.

“They fit.”

“I know. I asked the anchor woman your size.”

“She doesn’t know my size.”

“She guessed. She’s very good. She said you’ve got shoulders like her husband had and he worked the cranes for thirty years.” He opened the taxi door for her. “You look wonderful. You look like you might hit someone.”

“I might.”

“Please do,” said Raiden. “There’s a man there called Deputy Director Hsu. Start with him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The party was in a new tower in the Coastal High-Rise, forty-one floors up, in a gallery that had been open for an hour and already smelled of money and lilies.

The walls were white and the floor was white and the art was mostly large and red. There were waiters with trays. There were women in dresses that cost more than her bike and men in suits who all seemed to be the same man, and there was a string quartet in the corner, playing something nobody was listening to, and a window that went the whole length of the room with the whole city spread out under it in lights, all the way down to the black water of the harbour.

Jinx stood just inside the door in her old jacket and her new boots and felt every head in the room turn and look at her and then look away.

Raiden took a glass of champagne from a passing tray. He didn’t drink it.

“Watch,” he said, under his breath, and then he went into the room.

✦ ✦ ✦

She watched.

She’d been watching men all her life. At the chop shop you learned it early, before you learned to read: who was in charge, who was frightened, who was carrying, who would hit you and who would only shout. She could stand in the corner of a room and know in five minutes which man in it was dangerous.

In five minutes, every person in that room had decided that Raiden was the least dangerous man they had ever met.

He was wonderful at it. He was awful. He went from group to group with his glass held up like a torch, and he was loud, and happy, and wrong about everything. He told a woman in green that the red painting behind her was clearly about her divorce. He told an old man the building had terrible feng shui and that the columns in the lobby were all wrong, Uncle, they’re fighting the river, you can feel it in your knees. He got the name of the gallery owner wrong twice. He laughed at things that weren’t jokes. He knocked a canapé off a tray and apologised to the waiter so long and so warmly that the waiter started laughing too.

And everyone smiled at him, the way you smile at a nice dog, and turned back to each other, and forgot he was there.

Jinx stood by the wall and watched him do it, and slowly the back of her neck went cold.

Because he wasn’t drinking. He’d had the same glass of champagne for forty minutes, and it was still full to the same line. And every time he moved through the room, he touched something: a wall, a column, a door frame. Just his fingertips, in passing, the way she ran her thumb over a weld. And every time somebody new came in, he knew. He didn’t look round. He just moved a little, so that he could see them.

And when he’d been round the whole room, he came back to her, smiling his silly smile, and stood beside her at the wall, and said in an ordinary voice, low:

“Three ways out. The door we came in. The service corridor behind the bar, which goes to the kitchen and the goods lift. And the fire stairs, past the toilets, which are propped open with a fire extinguisher because the caterers are smoking on the landing. That window’s not load-bearing, by the way. None of the glass is. The whole weight of this floor is on six columns and the core, and two of the columns are wrong. Not feng shui wrong. Actually wrong. Someone saved money on them in 2018.” He sipped his champagne, finally, a small sip. “Don’t worry. It’ll stand for a hundred years. Probably. Shall we eat?”

She looked at him.

He looked back at her, with his silly smile still on, and his eyes not silly at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her out through the service corridor.

Past the bar and the kitchen and two waiters smoking by the goods lift, who straightened up and then saw it was him and relaxed, and through a steel door onto the back stairs, which were concrete and bare and smelled of cigarettes and bleach, with a little window on each landing looking out over the dark side of the city.

He sat down on the stairs and took off his tie.

“Sorry,” he said. “That’s always the worst part. The first hour. After that they’ve made up their minds and you can do what you like.” He stuffed the tie in his pocket. “Mrs. Tong’s is still open. Or there’s a place on the eleventh floor of this building that does the best duck in the city, if you don’t mind a lift with a man in it who’ll want to talk to me about columns.”

Jinx didn’t sit down.

She stood two steps below him, so their faces were level, and folded her arms.

He looked at her for a moment. Then he reached out and caught the zip of her old jacket between two fingers, the one that only went up if you held your breath, and pulled her up a step, until her knees were against his and her face was right in front of his, in the bleach-and-cigarette light of the stairwell, and she could feel him breathing.

“I’ve wanted to do this since the third coffee,” he said.

He leaned in. She didn’t move. His mouth was a breath from hers. Her heart was going hard enough to hurt.

And he stopped. She could see what it cost him.

“No,” he said. “Not yet. There’s something you should hear first. You’d hate me if I did this before you’d heard it.” He let go of the zip.

She stepped back down. Her face was hot. She folded her arms again, harder.

“You’re not stupid,” she said.

He went still.

It wasn’t much. If she hadn’t been watching him for an hour, she wouldn’t have seen it. But the smile stopped moving. It stayed on his face, exactly the same shape, and stopped being a smile.

“No,” he said, after a moment. “I’m not.”

“Why do you do it?”

He looked at her for a while. Then he looked down at his hands on his knees.

“My name’s Raiden Lin,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d known a Lin, once.

Not known. Seen. When she was nine, a black car had come down the lane under the flyover, slowly, and stopped outside her father’s shop, and every man in the shop had stopped what he was doing and stood up, her father first. A big quiet man in a dark coat got out and went into the office. Ten minutes later he came out again and the car drove away. And afterwards her father had sat at his desk with his hands flat on it for an hour and not said anything, and when she’d asked who that was, he’d said, Lin. From the Walled City. Don’t ever go there.

She’d never gone there.

“Lin Jian,” she said.

“He’s my father.”

She took a step back, down. Her boot heel hit the edge of the next stair.

He didn’t move.

“I’m the son,” he said. “The only one. There are four girls and me. And when you’re the only son of Lin Jian, there are a lot of people who’d like to have you. To use, or to hurt him with, or just to have.” He turned his hands over on his knees. “I worked that out when I was ten. So I decided to be the son nobody would want. Pretty, and loud, and silly, and useless. The one who can’t find his own coat. The one who draws. Nobody’s worried about a boy like that. And nobody shoots a boy nobody’s worried about.”

“And what do you really do?”

He looked up at her.

“I draw,” he said. “That part’s true. I draw buildings for a firm in the south. And sometimes I draw them for my family. Walls that look like walls. Floors that look like floors.” He was quiet for a moment. “I make places safe. That’s all. I’m good at it. And nobody knows, because nobody looks at me.”

She thought of him walking round the gallery with his fingers on the walls.

She thought of Xiao Pan’s face in her doorway, and the lie, and the feeling under it. Xiao Pan worked at a flower shop in the old town. She knew whose wife owned that flower shop. Everyone in the Docks knew.

“Your sister’s married to Zhao Zhendong,” she said.

“Elowen. Yes.”

“You knew who Xiao Pan was. You knew Zhao sent him to me.”

“Yes.”

“Did Zhao send you?”

He looked genuinely shocked. Then he laughed, short and surprised, the first real laugh since the stairs.

“No,” he said. “God, no. Zhao only notices me when I’m standing on his foot. I didn’t know who you were until the boy walked in on Sunday. I just saw your intake.” He stopped laughing. “I’m sorry I didn’t tell you. On Sunday. I should have. I wanted one day where you didn’t know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood on the stairs and didn’t say anything.

She was thinking about her father’s hands flat on the desk. About the men at the shop, standing up. About being twelve and fourteen and seventeen in a chop shop that broke stolen bikes for the Syndicate’s buyers, and about how she’d got out, at twenty-two, with a van and a lathe and nothing else, and promised herself she would never be owned by any of them again. Not the buyers, not the crews, not the families in the Walled City who sat at the top of all of it.

And here was the top of all of it, sitting on a concrete stair with his tie in his pocket.

“I’m going home,” she said.

He stood up.

He didn’t come down the stairs after her. He stayed where he was, with one hand on the rail, and let her go down past him. Then she heard him following a flight behind, all the way down, not saying anything. They came out of a fire door into a lane at the back of the tower where the bins were.

She walked to the end of the lane, to the main road, and put her hand up for a taxi.

One stopped. She opened the door.

“Jinx,” he said.

She looked back.

He was standing in the lane under a security light, in his silver waistcoat, with his hands in his pockets. He didn’t look silly at all.

“I liked you before you got off the bike,” he said. “I want you to know that. You stopped two metres from me and held it, and I looked round and saw you, and that was it. Before you’d said a word. Before the intake, even.” He took a breath. “I’m coming to the garage tomorrow. At ten. With coffee. If you want me to go away, throw a spanner at me. I’ll go. And I won’t come back, and I won’t send anyone, and you’ll never hear the name Lin from me again. That’s a promise. I keep those.”

The taxi driver said, “Are you getting in or not?”

She got in.

She didn’t look back again. But the taxi had to wait at the lights at the end of the road, and in the side mirror she could see him, still standing in the lane under the light, with his hands in his pockets, watching her go.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t sleep.

She lay on her mattress in the room over the workshop with the window open and the noise of the Docks coming in, the cranes and the trucks and the horns, and she thought about it.

She thought about spanners.

At four in the morning she got up and went downstairs in her vest and shorts and put the lights on in the workshop and stood in front of the tool wall, where her spanners hung on hooks in order of size, from the tiny ones she used on carburettors to the big one at the end that was as long as her forearm.

She took down a thirteen, the one she used most, worn smooth at the grip from her hand.

She put it on the bench by the door, where she’d be able to reach it at ten o’clock.

Then she went back upstairs, and lay down, and slept until nine like the dead.

chapters.title: The First Kiss Smells Like Oil
chapters.desc: She throws the spanner. She misses on purpose. He has one rule, and he keeps it, and he pushes it as far as it will go, under a bike, on two creepers, in the dark.
chapters.epigraph: “I said I’d go if you threw a spanner. I didn’t say what happens if you miss.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
He came at ten.

She heard the taxi stop at the end of the street, because taxis never came down it, and then she heard him walking, the clean brown shoes on the cobbles, and she was standing by the bench with her back to the door when he stopped in the doorway with three coffees.

She picked up the thirteen and threw it.

She’d been throwing spanners since she was seven. She threw this one hard, flat, spinning, at the brick wall a metre to the left of his head, where it hit with a crack like a gunshot and dropped to the floor and skidded under a bike.

He didn’t flinch. He looked at the wall. Then at the spanner. Then at her.

“You missed,” he said.

“I never miss.”

“No,” said Raiden slowly. “No, I don’t suppose you do.”

And then he smiled, and it was a new one. It started in his eyes and took its time getting to his mouth, and when it got there it stayed. He came into the workshop and put the coffees down on the bench beside her, carefully, and said, “Good morning,” as if nothing had happened at all.

She drank the black one.

Her hands were shaking. She didn’t let him see.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t sit on the crate today.

He walked round the workshop, and looked at the bikes, and asked her things. Real things. What the lathe could turn. Why she used carburettors on the old bikes and injection on the new ones. How she got the tank on her own bike so smooth. She told him, in short sentences, without looking up from the gearbox she was stripping, and he listened to every word, and asked the next thing, and the next, and after an hour she realised she’d said more to him than she’d said to anyone in a month.

“Carbs are simpler,” she said. “Fuel goes in, air goes past, the air pulls the fuel through a jet. You change the jet, you change the mixture. You can hear it. You can fix it on the side of a road with a screwdriver. Injection’s a computer guessing. It guesses well. Still guessing.”

“And your bike? The black one?”

“Carbs. Four. I tuned them on the dyno at a shop in the north. Took two days.”

“What’s a dyno?”

She looked up at him.

“A rolling road,” she said. “You strap the bike down, back wheel on a drum. You run it. The drum measures the power at the wheel, and a sensor in the exhaust tells you if it’s running rich or lean. Then you change the jets, and run it again. And again. Until the line on the screen’s smooth all the way up.”

“And was it?”

“After two days.”

“And then you rode it in a race, and a man knelt in the road,” said Raiden, “and you stopped in two metres, and nothing came loose.” He shook his head. “I’d like to see it. The dyno. The line on the screen.”

“There isn’t one here. They cost a fortune.”

“Hm,” he said, the way Zhao Zhendong said it, and wrote something down.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve she lay down on the creeper and pushed herself under the black bike, because the scraped exhaust had been bothering her for a week and she wanted to see if the bracket had bent.

It was dark under there. It always was. Just the work light hooked to the frame and the smell of oil and hot metal, and the concrete cool under her shoulders. She liked it. It was the only place in the world nobody could stand over her.

She heard him move.

Then she heard the second creeper. She kept it by the bench, for when she needed to get under a bike from both sides at once. It rolled across the concrete with its little wheels rattling, and stopped, and there was a pause, and then, slowly, with a lot of creaking and one quiet word she pretended not to hear, Raiden lay down on it and pushed himself under the bike beside her.

His shoulder was against hers. His head was right beside hers, under the sump.

“I’ve never been under a bike before,” he said.

“Get out.”

“It’s very nice. It’s like a little house.” He looked up at the underside of the engine, lit orange by the work light. “Oh, look. You can see everything. Is that the—what’s that?”

“The oil filter.”

“It’s beautiful,” said Raiden. “Don’t laugh. It is.”

She wasn’t laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went back to the exhaust bracket. He lay beside her and watched her hands.

It was quiet. The street outside was asleep in the noon heat. A fly went round the work light. She could hear him breathing, and feel his shoulder against hers, warm through his shirt, and she undid one bolt and did it up again and didn’t know why.

“Can I tell you something?” he said.

“No.”

“I’ve made a rule.”

She stopped, with the spanner on the bolt.

“I made it last night,” he said. “In the lane, after the taxi. I stood there for ages and I thought, if she misses with the spanner, I’ll want to kiss her. And I’ll want to so much I won’t be able to think. And I’m not going to. Not until she tells me her name.”

“You know my name.”

“I know what they call you. Jinx.” His voice was low in the little dark space under the bike. “That’s not a name. It’s a thing men called you. I want the one you were given. And I’m not going to kiss you until you tell me what it is.”

She didn’t move.

“That’s a stupid rule,” she said.

“It’s a terrible rule,” said Raiden. “I’ve been regretting it since about half past ten.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She did the bolt up. She undid it again.

He turned his head on the creeper. She felt it, without looking, the way you feel a light come on in another room. He was looking at her face in the orange light.

“I could ask nicely,” he said. “Please. Look, I’m asking. Jinx. What’s your name?”

“No.”

“I could beg.” He sounded serious. “I’m a good beggar. I’m a Lin. We’re brought up to it. Please. I’m begging. I’m lying on a concrete floor under a motorbike, begging. Nobody’s ever made me do that before.”

She pressed her mouth flat.

“I could guess,” said Raiden. “Mei. Lan. Xiu. Fen. Ah Lam. Little Cabbage.” He waited. “Was it Little Cabbage?”

“No.”

“Then it’s something better.” He moved his hand, slowly. She saw it, at the edge of the light: his hand coming across the gap between the creepers, with pencil on the side of his finger, and stopping, just above hers, where it lay on the concrete by her hip. Not quite touching. She could feel the warmth of it. “Can I?”

She didn’t say anything.

He waited.

“Please,” he said, and she didn’t know how he’d got that close, and she turned her hand over on the concrete, palm up, under his.

He put his hand down on hers.

That was all. His hand on hers, on the cold floor, under the bike. His thumb moving once, across her palm, across the calluses and the old burn. She felt it all the way up her arm and into her chest and down into her stomach, and it was ridiculous, it was only a hand, she’d had men’s hands on her before, and none of them had felt like this, like a key going into a lock that had been rusted shut.

“That’s not fair,” she said.

“No,” he agreed. “I’m an unfair man. I’ve got lots of rules and I cheat at all of them except the important ones.” His thumb went across her palm again. “Tell me your name, Jinx.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She turned her head.

He was right there. In the orange light, with grease on his cheek where he’d touched the frame, and his eyes dark, and his face serious, and not one bit of silly in it anywhere.

“Cao Jia,” she said.

He shut his eyes.

He shut them for a second, as if she’d said something that hurt. Then he opened them.

“Jia,” he said. Properly this time. Like it was a word in a language he’d been learning and had finally got right.

And he kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was awkward. It was under a bike. Her elbow hit the sump and his head hit the frame and he said ow against her mouth and she laughed, she actually laughed, out loud, and he laughed too, and kissed her through it, and then neither of them was laughing.

His hand came up out of hers and went to her face. Her jaw. The back of her neck. He kissed her slowly, the way he drew, as if he wanted to get every line right, and then not slowly at all, and she grabbed the front of his shirt in both fists and pulled him across the gap between the creepers, and one of them rolled, and they both slid sideways, and she ended up half on top of him on his creeper with her knee on the concrete and her hair falling on his face and his hands in it.

“Your bike,” he said, against her mouth. “We’re going to knock your bike over.”

“It’s on the stand.”

“I’ll buy you a new mirror,” he said, and kissed her again.

“I don’t want a new mirror.”

“What do you want?”

She stopped. With her mouth on his, and her hands in his shirt, and her heart banging against his chest.

“You talk too much,” she said.

“I always talk,” said Raiden. “It’s the worst thing about me. You’ll have to stop me.”

So she did.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came out from under the bike at about half past one, because the creeper wheels had run over his sleeve and trapped him, and he couldn’t get up, and she had to roll him out by the shoulders.

He lay on the concrete on his back in the light from the door with oil on his face and his shirt half undone and his hair everywhere, laughing.

She sat on the floor beside him with her back against the bench and her heart still going, and wiped her mouth with the back of her hand, and found it was black.

“You’ve got oil on your face,” she said.

“So have you. All over. I did that.” He looked up at her from the floor, pleased with himself. “You look like you’ve been in a fight.”

“I nearly was.”

“You won,” said Raiden. Then he stopped laughing. He lay there on the concrete and looked at her. “Cao Jia. Thank you for telling me.”

She didn’t say anything.

She’d never told anyone. Not since the shop. The men there had stopped using it when she was twelve and they’d started calling her Jinx, because every bike she touched got away clean and never got caught, and she was bad luck for the police. Her father called her girl. The collectors called her Jinx, or Miss Jinx, or nothing. She’d almost forgotten she had another name, until he’d lain on a cold floor under a bike and begged for it.

“Don’t tell anyone,” she said.

“I won’t. I’ll only use it when it’s important.” He sat up, slowly. “Can I still call you Jinx the rest of the time? I like Jinx. It suits you. It’s a good name for a woman who throws spanners.”

“I missed.”

“You missed on purpose,” said Raiden. “I’m going to remember that for the rest of my life.”

He leaned over and picked up the thirteen from under the bike, where it had skidded, and turned it over in his hands, and looked at the worn place on the grip where her hand had been for years.

Then he got up and hung it back on the tool wall, between the twelve and the fourteen.

chapters.title: Raiden Gets Hit by a Car
chapters.desc: June 2021. It isn’t her fault. She stays at the hospital all night anyway. At dawn he asks her to go out the back before his family comes, and she goes.
chapters.epigraph: “I said go. I meant stay. I’ve never been so frightened of anything in my life as I was of them seeing you.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
For two weeks he came every day.

He came at ten with coffee, three, and she drank all three. He sat on the crate and drew. He went out at one and came back with Mrs. Tong’s noodles and put the greens on the side for her without being asked. He watched her work, and asked things, and sometimes he didn’t talk at all for an hour, and she found she didn’t mind that either. In the evenings he took her to eat in places she’d never been, where the waiters knew him, and he ordered for both of them without looking at the menu and was always right.

And every night, at the black door, he kissed her goodnight.

Not under a bike: on the step, with the street empty and the cranes lit up over the roofs, his hands on her face. Every night she thought she’d ask him in, and every night he stepped back first. He’d smile at her and say, “Tomorrow,” and walk away up the street, and she’d stand in the doorway listening to him go and thinking idiot, and not know which of them she meant.

On the second Thursday she said, “Why do you always leave?”

He was on the step. He turned round.

“Because if I come up those stairs,” he said, “I’m not leaving till you throw me out. And I want you to be sure you won’t.” He looked at her in the light from the door. “I’m not in a hurry, Jia. I want all of it. I want it to take years.”

Then he kissed her again, harder, and went.

She shut the door and leaned on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Friday he wanted to draw the cranes.

He’d been wanting to for days. The big ones at the end of the Docks road, the ones that went all night under floodlights, lifting containers off the ships in the basin like a child lifting blocks. He said they were the most beautiful machines in the city and nobody ever looked at them.

“I’ll come and get you,” she said. “Eleven. On the bike. Don’t stand in the road.”

“I never stand in the road.”

“You knelt in the road.”

“That’s different,” said Raiden. “That was for art.” He kissed her, at four in the afternoon, in the doorway, with a customer watching. “Eleven. I’ll be on the pavement like a good boy. You can check.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was late.

A man came at half past ten with a bike he’d dropped on the expressway, a big touring bike with the fairing smashed and the clutch lever gone, and he’d ridden it to her across the city in first gear because nobody else would open at that time of night. He was shaking. He had a wife at home and a job at six. She did the lever and taped the fairing and checked the forks, and it took forty minutes, and she didn’t think about the time until she was wiping her hands and looked at the clock over the door.

Ten past eleven.

She rang him. It rang and rang.

She rang again on the bike, at the lights at the top of the street, with her helmet off. It rang and rang.

She put her helmet on and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was an ambulance on the Docks road.

She saw the lights from a kilometre away, blue, going round and round against the side of a container stack, and her whole body knew before she did. Her hands went cold on the bars. She rode toward the lights and didn’t remember riding there.

A van was stopped across the road at an angle. A delivery van, white, with its front wing caved in and one headlight out. The driver was sitting on the kerb with a policeman beside him, holding his head in his hands. There was glass everywhere, glittering in the blue.

And on the pavement, by the railings, under the floodlights from the cranes, there was a stretcher, and two paramedics, and a man on it, in a white shirt.

There was a sketchbook in the road.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember getting off the bike.

She remembered the paramedic, a woman with short grey hair, putting an arm out to stop her. She remembered pushing past it. She remembered his face, on the stretcher, with blood on it, all down one side from a cut above his eye, and the eye swelling shut, and his left arm in a splint across his chest, and his shirt cut open, and his skin white under the floodlights.

His other eye was open.

He looked at her and tried to smile. “You came.”

“I was late.”

“You came,” said Raiden again. His voice was thick and slow. “I was on the pavement. I promise. I was on the pavement. He came round the corner too fast. He didn’t see me. He was on his phone. It wasn’t—” He stopped, and breathed in, and something hurt him, badly, she saw it go across his face. “It wasn’t you. Jia. It wasn’t you.”

She took his good hand. It was cold.

“Don’t try to talk,” she said.

“I always talk,” said Raiden, and shut his eye.

✦ ✦ ✦

They took him to the City Hospital.

She followed the ambulance on the bike, through every red light, and left it on the pavement outside the emergency entrance with the key in it. She went in after the stretcher with her helmet still on. A nurse told her to sit down, and she didn’t.

She stood in the corridor outside the room where they took him while they cut the rest of his shirt off and put a line in his arm and shone lights in his eyes. She stood outside X-ray, and then outside the CT scanner, by a window with a blind half down, while a machine looked inside his head, and a doctor came out and said she couldn’t tell her anything because she wasn’t family.

“I’m his,” said Jinx.

The doctor looked at the helmet, the grease, her face.

“His what?”

“His.”

The doctor looked at her for a moment more. Then she told her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three ribs cracked, on the left, where the van’s wing had hit him. A broken wrist, the left, the end of the big bone above the hand, which they’d put back in place and would put in plaster in the morning when the swelling had gone down. Seven stitches over his left eyebrow. A concussion. The scan was clear. No bleeding inside his head. He’d been lucky. If he’d been half a step further out, or the van a little faster, it would have been a different conversation.

They were keeping him two nights, for the concussion. Somebody would have to wake him every few hours tonight and check he knew his name.

“I’ll do it,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

They put him in a room on the sixth floor at two in the morning, a small room with one bed, because he was a Lin and somebody had looked at his wallet.

She sat on a plastic chair beside the bed in her helmet, until a nurse told her to take it off, and then she sat in her jacket. The old one with the burn on the cuff. He was asleep, or something like asleep, on his back, with his arm strapped up and his face swollen and the stitches black above his eye, and a machine beside him doing a small green line that went up and down.

She watched the line.

At three she woke him, the way the nurse had told her. She said his name. He opened his good eye and looked at her.

“What’s your name?” she said.

“Raiden Lin. I’m twenty-three. It’s Friday. No. Saturday. You’re Cao Jia, and you’re beautiful, and you came.” He shut his eye again. “Is that enough?”

“That’s enough.”

“Hold my hand,” he said, with his eye shut. “Please. I won’t tell anyone.”

She held it.

At five she woke him again, and he said his name, and the day, and then he said, “I dropped my sketchbook.”

“I’ve got it.”

She’d picked it up from the road. It was in her jacket. The cover was wet, and there was a tyre mark across the back of it, and inside, on the last page, there was the crane. Half drawn. The long arm of it reaching out over a ship, and the floodlights, and the line of the cable going down and stopping in the middle of the page, where he’d been drawing when the van came.

“Is it ruined?” he said.

“No.”

“Good,” said Raiden, and slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t cry.

After that the room got warm, and she took off her jacket and hung it on the back of the chair, and put his sketchbook on the seat beside her.

She sat in the plastic chair for the rest of the night and watched the green line and his face and the window, where the sky over the Symmetrical Ward went from black to grey to a dirty pink. She’d stopped crying at the shop when she was eight. She’d learned that there was no point. Crying didn’t fix anything. You found what was broken and you fixed it, or you couldn’t, and either way you didn’t stand there with your face wet.

But she sat there, and she held his hand, and she thought, he was on the pavement. And she thought, I was forty minutes late. And she thought about the sketchbook in the road, and the line of the cable going down and stopping, and something in her chest went tight and stayed tight, like a bolt done up past where it should go.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six his phone rang.

It was in a plastic bag on the cupboard with his wallet and his keys and his watch, all of them in blood. It kept ringing. She looked at it.

Elowen.

It stopped. Then it rang again.

Baba.

He woke up.

He woke up properly this time. She saw it. His good eye opened, and looked at the ceiling, and then went to the phone ringing on the cupboard, and then to her, and his face, the bit of it that wasn’t swollen, went white.

“The hospital rang them,” he said. “They’ll have rung the house. When they saw the name.” He tried to sit up, and stopped, because of the ribs, and lay back down, breathing badly. “Jia. They’re coming. My father’s people. My sister. They’ll be here in twenty minutes.”

“Good,” she said. “Someone should be.”

“No.” He was holding her hand hard now, with his good one. Harder than she’d have thought he could. “No. Listen. Listen to me. They can’t see you.”

She went still.

“You have to go,” said Raiden. “Now. Before they come. There’s a lift at the end of the corridor, by the linen room, that goes down to the service entrance. Take your bike and go home, and I’ll ring you. Tonight. I promise. But you have to go before they see you here.”

She looked at him.

She looked at his hand, holding hers. At his face, white and swollen, with the black stitches over his eye.

She thought: he’s ashamed of me.

She thought it so clearly it was like hearing it said out loud. A girl from a chop shop under the flyover, in a dead man’s jacket, with grease under her nails. Sitting beside the bed of Lin Jian’s only son. Of course he didn’t want them to see her. Of course he’d want her out the back, by the linen room, by the service lift, like the rubbish.

She took her hand away.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Jia,” he said.

She stood up. She picked up her helmet off the floor. She didn’t think about the jacket. She didn’t think about anything.

“Jia, please. It isn’t—you don’t understand. It’s not—”

“I understand,” she said.

She did. She’d always understood. That was the trouble. She’d let herself not understand, for two weeks, because of three coffees and a drawing and the way he looked at her intake, and the way he kissed her on the step and said tomorrow. She’d let herself forget who he was and who she was. And now it was six in the morning, and the sun was coming up over the Symmetrical Ward, and his family was coming, and she remembered.

“Your sketchbook’s on the chair,” she said.

“Jia—”

She went out.

She walked down the corridor to the end, past the nurses’ station, past the linen room, and pressed the button for the service lift, and stood there with her helmet in her hand. She could hear him saying her name, from the room, louder, and then a nurse’s voice, sharp, telling him to lie still, and then nothing.

The lift came. She got in. The doors shut.

In the steel of the lift doors she could see herself, small and dark, with her helmet, and her face, and she looked at it all the way down six floors and it didn’t do anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, eleven minutes later, Elowen Zhao came along the corridor fast, in a green coat, with her husband a step behind her.

She stopped in the doorway of the room. She looked at her brother in the bed, with his face swollen and his arm strapped up and his eye shut, pretending to be asleep, badly. She said his name in a voice that went right up the corridor, and he opened his eye and said, “Hello, Elowen, I’m fine, it’s nothing, I was drawing a crane,” in his silly voice, and she sat down on the edge of the bed and took his face in both hands, very carefully, and didn’t say anything at all.

Zhao Zhendong didn’t come in.

He stood in the doorway with his hands in the pockets of his black coat and looked at the room: the machine, the bag of bloody things on the cupboard, the sketchbook on the chair with a tyre mark across the back of it.

And at the plastic chair beside the bed, which still had the shape of someone in it, and over the back of which somebody had left a jacket. An old black leather jacket, much too big across the shoulders for a woman, with a cigarette burn on the left cuff and grease ground into the collar.

He looked at it for four seconds.

Then he looked at Raiden.

Raiden looked back at him from the bed, over his sister’s shoulder, with his good eye, and gave a very small shake of his head.

“Hm,” said Zhao.

He picked up the jacket off the chair and folded it, once, over his arm, and took it out of the room before Elowen could turn round and see it.

chapters.title: A Bike That Goes Twenty Kilometres an Hour
chapters.desc: Three weeks of silence, one visit from Zhao Zhendong, and a pale green bike with a drawing board on the tank. Then the thirty-first floor, his rule, and a man in plaster who begs.
chapters.epigraph: “If you’re going to draw in roads, you do it on this.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
He rang that night. She didn’t answer.

He rang the next night. She didn’t answer that either.

On the third day he stopped ringing and started sending things instead. One a day, always at ten in the morning, which was when he used to come with the coffee. No words. Just a photograph of a drawing.

The first one was her lathe, from memory. The second was Mrs. Tong’s noodle shop, with Mrs. Tong in the window glaring. The third was the black bike. The fourth was the thirteen, the spanner, lying on the floor where it had skidded, with a little arrow pointing at the wall a metre away and a note in small capitals: MISSED.

He was drawing right-handed. The plaster was on the left. She could see it at the edge of the fourth photograph, white, with something written on it she couldn’t read.

She looked at every one. She didn’t answer any of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the sixth day Zhao Zhendong came to the garage.

She heard the car stop. It wasn’t a taxi; it was something heavy that idled like a cat. Then nothing for a while. When she looked up from the bench he was in the doorway, in a black coat, in June, with her old jacket folded over his arm.

She’d seen him twice. Once at a distance, at a race, years ago, standing at the back with his arms folded while the whole crowd made a space round him without knowing they were doing it. And once in November 2018, the night she’d opened the black door for the first time, when three men from her father’s buyers had come down the street to drag her back and his men had come out of the dark and stopped them, and he’d stood in the street afterwards and looked at her and said, You owe me one.

She’d paid it in February, with Xiao Pan’s bike. They were even.

He came in. He put the jacket down on the bench beside her, folded.

He looked at her for four seconds.

“He hid you,” said Zhao.

She didn’t say anything.

“He was hidden,” said Zhao. “Ten years. A farm in the borderland. So nobody could use him.” He looked at the drawing of her bike, pegged on the string. “He thinks hiding is how you keep someone.”

He turned round and went out.

She heard the car door, then the engine. The car went away up the street, slowly, and Mrs. Tong came out of her shop and watched it go with her hands in her apron.

Jinx stood by the bench with her hand on the jacket.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she started building the bike.

She didn’t decide to. She just found herself, at eleven, at the back of the workshop, pulling the frame of an old step-through off the hook where it had hung for a year. A cheap commuter frame, light and low, that she’d bought for parts and never used. She stood it on the floor and walked round it and looked at it, the way she looked at every bike, until she could see what it wanted to be.

Then she started.

She did it at night, after the customers had gone, for two weeks. She stripped it to the bare frame and straightened the bent bits and painted it. Pale green, the colour of the old trams in the Walled City, because she thought he’d like that. She gave it fat tyres and wide bars, so he couldn’t fall off it if he tried, and the softest springs she had. She took the little engine out and put in a quieter one, and gave it the lowest gearing she could make, and then she put a stop on the throttle and a limiter in the wiring so it would never go faster than twenty kilometres an hour, not downhill, not with a wind behind it, not if he begged.

She put big lights on it, one on the front like a train and two at the back, and strips of reflective tape down the forks and along the frame, so that anything coming round a corner at night would see it from half a kilometre away.

And over the tank, on a steel arm that swung out and locked, she put a board. A flat board, the size of a sketchbook, covered in cork, with a clip at the top and a little tray underneath for pencils. So that when he stopped, wherever he stopped, he could swing it out and sit sideways on the wide seat and draw, up on the pavement, with the lights on.

She put a bell on it, too. She told herself it was for safety.

On the last night she sat on it in the workshop at three in the morning with the lights on, and rang the bell, once, and it made a small silly cheerful sound in the dark, and she put her face in her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

The building in the Symmetrical Ward was called the Meridian, and it was all glass, and the man on the desk in the lobby looked at her pale green bike with the bell on it as if she’d brought in a horse.

“Lin,” she said. “Thirty-one.”

“Is Mr. Lin expecting you?”

“No.”

The man looked at her old jacket with the burn on the cuff, at her new boots, at the bike. He picked up the phone.

She heard it ring. She heard someone answer. She heard the man say a lady with a bicycle, sir, well, a sort of bicycle, and then she heard, through the phone, small and clear across the whole lobby, Raiden’s voice say something, and the man on the desk took the phone away from his ear and looked at it.

“He says to send you up,” said the man. “He says to send you up immediately. He says if the lift’s too small for the bicycle, I’m to carry it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The goods lift was big enough. She rode it up thirty-one floors standing beside the pale green bike with her hand on the seat, and her heart going, and when the doors opened he was already there.

He was standing in the corridor in a T-shirt and old trousers and bare feet, with his left arm in plaster to the elbow, and the stitches gone from his eyebrow and a thin pink line in their place. He was thinner. His hair needed cutting. He looked as if he hadn’t slept since the hospital.

He looked at her.

Then he looked at the bike.

He didn’t say anything. She’d never seen him not say anything. He came forward slowly, in his bare feet, and put his good hand on the handlebar, and looked at the lights, and the tape, and the wide soft seat. And the board, folded down over the tank. He found the catch. He swung it out, and it clicked into place, and he stood looking at the cork, and the clip, and the little tray for pencils.

He rang the bell.

It made its small silly sound in the corridor of the thirty-first floor.

“It does twenty,” she said. “It won’t do more. Not downhill, not anything. If you’re going to draw in roads, you do it on this. On the pavement, lights on. Or I break your other arm.”

He looked up at her.

His eyes were wet.

“I’m sorry,” he said. “Jia. At the hospital. I’m so sorry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His flat was enormous and nearly empty.

White walls. A grey floor. A whole wall of glass looking out over the Symmetrical Ward and the hospitals and the harbour beyond, blue and silver in the afternoon. A long table with nothing on it. A drawing table by the window, tilted, with a lamp, and a stool, and drawings everywhere around it, on the floor, in piles, pinned to the wall. A kitchen that looked as if it had been used, properly, by someone who knew how. Not much else. No pictures, no clutter.

She stood in the middle of it with the bike parked by the door like a pale green animal.

“I wasn’t ashamed of you,” he said.

He was standing by the window. He hadn’t sat down. He kept moving his good hand, and stopping it.

“I know what it looked like,” he said. “I know what you thought. The service lift. The back way. I saw your face. I’ve seen it every night for three weeks.” He took a breath, and it hurt him, she saw it, the ribs still. “I’ve never been ashamed of anything less in my life. Jia. I was frightened.”

“Of what?”

“Of them seeing you.”

He told her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her about being a baby in a farm in the borderland, with a white water tower and a brick kiln and a couple his father paid. About being sent away before he could remember being anywhere else, and not knowing why, for ten years, and growing up thinking that was what love was: being put somewhere far away, where nobody could find you.

“My father loves us,” he said. “All of us. He’d kill for us. He has. And everyone knows it, that’s the problem. So anyone he loves is something somebody else can take. I got sent away because I was the son, and the son’s the one they’d take first.” He looked out at the harbour. “When the phone rang at six and it said Baba, I didn’t think, oh good, my family. I thought, in twenty minutes the whole Walled City knows Raiden Lin has a girl. What she looks like. Where she works. That she sat by his bed all night. And then you’re something somebody can take.”

He turned round.

“I wanted to keep you out of it,” he said. “That’s all. I wanted you to be mine and nobody else’s business. And I did it like a coward, by the linen room, and I’m sorry. I’ll never do it again. If anybody ever comes through a door when you’re with me, I’ll stand in front of you. I won’t send you anywhere.”

She didn’t say anything.

“I’m not going to the Walled City,” she said at last.

He looked at her.

“I don’t want your father,” she said. “Or his business. I grew up with my father’s buyers in and out of the shop. I got out. Nobody owns me again. Not the buyers, not the crews, not Lin Jian.” She folded her arms. “I’m not going out with a Lin. I’m going out with you.”

“Yes,” said Raiden. “Yes. Good. That’s—yes.”

“So we keep it separate. My side and your side. I don’t go there. Your people don’t come to the garage.” She looked at him. “And you don’t ever put me out of a room again. If someone comes, I stay. I can stand in front of myself.”

“I know you can,” said Raiden. “I’ll stand in front of you anyway. You can stand in front of me. We’ll take turns.”

Her mouth moved. She pressed it flat.

He saw.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came across the room.

He came slowly, in his bare feet, with his arm in plaster, until he was standing right in front of her. He didn’t touch her. He looked at her face, the way he looked at buildings, as if he was learning where everything went.

“Can I tell you what I’ve been thinking about?” he said. “For three weeks? Apart from being sorry?”

“No.”

“I’ve been thinking about my rule.”

“Which one? You’ve got a lot.”

“The one on your step. That if I came up your stairs, I wouldn’t leave until you threw me out. So I wasn’t coming up until you were sure you wouldn’t.” He was very close now. He lifted his good hand and put two fingers under her chin and tipped her face up. “Well. These are my stairs. And you came up them. On a pale green bike. With a bell.”

“That’s not the same.”

“It’s exactly the same,” said Raiden. “It’s better.” His thumb moved along her jaw. “So I’m asking. I’m not going to do anything until you say. I’m in plaster and three of my ribs are held together with hope, and I’m going to be absolutely useless, and I don’t care, I’ve wanted you since you stopped two metres from me and I’d have crawled to the Docks on my knees if I’d thought you’d open the door.” He took a breath. “Jia. Will you stay? Tonight. Please.”

She looked at him.

At the pink line through his eyebrow, his mouth, his good hand under her chin, not quite steady.

“Yes,” she said.

He made a sound she’d never heard a man make. Low and rough, as if something had come loose in him.

Then he kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a disaster.

It was the best disaster of her life. He kissed her against the glass wall with the whole harbour behind her, one-handed, and his plaster knocked on the glass like someone at a door, and she laughed into his mouth. She pulled his T-shirt over his head and he said ribs, ribs, ribs and she stopped, horrified, and he laughed so hard he had to sit down on the floor. And then she was on the floor with him, on the grey floor in the sun, and he was kissing her neck and her shoulders and the carp on her arm, all the way up, slowly, the whole length of it, as if he was reading it.

“I can’t do anything,” he said, against her collarbone. “I can’t do anything. I’ve got one hand. I’ve thought about this for six weeks and I’ve got one hand.”

“Then lie still.”

“I don’t want to lie still.”

“Raiden.”

“I’m begging,” he said. “Look. I’m on the floor. I’m begging again. You’ve made me beg twice in a month. Nobody’s ever—”

She put her hand over his mouth.

He looked up at her over it, from the floor, with his hair everywhere and his whole face shining.

She took her hand away and kissed him instead, and pushed him down onto his back on the grey floor, minding the ribs, and he let her, for about one breath, and then he didn’t, and pulled her down with his good arm, and after that neither of them was careful at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ended up in the bed eventually.

It was enormous, and white, and he’d never slept in the middle of it. She could tell. Only one side was creased. She lay in the middle of it in the evening, with the sheet round her waist and the light going gold on the glass wall and then pink and then blue, and him beside her on his good side with his plaster across her stomach, and his face in her neck.

Neither of them said anything for a while.

She could feel his heart against her arm. It was still going fast.

“I’ve got a new rule,” he said eventually, into her neck.

“No.”

“It’s a good one. You don’t ever have to leave. That’s the rule. You can, whenever you want. You don’t have to.”

She lay there.
