She thought about the two rooms above the garage, and the mattress on the floor, and the shower you had to hit. She thought about the black door. About her old jacket folded on the bench, and Zhao standing in her doorway, and the van with its wing caved in, and the sketchbook in the road.

She turned her face, and put her mouth against his hair.

“Idiot,” she said into his hair. It came out softer than she meant it to.

He laughed. She felt it all down her side.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when it was dark, he got up, and found his sketchbook, and a pencil, and sat on the edge of the bed by the lamp, and tried to draw her.

She lay where she was and let him.

She watched his face while he drew. He frowned and rubbed things out and started again, then turned the page and started again. He drew fast and then slowly and then not at all, and sat there with the pencil in his hand, looking at her, and then looking at the paper.

At last he tore out the page, and the two before it, and folded them up small and put them on the bedside table.

“I can’t do it,” he said.

He sounded astonished.

“I can draw anything,” said Raiden. “Anything. I can draw a building from the other side of the harbour and get the windows right. I drew your bike in a minute, in the dark, upside down. And I can’t get you.” He looked at her across the lamp. “I’ve tried for a month. I can’t get your face. I don’t know what it is.”

“Then don’t.”

“I have to,” he said. “One day. I’m going to get it right one day if it takes me my whole life.”

He put down the pencil, and lay back down beside her, and pulled her against him with his good arm.

In the morning the pale green bike was still by the door, with the board swung out, and he went down thirty-one floors in the goods lift in his bare feet with his plaster on to ride it round the car park, at twenty kilometres an hour, ringing the bell.

chapters.title: Her Father’s Chop Shop
chapters.desc: August 2021. A roof across the road from a shop under the flyover, where she learned engines before letters. She doesn’t go in. He draws the window with her father in it.
chapters.epigraph: “I could strip a carburettor before I could write my name. My father thought that was a good thing. So did I, for a while.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
The plaster came off in July.

He came to the garage the same afternoon with his arm thin and pale and strange-looking, like something that had been kept in a drawer, and held it out to her across the bench as if he were showing her a new bike.

“Look,” he said. “Two hands.”

She looked at it. She took it, and turned it over, and pressed her thumb along the inside of his wrist where the bone had broken, feeling for it the way she felt for a crack in a frame.

“Does it hurt?”

“Only when you’re not holding it,” said Raiden.

She dropped it.

He laughed, and picked her up off the floor with both arms, and his ribs must still have been sore because he said ow in her ear, and didn’t put her down.

✦ ✦ ✦

By August he knew everything about her workshop and almost nothing about her.

She noticed it one Sunday, lying on the floor of his flat on the thirty-first floor with her head on his stomach and his hand in her hair, while he told her about the borderland. Not the bad parts. The farm. The water tower he used to climb. The couple who ran it, who were called Uncle and Auntie and nothing else, and who fed him well and taught him to milk a goat and never once said his surname out loud. The kiln, where he’d learned that a brick arch holds up because every brick is pushing against the one beside it, and if you take one out, the whole thing falls down.

He talked and talked. He always did.

And he’d ask her things, sometimes, in between. Where she grew up. What her father did. And she’d say under the flyover, and bikes, and he’d wait, and she wouldn’t say anything else, and he’d go on talking about goats.

He never pushed. He asked once, and waited, and let it go.

“Ask me,” she said.

He stopped talking. His hand stopped in her hair.

“Ask me what?”

“The thing you want to ask. About the shop. You keep not asking.”

He was quiet for a moment.

“I don’t want you to tell me because I asked,” he said. “I want you to tell me because you want to.”

She lay on his stomach and looked at the ceiling.

“I’ll show you,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him on the black bike.

He’d never been on the back of a motorbike. She found that out in the car park of the Meridian, when she gave him the spare helmet and he put it on backwards. She turned it round. She did up the strap under his chin. She showed him where to put his feet, and told him to hold on to her and not the bike, and to lean when she leaned and not to fight it, and if he did anything stupid she’d stop and leave him on the expressway.

“Can I hold on tight?” he said, through the visor.

“Yes.”

“How tight?”

“Raiden.”

He held on tight.

She took the expressway north, across the Symmetrical Ward and over the river and past the Iron Docks, and at the first long straight she opened it, just once, just to feel him. The black bike went from a hundred to a hundred and sixty like something let off a chain, and his arms locked round her waist and his whole body pressed against her back, and over the wind she heard him, inside his helmet, laughing. He wasn’t frightened at all. He laughed like a boy the whole way down the straight.

She slowed down, though she didn’t want to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Slums of the Industry weren’t called that on any map.

On the map they were an industrial zone, the old one, built in the sixties and seventies and then left behind when the factories moved north. A grid of grey streets under the flyovers where the expressways crossed, three of them, one on top of the other, so that the streets underneath never saw the sun. Workshops, scrapyards, small factories that made small things, and rooms above them where people lived who had nowhere better. And under the lowest flyover, at the end of a lane where the concrete pillars went down into the ground like the legs of something enormous, her father’s shop.

She didn’t take him down the lane.

She stopped two streets away, outside a noodle factory that had closed when she was fifteen, and took him round the back, and up a fire escape that she’d climbed a thousand times. Six flights of rusty iron steps, to a flat roof covered in pigeon droppings and broken tiles and an old water tank, right on the level of the lowest flyover, with the traffic going over their heads so close that you could feel it in your teeth.

From the edge of the roof you could see straight down the lane to the shop.

✦ ✦ ✦

It hadn’t changed.

A long low building of grey block, with a corrugated roof and three roll-up doors, all of them up. The sign over the middle one, hand-painted, older than her: CAO MOTOR REPAIR. Bikes on the pavement outside. Bikes inside. Bikes in pieces in the yard at the side, in heaps, stripped, their frames grinding off under a man with an angle grinder, the sparks going up orange in the shadow under the road.

“It’s a chop shop,” she said.

“I know.”

“Do you? Do you know what that means?”

“Stolen bikes come in,” said Raiden. “Parts go out. The frames get cut up, so nobody can trace the numbers. The engines get new numbers. Some of the bikes go out whole, with new papers, to buyers who don’t ask.” He was standing beside her at the edge of the roof, with his hands in his pockets. “My father’s people used to buy from places like this. Not this one. Places like it.”

“They bought from this one,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him.

Not all of it. She sat on the edge of the roof with her boots over the drop and the traffic going over their heads and told him the parts she could.

That her mother had left when she was four. Gone south, with a man who sold refrigerators. She didn’t remember her face. She remembered a red dress, and the sound of the door.

That her father had brought her up in the shop because there was nowhere else to put her. That she’d slept in the office on a camp bed, and played on the floor among the parts, and the first thing she’d ever taken to pieces was a carburettor, when she was five, and she’d put it back together, and it had worked, and her father had laughed and shown everyone.

That she couldn’t read until she was nine. Nobody had thought to teach her. She’d taught herself, in the end, from the workshop manuals, the big greasy books with the diagrams, so that the first words she’d ever read were torque, and clearance, and do not overtighten.

That by twelve she could strip and rebuild any engine that came through the door, faster than any of the men. And that every bike she touched got out of the shop clean and was never traced, and the police never once caught one, and the men had started calling her Jinx, because she was bad luck for the police, and it had stuck.

“I was proud of it,” she said. “Bad luck for the police. I thought it was the best thing anyone had ever called me.”

“How old were you?”

“Twelve.”

He didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

“And then?” he said, after a while.

She looked down the lane at the shop.

“And then something happened, when I was seventeen,” she said. “I’m not telling you that one.”

“All right.”

“I mean it. Not today.”

“I said all right,” said Raiden. “I meant it. Whenever you want. Or never.” He sat down on the edge of the roof beside her, carefully, because he wasn’t used to heights without walls. “Is he there? Your father?”

She looked.

There was a window in the side of the shop, a small square window with wire in the glass, where the office was. Where her camp bed had been. There was a light on in it, a desk lamp, yellow. And a man at the desk, bent over something, grey-haired and big in the shoulders, in a vest. He was writing in a book, slowly, the way he always had, as if every number cost him money.

“That’s him,” she said.

“When did you last talk to him?”

“November 2018. The night I left.”

“Do you want to go down?”

She didn’t answer.

She sat on the edge of the roof and watched her father write in his book under the yellow lamp, and the man with the angle grinder in the yard put it down and lit a cigarette, and a truck went over the flyover above them with a sound like the end of the world.

“No,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drew it.

He didn’t ask. He took the sketchbook out of his jacket and drew it, sitting beside her on the edge of the roof, fast, in the grey light under the road. The lane. The pillars going down into the ground. The shop with its three doors, and the sign, and the bikes on the pavement. The sparks from the grinder going up. And the little square window with the wire in it, and the lamp, and the man at the desk, small and bent, writing in his book.

It took him twenty minutes. She watched him the whole time.

When he’d finished, he tore it out and held it out to her.

“No,” she said.

“All right.” He didn’t put it away. He held it a bit longer, then folded it in half, carefully, and put it inside his jacket, against his chest. “I’ll keep it. In case you ever want it.”

“I won’t.”

“Then I’ll keep it anyway,” said Raiden. “It’s the best thing I’ve done all summer. It’s got your father in it, and you can see from here he doesn’t know what he lost.”

She turned her head and looked at him.

He was looking at the shop. His face was still and serious. She thought he was angry. She’d never seen him angry.

“He let you sleep in an office in a chop shop,” he said. “He never even taught you to read. He let a lot of men call you a name for being useful to them, and he was proud of you for it.” He stopped. “And something happened when you were seventeen, and I can see from here he didn’t stop it. Sorry. I said whenever you want. I’m not asking. I just—I can see it from here.”

She didn’t say anything.

She put her hand out, on the dirty roof between them, among the pigeon droppings, palm up.

He put his hand in it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed until it got dark.

The lights came on under the flyover, the orange ones on the pillars, and the man with the grinder pulled down the yard door, and her father turned off the lamp in the office and came out and pulled down the three roll-up doors, one after another, the way he did every night, with the same three crashes. Then he walked away down the lane under the road, slowly, a big grey man with his hands in his pockets, and didn’t look up.

She watched him go.

Raiden got up and knelt behind her on the roof and put both arms round her, and held on. He put his chin on her shoulder. She felt him breathing, slow and even, against her back.

She leaned back into him.

“I’m never going to be owned again,” she said, under her breath. “By him or his buyers. Or anyone.”

“I know.”

“That means you too.”

“I know,” said Raiden, against her ear. “I don’t want to own you. I want you to let me stay. That’s the opposite.”

She sat there in his arms on the roof of the noodle factory in the dark, with the traffic going over, until her legs went numb.

Then she turned round in his arms, on her knees, and kissed him, hard, with her hands in his hair, the way she’d kissed him under the bike, and he made a surprised sound and kissed her back, and they nearly went off the edge of the roof, and he swore, for the first time she’d ever heard, and she laughed so hard she had to hold on to the water tank.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the way home he held on round her waist without talking, and she stayed in the slow lane all the way.

At the black door she found out he’d been drawing again, the whole ride, in his head. He went straight upstairs to her two rooms, and sat at her kitchen table under the bare bulb, and drew the shop again from memory, the lane, the pillars, the roof they’d sat on, and then the next street, and the next: every street under the flyover they’d ridden through, every corner and alley and fire escape.

“What are you doing?” she said, from the bed.

“Making a map,” said Raiden, without looking up. “Of every way out.”

“Why?”

He looked up then.

“Because I’m a Lin,” he said, “and I make places safe, and that’s the most dangerous place I’ve ever seen you look at. And because one day you might want to go down that lane. And if you do, I want to know every way you could come back.”

He went on drawing until two in the morning.

She fell asleep watching him, with the light on.

chapters.title: He Asks Her to Marry Him on a Napkin Drawing
chapters.desc: September 2021. Mrs. Tong’s noodle shop, a paper napkin, a plan of their whole life drawn to scale. She says not yet. He says he’ll ask every month until she doesn’t.
chapters.epigraph: “One to fifty. The scale’s at the bottom. I wanted you to see I’d measured.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
By September he lived in two places and she lived in two places, and they’d stopped pretending otherwise.

Some nights they slept on the thirty-first floor in the enormous white bed, and she woke up to the whole harbour going gold and him already up, at the drawing table by the window in his shorts with a pencil behind his ear, drawing something for the firm in the south and humming. Some nights they slept above the garage, on her mattress on the floor, with the window open and the cranes going and the shower you had to hit, and he woke up with his feet hanging off the end and said it was the best night’s sleep he’d ever had in his life, every time, and seemed to mean it.

He’d won a prize in August. A library he’d drawn for the firm, in a town in the south, with a roof like an open book. There’d been a dinner, and a speech, and a glass thing with his name on it. He’d brought the glass thing to the garage and put it on the shelf over the bench between a tin of washers and a jar of brake fluid, and when she asked why, he said that was where the important things went.

He’d got the pale green bike out every day. He rode it everywhere at twenty kilometres an hour with the lights on in broad daylight and the bell going, and drew from the pavement, and stopped people in the street to tell them his girlfriend had built it. The man on the desk at the Meridian had started calling it the tram.

And every morning at ten there were three coffees.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You should get a car,” she said, one evening, at Mrs. Tong’s.

It was a Friday in the middle of September, still hot. The noodle shop was full of men off the container ships, big men in vests and work boots who ate fast and didn’t talk, and Mrs. Tong was behind the counter shouting at the kitchen, and they had the table in the corner by the fridge where she always sat, because it was the only one with its back to the wall.

Raiden looked up from his noodles.

“I don’t drive.”

“You should learn. You can afford a driver. You can afford a hundred drivers. You take taxis everywhere and you ride that thing on the pavement and you nearly got killed by a van.”

“I nearly got killed by a man on his phone,” said Raiden. “A car wouldn’t have helped. And anyway.” He pointed his chopsticks at her. “You said cars were for cowards.”

“Cars are bikes for cowards.”

“Exactly. So I can’t have one. I’d lose all your respect.”

She snorted and ate her noodles. She left the greens on the side. He reached over without looking and took them, the way he always did now, and ate them himself.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was drawing on the napkin.

He’d been doing it since the food came. He did it everywhere. Napkins, receipts, the backs of menus, the margins of her invoices, which drove her mad. He drew while he ate, and while he talked, and while he listened, and most of the time she didn’t look, because it was just what his hands did, like hers turning a bolt over and over in her pocket.

But tonight he was taking care over it, with the pencil and a little ruler he kept in his jacket and never used for napkins. Every so often he looked up at her, and then back down. She noticed he hadn’t said a word in nearly ten minutes, the longest she’d known him go in a noodle shop.

“What are you drawing?”

“Nearly finished,” said Raiden.

He drew one more line. He looked at it. He wrote something small at the bottom. Then he put the pencil down on the table, and turned the napkin round, and slid it across the table to her, past the chilli oil and the soy sauce and the little dish of her greens that he hadn’t finished.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the garage.

Not as it was. As it could be. A plan, from above, the way an architect draws a building, with the walls as thick black lines and the doors as little arcs. Her workshop, downstairs, with the benches and the lathe and the bikes, all in the right places. And the stairs. And upstairs, where her two rooms were, not two rooms any more but one big long one, with windows down the whole side looking out over the street, and a kitchen at one end with a long table, and a bed at the other end, a big one, and a bathroom with a bath, a real bath, drawn in with its taps. A drafting table by the window. A bench by the other window, with a vice on it. A sofa. A shelf over the bench, and on it, tiny, the glass prize and the tin of washers and the jar of brake fluid.

And in the middle of the long room, in the kitchen, at the table, two little circles, side by side. And beside them, in his small neat capitals: J. R.

At the bottom, in the corner, there was a scale bar. 1:50.

And under that, so small she had to bring it close to her face:

Will you marry me?

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat still.

The noodle shop went on around them. Mrs. Tong shouted. A man at the next table scraped his bowl. The fridge beside her hummed and shuddered the way it always did. And she sat there with a paper napkin in her hands that had their whole life drawn on it to scale, and for a second she couldn’t breathe. Then her heart went off too fast, worse than in any race.

She looked up.

He was watching her across the table. He wasn’t smiling. He was pale. His hands were flat on the table on either side of his bowl, as if he was holding it down.

“I measured,” he said. “Everything. I went round with a tape when you were at the dyno shop in the north last week. The walls are right. I checked the beams. You can take out the wall between your two rooms, the one with the crack, it’s not holding anything up, it’s only partition, somebody put it in in the eighties. The bath’ll fit if we move the water tank to the roof. I’ve drawn the tank on the roof. It’s on the other side.” He turned the napkin over for her. It was. “I wanted you to see I’d measured. I didn’t want you to think it was just a drawing. It’s a plan. It’s a real one. It’ll stand up.”

She didn’t say anything.

“It’s four months,” he said. “I know. I know it’s four months. I don’t care. I’ve known since the shipyard road. You grabbed my shirt and I looked at you and thought, oh, it’s her, that’s who it is. I’m not going to know it any better in a year. I’ll just know it longer.” He took a breath. “Jia. I love you. Marry me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The man at the next table had stopped eating.

Mrs. Tong had stopped shouting. Jinx could feel it. The whole noodle shop had gone quiet behind her, everyone in it pretending not to listen.

She looked at the napkin.

She looked at the two little circles at the table. J. R. The bath. The tank on the roof. The glass prize on the shelf between the washers and the brake fluid, where the important things went.

She wanted to say yes so much that her hands shook.

And she thought of her father’s hands, flat on the desk, the day the black car came down the lane, and the men at the shop standing up when it stopped outside. Lin, from the Walled City, don’t ever go there. She thought of what it would mean to marry the only son of the man in the dark coat. Not Raiden. Him. The Walled City, the family, the thing she’d got out from under with a van and a lathe and nothing else.

“Not yet,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t move.

She saw it land. She wanted to take it back, and didn’t.

“Not no,” she said. “Not yet.”

“All right,” said Raiden. His voice had gone quiet. “Can I ask why? You don’t have to say.”

“Because I’d be marrying your father too.”

“You wouldn’t. You’d be marrying me.”

“You’re his son. Everyone knows. You said it. Everyone he loves is something someone can take.” She put the napkin down on the table between them, flat, the right way up. “I marry you, I’m his. In the Docks. In my father’s shop. Lin Jian’s daughter-in-law. I’d say yes tomorrow if it was just you. It isn’t.”

He didn’t say anything.

Then he looked down at the napkin.

“Ask me,” she said. Her voice wasn’t working properly. “Ask me when I can say yes without walking into your father’s house.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She thought he’d be angry. Or hurt. Or that he’d do the silly face, the one from the gallery, and make a joke, and go away inside himself where she couldn’t follow.

He didn’t.

He picked up the napkin. He folded it in half, and then in half again, neatly, along the scale bar, so it didn’t crease the bath. He took out his wallet, a soft old brown leather one with the corners worn, and opened it, and put the napkin inside, behind his cards, in the place where other people kept photographs. He put the wallet back in his jacket, against his chest, where he’d put the drawing of her father’s shop.

Then he looked up at her.

“I’ll ask every month,” he said.

She stared at him.

“On a napkin,” said Raiden. “Every month. A new one. A new plan. I’ll draw you every house in the city, if I have to. Every flat. Every garage. Every barn. A lighthouse, if you want one. A boat. I’ll draw them all to scale and I’ll put the scale bar on and I’ll ask you at the bottom of every single one. And one day you’ll say yes, and I’ll have a wallet full of napkins, and I’ll show them all to you at the wedding.” He picked up his chopsticks again. “Eat your noodles. They’re getting cold.”

She didn’t eat her noodles.

She got up. She came round the table, past the fridge, in front of every man off the container ships in the noodle shop and Mrs. Tong behind the counter, and took his face in both her hands and kissed him hard, in front of all of them, with his chopsticks still in his hand.

When she let him go, he was red to the ears.

“That’s a no,” he said, a bit breathless. “Officially. For tonight. I just want to be clear. That was a no.”

“It was a not yet,” she said, and sat back down and ate her noodles.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Tong came over with a plate of extra beef and put it down between them without a word, hard, and went away again.

The men off the container ships went back to their bowls.

And under the table, all through the rest of dinner, his foot stayed against hers, pressed there, the whole length of it, as if he was making sure she didn’t go anywhere. She didn’t want to. She sat in the corner with her back to the wall and her foot against his and thought about the napkin folded in his wallet, behind his cards.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the seventeenth of October, at Mrs. Tong’s, at the same table, he drew a lighthouse.

It was on a rock, in a sea, with a workshop in the bottom for her bikes and a bedroom at the top under the lamp, and the stairs went round and round inside it, every step drawn in, and at the bottom, beside the scale bar, 1:100, it said: Will you marry me? (The view is good.)

“Not yet,” she said.

“I’ll take that,” said Raiden, and folded it up, and put it in his wallet behind the first one.

That was number two.

chapters.title: The Trophy Husband Has Dinner Ready
chapters.desc: Autumn 2021. He moves into two rooms above a garage and cooks every night. She comes up the stairs to soup and a clean floor. Then flour, the kitchen counter, and an argument they don’t finish.
chapters.epigraph: “Somebody has to cook. You’d put soup in a gearbox if I let you.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
He moved in on a Wednesday at the end of October with two suitcases, a drawing table in four pieces, and a wok.

She came up the stairs at nine that night, after a clutch job that had gone wrong three times, with oil to her elbows and a burn on her thumb and her shoulders up round her ears, and stopped in the doorway.

The room smelled of ginger.

He’d swept the floor. He’d washed the window, the one that didn’t close, so that the lights from the street came in clean for the first time in three years. He’d put his drawing table up in the corner by it, and his lamp, and his pencils in a jar. He’d found a tablecloth from somewhere, a blue one, and put it on the little table under the bare bulb, and two bowls, and spoons, and a pot in the middle with steam coming off it.

He was standing at the hot plate in an apron that said TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS on it, which he must have found in the box of old things under the stairs, stirring something.

“Sit down,” he said, without turning round. “Don’t touch anything. Wash your hands first. Twice. With the orange soap, not the other one, the other one smells of petrol.”

She stood in the doorway.

“What is that?”

“Fish soup. With ginger. And tofu. And the greens you don’t eat, so I can eat them.” He turned round, finally, with the spoon in his hand. “You’ve burned your thumb.”

“It’s nothing.”

“Let me see.”

She held it out. He looked at it, and put the spoon down, and took her wrist and held her hand under the cold tap at the sink for a full minute, not letting go, while she stood there dripping oil on his clean floor and didn’t argue.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was good soup.

She ate two bowls. She didn’t say anything. He didn’t either, much. He sat across the little table from her under the bare bulb with his chin on his hand and watched her eat, the way he watched her work.

“Who taught you to cook?” she said, on the second bowl.

“Auntie. At the farm. She said a boy who can’t feed himself is a boy who’ll marry the first girl who feeds him.” He smiled. “Then my father’s cook, in the Walled City, when I came home. She was called Ah Sim and she was the most frightening woman I’ve ever met and she thought I was too thin. So I used to sit in the kitchen. Nobody else ever went in there. I used to sit on the step by the door and draw her, and she used to make me chop things.” He looked at her bowl. “Good?”

“It’s all right.”

“You’ve had two bowls.”

“I was hungry.”

“You’ve been hungry for three years,” said Raiden. “I can tell. You’ve got one pan and a hot plate and a cupboard full of beans. You eat at Mrs. Tong’s or you don’t eat.” He reached across the table and took the greens out of her bowl, which she’d pushed to the side. “That’s finished now. I’m here. Somebody has to cook. You’d put soup in a gearbox if I let you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It became the shape of every day.

She worked. He worked. In the mornings he drew at the table by the window for the firm in the south, and in the afternoons he went out on the pale green bike and drew the city, and in the evenings, at six, he came back with bags of shopping hanging off the handlebars and went upstairs.

And at nine, or ten, or once at half past midnight, she came up the stairs.

Every night there was something. Soup. Rice. Noodles he’d made himself, with his hands, on the little table, rolled out with a wine bottle because they didn’t have a rolling pin. A whole fish, steamed, with ginger and spring onions, that he took the bones out of for her with his chopsticks without saying anything. Dumplings. Fried eggs with tomato, the way Ah Sim had made them for him when he was ten. Once, when she’d had a bad day, a cake, a lopsided one, with JINX on top in chocolate in his architect’s capitals.

And the room was clean every night: her overalls washed and folded, her boots by the door with the laces undone, the bed made, the window open or shut depending on the weather, a towel on the hook by the shower that was warm because he’d hung it over the hot plate.

She’d never come home to anything in her life.

She came home, every night, up the stairs with her shoulders round her ears, and opened the door, and the room smelled of ginger, and he looked up from the hot plate and said wash your hands, the orange soap, and her shoulders came down.

She could feel it happen, like letting off a clamp.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell him that.

She told Mrs. Tong, by accident, at lunch, in the second week of November, when Mrs. Tong asked why she hadn’t been in for dinner in three weeks.

“He cooks,” said Jinx.

Mrs. Tong looked at her over the counter.

“Every night?”

“Yes.”

“And cleans?”

“Washes my overalls.”

Mrs. Tong put down her ladle.

“In thirty-one years,” she said, “my husband washed one bowl. Once. In 1997. I remember the day.” She shook her head. “Marry him. Marry him tomorrow. If you won’t, I will.”

“He’s asked.”

“And?”

“Not yet,” said Jinx.

Mrs. Tong said something in a dialect from the coast that Jinx didn’t understand and that the men off the container ships at the counter clearly did, because they all laughed, and one of them choked on his tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third Wednesday in November he made dumplings.

He’d bought the flour that afternoon, a whole bag, and the pork, and the cabbage, and the little round wrappers he said were cheating, so he wasn’t using them, he was making his own. He had the little table covered in flour. He had flour on the floor. He had flour on his face, a long white streak down one cheek where he’d pushed his hair back, and on his apron, and up his arms to the elbows.

She came up the stairs at ten past nine. She’d been under a bike for four hours. She was black from her hair to her boots.

“Don’t touch anything,” he said.

She stopped in the doorway.

He was standing at the table with a dumpling in one hand and a spoon in the other, and she looked at him, with the flour on his face and his sleeves rolled up and the bare bulb over his head, and something in her chest went loose all at once, the way a stuck bolt does when you finally get the heat in.

She walked across the room. She didn’t wash her hands.

“Jia,” he said, warning. “Jia. Your hands. I’ve got forty dumplings here. They’re perfect. They’re the best dumplings anyone’s ever made. Ah Sim would weep. Don’t you dare—”

She put both hands on his face.

Two big black handprints, on his cheeks, over the flour.

He stood there with a dumpling in his hand and looked at her.

“You did that on purpose,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I’m going to have oil in my eyebrows for a week.”

“Yes,” she said.

He looked at her one second more, with her handprints on his face, and then he kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He dropped the dumpling.

He put the spoon down, somewhere, she heard it hit the table, and put his floury hands on her waist and pulled her in, and kissed her like he’d been waiting all day, which he told her afterwards he had, since about two o’clock, when he’d seen her through the floor of the room, through the gap by the pipe, lying under the bike with only her boots sticking out, and had had to go out and buy flour to calm down.

“You can’t see through the floor,” she said, against his mouth.

“There’s a gap by the pipe. I measured. I’m going to fill it in tomorrow.” He backed her into the counter by the sink, the narrow wooden one with the cracked edge, and lifted her up onto it, in one go, both hands under her thighs, and she put her arms round his neck and her boots round the backs of his legs. “Or maybe not. Maybe I’ll leave it.”

“Your dumplings,” she said. “You’ll ruin them.”

“They’ll be fine.”

“They’ll go soggy. You said. You said if you leave them out they go soggy and stick. You said it on Monday.”

“Jia,” said Raiden, with his mouth on her neck, “are we arguing about dumplings?”

“You started it.”

“I didn’t. I was very calm. I was making dumplings. You came in and put your hands on my face.” His hands were in her overalls, at the waist, where she’d tied the sleeves. He was undoing the knot. “I want to be clear. I’m going to stop if you tell me. Right now. And go back to my dumplings, and you can go and wash your hands with the orange soap, and we’ll have dinner like civilised people.” He lifted his head and looked at her, close, with her black handprints on his face and flour in his eyebrows. “Do you want me to stop?”

She looked at him.

“Don’t stop,” she said. “Your dumplings are going soggy.”

He laughed into her neck, helplessly, and didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

They argued about the dumplings the whole time.

Not all the time; in the gaps. When he had his mouth on her shoulder and said they’ll be fine, I promise you they’ll be fine, and she said they’re sticking, I can hear them sticking, and he said you cannot hear a dumpling stick, and she said I can hear a valve stick from across a workshop, I can hear your dumplings, and he laughed so hard he had to put his forehead on her chest. When the flour got everywhere. When her elbow went into the bag of flour on the counter and a white cloud went up round both of them, and they stopped, and looked at each other through it, coughing, white and black and ridiculous, and she started laughing and couldn’t stop, and he kissed her through it, and through it, until she did.

The bare bulb swung on its wire. The window that didn’t close let in the sound of the Docks, a horn, a truck. Somewhere on the floor, the dumplings went soggy, all forty of them, and stuck to the table, and nobody cared.

Afterwards she sat on the counter wrapped in his apron, the one that said TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS, with her hair full of flour, and he stood between her knees with his forehead on her shoulder, breathing.

“They’re soggy,” she said.

“I know,” he said into her shoulder. “You were right. You’re always right. It’s unbearable.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They had dumplings at eleven o’clock, the ones that could be saved. They were lumpy and torn and stuck together in pairs, and they were the best thing she’d ever eaten in her life, and she ate seven, and gave him the rest.

He drew her afterwards, in bed, with flour still in her hair. Her shoulder. Her hand on the sheet. The edge of her jaw.

Not her face. He tried. He got as far as her mouth and stopped and turned the page.

And at two in the morning she woke, cold, because the window that didn’t close had let the whole November night in, and found him already up, in his shorts, with a roll of tape, taping cardboard over the gap at the top of the frame. He was shivering. The room was freezing. The hot plate was on, for warmth, glowing red in the dark.

She lay on the mattress and watched him tape the cardboard. Then go and put a hand on the wall, the outside wall, where the damp came through in a long dark stain behind the bed. Then look up at the ceiling, where the plaster was cracked. Then look at the shower, the one you had to hit.

He didn’t know she was awake. He stood in the middle of her two rooms, in the cold, in his shorts, with the tape in his hand, and looked at all of it, slowly, every bit, the way he’d looked at the gallery with his fingers on the walls.

There was nothing silly in his face.

“No,” she heard him say, under his breath. “No. That’s not good enough for her.”

She shut her eyes before he turned round.

She found out in December what he meant.

chapters.title: The Roof That Will Never Fall
chapters.desc: Winter 2021 to spring 2022. A letter says her building has been sold. It has: to her. Then he shows her what the new walls are really made of, and what’s behind the tool wall, and the dyno.
chapters.epigraph: “Every wall in here is lying. Every one. They all look like plaster. I promise you none of them will ever fall on your head.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
The letter came on the second Monday in December.

It was from the lawyers for the Tai Hing Rope & Canvas Company, which had stopped making rope in 1994 and existed now only as three elderly cousins in three different countries who owned the building and argued about it by email. She’d rented from them for three years. She paid on the first of every month, in cash, to a man who came on a scooter.

Dear Tenant, the letter said. We write to inform you that the property at the above address has been sold. The new owner’s representatives will be in contact regarding your tenancy.

She read it standing by the black door with grease on her hands.

Then she read it again.

She went cold all over, the way she had on the Docks road when she saw the ambulance lights. She thought about the lathe, which weighed a tonne and a half and had taken four men and a crane to get in. About the benches. The bikes on their chains. Her customers, who came because they knew where the black door was. About finding somewhere else near the Docks, where Zhao’s name kept the crews off, at a rent she could pay, with a ceiling high enough, in a city where nothing was ever for rent and everything was for sale.

She went upstairs. He was at his drawing table by the window.

“They’ve sold the building,” she said.

He looked up.

He looked at the letter in her hand, then at her face, and she saw it before he said anything. She’d got good at that. There was something under the smile, like a valve sticking under a clean idle.

“Raiden.”

“Yes,” he said. “I know.”

“How do you know?”

He put his pencil down.

“Because it was me,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t throw a spanner.

She stood in the middle of the room with the letter in her hand and couldn’t think of anything to say at all, and in the end what came out was, “You bought my building.”

“No,” said Raiden.

He got up. He went to his suitcase, the one under the bed that he hadn’t fully unpacked, and took out a brown envelope, a thick one, and came and held it out to her.

“I bought your building,” he said. “Yours. Not mine. It’s in your name. Only yours. Cao Jia. I had to give them your name for the papers. I’m sorry, I know I said I’d only use it when it was important. This was important.” He held the envelope out a bit further, because she wasn’t taking it. “There’s nothing of mine on it. Not my name, not my father’s, not anything Lin anywhere. You own it. The whole thing. The ground and the walls and the roof. And next door. The old sailmaker’s. I bought that too. It’s in your name as well.”

She took the envelope.

She opened it. It was a deed. Two deeds. In a lawyer’s language she couldn’t read very well, with stamps on them, and her name, in black type, on the line that said Owner. Twice.

Cao Jia.

“Why?” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Because you said you’d never be owned,” said Raiden.

He was standing still in front of her, with his hands at his sides.

“You said it on the roof. And at Mrs. Tong’s. I’ve thought about it every night since.” He took a breath. “I can’t fix your father. Or your mother. I can’t make the Walled City not be the Walled City, or me not be his son. But nobody can put you out of your own door now. Not a landlord, not a crew, not my father. Not me. If we ever—if one day you want me gone, you put my suitcases on the step and I’ve got no right to argue.” He stopped. “That’s the point. It’s yours.”

She looked at the deed.

“And,” said Raiden, slightly differently, “your window doesn’t close, and the wall behind the bed is wet, and the shower only works if you hit it, and you had a cold for a week in November, and I had to watch. So I’m also going to rebuild the top two floors. If you’ll let me. It’s your building. You can say no.”

She looked up at him.

“You’ve already drawn it,” she said.

“I drew it in September. On a napkin.”

“That was a proposal.”

“It was both,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went downstairs.

She walked through the workshop and out of the black door and across the street to her van, parked by the anchor woman’s. She got in and shut the door. She turned the radio up loud, the station that only played old songs, and sat there with her hands on the wheel and the deed on the seat beside her.

He didn’t follow her.

He stood in the black doorway with his hands in his pockets, and waited, and after a while the anchor woman came out of her shop and stood beside him and looked at the van too.

“What did you do?” said the anchor woman.

“I bought her the building.”

The anchor woman looked at the van. The radio was loud. You could hear it all down the street. Something from the seventies, a woman singing about a boat.

“She’ll be in there twenty minutes,” said the anchor woman. “She did it when her best customer died. Twenty minutes, with the radio.” She went back into her shop. “Don’t knock on the window.”

He didn’t knock on the window.

It was a bit over twenty. Then the radio went off, and she got out, with her face white and dry, and walked back across the street with the deed in her hand, and stopped in front of him on the step.

“Fine,” she said. “Rebuild it.”

He held out his arms. She walked into them, and stayed there, on the step, with her face in his shoulder, in front of the anchor woman’s window.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took three months.

She slept at the Meridian while they did it, in the enormous white bed, and went down to the garage every morning at seven on the black bike and worked downstairs while the builders worked upstairs, with the whole building shaking and dust coming down through the floor onto her benches, and she didn’t complain once, because every time she looked up, there was something new.

He was there every day in a hard hat with his drawings. He didn’t play the fool with the builders. He talked to them in short plain sentences, and they listened, and when the foreman said something couldn’t be done he took the foreman to the wall and showed him how it could, and the foreman went red and did it. They called him Mr. Lin. Not young master, the way the men at the gallery had. Mr. Lin.

He wouldn’t let her go up.

“Not till it’s finished,” he said, every evening, at the bottom of the stairs, which were now behind a plastic sheet. “I want you to see it all at once. Like the bike. You didn’t show me the bike in bits.”

“I didn’t show you the bike at all.”

“Exactly,” said Raiden. “So you know how it feels.”

At Mrs. Tong’s in January he drew a workshop inside an old ship, with the engines still in it, and asked her at the bottom. Not yet. In February, a house in a tree. Not yet. In March, a tiny flat on the top of a crane, with a garage for one bike in the cab. Not yet. That one made her laugh out loud, and Mrs. Tong brought extra beef.

Number seven. He folded it into his wallet behind the others.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Saturday in April he took the plastic sheet down.

He took her hand at the bottom of the stairs. The stairs were new, oak, wide, with a steel rail. He walked her up them slowly, one at a time, and at the top he opened the door, and stood back, and let her go in first.

She stopped.

It was the napkin.

All of it. The long room, the whole length of the building, where her two rooms had been, with the crack and the damp and the bare bulb. Windows down the street side, tall, five of them, in steel frames, that opened and closed and let the light in from morning to night. A floor of wide pale boards. A kitchen at one end, a proper one, with a long table, oak, with eight chairs. Lamps that hung down over it from the beams. A bed at the far end, under the windows, big and low. A drafting table by the first window, his, with his lamp. A bench by the second window, hers, with a vice bolted to it, and her own lamp, and a rack of small tools she hadn’t had to ask for. A sofa, long and soft and dark green. A shelf over the bench, and on it, the glass prize and the tin of washers and the jar of brake fluid.

And at the other end, through a door, a bathroom: white tiles, a shower with a head as big as a plate, and a bath, a real one, deep and long.

She stood in the middle of it all.

He’d even filled the gap by the pipe.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Now,” said Raiden.

He was standing behind her in the doorway. His voice had gone quiet and serious, the way it had on the back stairs of the gallery.

“Now I’m going to show you what it’s really made of,” he said. “And you can tell me if it’s too much.”

He walked her round it. Wall by wall.

The outside walls, the brick ones, had been lined. Behind the new plaster there was steel mesh, set in concrete, all the way round, so that if anyone ever drove a truck into the building, or worse, the outside would come down and the inside wouldn’t. The five tall windows were laminated glass, three layers, that would crack and hold and not fall in. The front door at the top of the stairs looked like oak, and was oak, on the outside. Inside it was steel.

“You’d need a lot of time and a lot of noise to get through that,” he said. “And you’d have woken up the whole street. The anchor woman would come out with an anchor.”

He showed her the roof. The new stair to the roof, behind a narrow door in the bathroom that looked like a cupboard, that went up past the water tank to a hatch, and out onto the flat roof, and across to the roof of the sailmaker’s next door, and down an iron ladder bolted to its back wall into the lane behind, where nobody went. Another way out, one nobody else knew.

And then he took her downstairs, into the workshop, to the tool wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her tool wall.

The spanners on their hooks, smallest to biggest. The sockets. The screwdrivers. The thirteen in its place between the twelve and the fourteen. She’d hung every one of them herself, three years ago, on a board screwed to the back wall.

He reached up, behind the biggest spanner, the one as long as her forearm, and pressed something she couldn’t see.

The whole wall moved.

It swung out on hinges she’d never known were there, without a sound, with every tool still hanging on it in its place. Behind it, where the old back wall had been, there was a grey steel door with a handle and a keypad.

“I built it in February,” said Raiden. “When you were at the dyno shop. I’m sorry. It’s the only thing I’ve done without asking. Because if you knew it was here, and someone ever made you tell them, you’d be able to say you didn’t.”

He typed four numbers. The steel door opened.

It was a small concrete room, with a light that came on by itself, and a vent in the ceiling that hummed, and a bench with a mattress on it, and shelves with water and food and a first-aid box and a radio and a torch. A phone on the wall. Nothing else.

“Nobody gets in,” he said. “Not with anything they could carry. The walls are thicker than the ones upstairs. It has its own air. It has a line out that doesn’t go through anyone’s exchange. You could sit in there for three days.” He looked at it, not at her. “I hope you never go in it. Not once. I built it so that I’d never have to think about you, at two in the morning, the way I did at the hospital. Not knowing.”

She didn’t say anything.

“What’s the code?” she said.

He looked at her.

“Your birthday,” he said. “Fourteen, oh-two. I’m sorry. I know you hate it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood in front of the open steel door.

Then she said, “Show me the rest.”

“What rest?”

“You said and you can tell me if it’s too much. That’s not all of it. There’s something else. You’ve got that look.”

He looked at her. Then he laughed, a short helpless laugh.

“How do you always know?”

“I can hear it,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her next door.

Through a new door in the side wall of the workshop, into the sailmaker’s, which had been empty for ten years and full of pigeons. There were no pigeons now. It was clean, and white, and lit, and empty except for one thing in the middle of the floor, under a cover.

He pulled the cover off.

It was a dyno.

A rolling road. New. A big steel drum set into the floor in a pit, with straps and frames to hold a bike down, and a fan as tall as she was to cool it, and a long desk along the wall with screens on it and a computer and a sensor on a lead for the exhaust. The kind they had at the shop in the north, where she paid by the hour and booked three weeks ahead, only newer.

“You said they cost a fortune,” said Raiden. “In May. Over the gearbox. I wrote it down.”

She stood there.

“It is too much,” she said.

“Yes,” said Raiden. “I know. I’m sorry. I’m a Lin, and I’m rich, and I like you, and that’s what happens. I’m going to keep doing it. You’ll have to get used to it.”

She turned round.

She walked back across the empty white room, past the dyno, and took his face in her hands, the way she had with the flour, except her hands were clean. And she looked at him, so long that he started to look worried.

“Thank you,” she said.

He went still.

She’d never said it to him, not for the coffee or the soup or anything else. She didn’t say it to anyone. Nobody had ever said it to her in the shop, and she’d never learned how.

“Oh,” said Raiden. It came out small.

✦ ✦ ✦

They had the first bath that night.

It took twenty minutes to fill, and she sat on the edge of it in his shirt and watched it, and didn’t believe it. And then they got in, both of them, though it wasn’t really big enough, with her back against his chest and his arms round her and his chin on her shoulder and the water up to their necks, and the five tall windows next door showing the cranes lit up over the roofs.

She’d had a bath twice in her life. Once at a hotel, for a race, when she was nineteen. Once in a borrowed flat, years ago.

She lay against him in the hot water and felt her body let go, her shoulders and her back and then her hands, which were always tight, even when she slept. She felt them open, under the water, as if she was letting go of a tool she’d been holding for years.

“Is it all right?” he said into her hair.

She didn’t answer. She took his hand, under the water, and put it flat on her stomach, and put hers over it.

He kissed the side of her neck, under her ear, and again, lower, and his hand moved under hers, and she turned her head on his shoulder, and he said, against her jaw, “I want to. Can I?” and she said yes, and the water went everywhere, all over the new white floor, and neither of them cared about that either.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, wrapped in towels on the long green sofa, she said, “You built it anyway.”

“Built what?”

“The napkin. The first one. You built it. It’s all here. Except the two circles.” She looked at the long table, with its eight chairs. “You built the house anyway, without the yes.”

“I built the house,” said Raiden. “The question’s still open. They’re different things.” He kissed her temple. “It’s your house. I’m just the man who lives in it and cooks. I don’t need the yes to cook. I’ll need it one day for the rest.”

He reached for his jacket on the back of the sofa and took out a pencil.

And on the back of the dyno’s instruction manual, which was lying on the floor, he drew the long room, from above, fast, with the two of them on the sofa, two little circles. And at the bottom, the scale bar.

Will you marry me? (You’d have a bath.)

“Not yet,” said Jinx, and kissed him.

He folded it up and put it in his wallet with the other seven. He hadn’t even waited for the end of the month.

chapters.title: The Meanest Engineer in the City
chapters.desc: April 2022. A charity gala, a column with terrible feng shui, and a racing driver with kitchen-scissor hair who finds his act very funny until he forgets to do it. Serafina Song becomes a client.
chapters.epigraph: “She could build a bike faster than you could crash it. I’d bet money. I’d bet your money.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
The gala for the children’s hospital was on the eighth of April, a Friday, in the ballroom of the Harbour Hotel, and for the first time she went because she wanted to.

He hadn’t asked her to. He’d mentioned it, on the long green sofa, the week before, the way he mentioned every party: as a thing he had to do, like a dentist. Seven hundred people. A dinner. An auction. Speeches. I’ll be an idiot from seven till eleven and then I’ll come home and you can tell me what was wrong with everyone.

“I’ll come,” she’d said.

He’d turned his head on the sofa cushion and looked at her.

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

“There’ll be people from the Walled City. Not my family. But people who know my father. People who’ll see you with me and go home and talk.”

“Let them,” said Jinx.

He hadn’t said anything for a moment. Then he’d pulled her down on top of him on the sofa and kissed her so long that the rice burned.

✦ ✦ ✦

She wore the new jacket this time.

Over a black dress she’d bought herself, in a shop in the Coastal High-Rise where the woman behind the counter had looked at her tattoos and her shoulders and then gone into the back and come out with the only dress in the shop that would fit her, which was plain and well cut and cost more than a carburettor rebuild. And the boots. And her black nails, which she’d done herself at the bench with the vice holding the bottle.

He stopped dead at the top of the stairs when she came out of the bathroom.

He didn’t say anything at all. He stood there in his dark suit and his silver waistcoat, the new one, with the pattern like gears that he’d designed himself and had made by a tailor in the old town, and looked at her from the boots up, and went red to the roots of his hair. She’d never seen him blush.

“Say something,” she said.

“I can’t,” said Raiden. “I’m a Lin. We’re well brought up. Everything I want to say is something I can’t say in a taxi.”

He said some of it in the taxi anyway, in her ear, all the way across the harbour.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ballroom was gold and white and full, and it went quiet when they came in.

Not all of it, just the bit near the door. She felt the heads turn, the way they had at the gallery, and look at her, and look at him beside her, and look at his hand on the small of her back. And this time they didn’t look away.

She looked back.

She’d learned at the shop how to look at a man so he looked away first. She did it now. To the whole bit of the room near the door, one after another: a man in a grey suit, a woman with pearls, a bald man who’d been staring at her tattoos. They all looked away.

“Oh,” said Raiden, under his breath, delighted. “Oh, do that again.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He did his act.

She’d seen it twice now and it still amazed her. He let go of her back at the edge of the room and threw himself into it, arms out, as if into the sea, and in thirty seconds he was the silliest person there. He hugged an old man who clearly didn’t know him. He told a famous banker his tie was a crime against silk, Uncle, a crime. He got the name of the hospital wrong. He knocked over a little gold chair and apologised to the man sitting on the next one for ten minutes. And he did the columns.

There were twelve of them down the sides of the ballroom, white marble, with gold at the tops, and he stopped in front of one with a glass of champagne he wasn’t drinking and stared up at it with his mouth open.

“No,” he said, loudly. “No, no, no. This is terrible. Who did this? The feng shui is a disaster. Look at it. It’s fighting the harbour. You can feel it in your teeth. This whole room is unlucky. I’m going to lose money at the auction, I can feel it, it’s coming up through the floor—”

People laughed. People always laughed. A woman in green patted his arm.

Jinx stood by the wall and watched him do it and didn’t laugh.

And beside her, someone else laughed, a real laugh, short and loud, like a cough.

✦ ✦ ✦

She turned her head.

There was a woman leaning on the wall beside her. Tall, thin, wiry. Short dark hair that looked as if she’d cut it herself with kitchen scissors, which she had, Jinx found out later. A red dress she clearly hated, and flat shoes, and a burn scar on the back of her right hand, an old one, shiny, the shape of an exhaust pipe.

Jinx knew who she was. Everyone who’d ever been near a track knew who she was. Serafina Song. The one who raced. Team AURELIA, the black car with the gold on the bonnet, in the Asian GT series. The one whose sister was a jeweller and whose family had more money than the harbour.

“Is he yours?” said Serafina Song.

Jinx looked at Raiden, under the column, telling a man in a dinner jacket that his whole life would go wrong if he didn’t move his table.

“Yes,” she said.

“He’s very good,” said Serafina. “I’ve never seen anyone do it that well. My mother would believe him. My mother believes nothing.” She drank her champagne. “Why does he do it?”

Jinx didn’t answer.

Serafina looked her over sideways: the jacket, the tattoos, the black nails, the grease ground into the creases of her knuckles that wouldn’t come out whatever she used.

“You’re a mechanic,” she said.

“Engineer.”

“What kind?”

“Bikes.”

“I hate my mechanics,” said Serafina Song, with feeling. “They’re too careful. Everything takes three days. Everything needs a part from Germany. I ask them to try something and they look at each other and say Miss Song, the regulations.” She finished the champagne. “I want someone who’ll just build the thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden had come back.

He’d come back along the wall from the column without either of them noticing, and he was standing on Jinx’s other side, holding his full glass, looking at Serafina Song with his silly face on. But his eyes weren’t silly. Jinx could see them going over Serafina the way they went over a building: the scar on her hand, her shoulders, her flat shoes, the way she stood with her weight on the balls of her feet.

“You want my wife,” he said.

Jinx turned her head and looked at him.

“Well,” said Raiden. “Not my wife. Not yet. She says not yet. I’ve asked seven times. Eight if you count the bath.” He smiled at Serafina with every tooth he had. “But she’s the meanest engineer in the city. She built a bike in a garage near the Docks with an intake you could hang in a gallery, and she stopped it in two metres from a hundred and ninety, and it didn’t drop a bolt. She could build a bike faster than you could crash it. I’d bet money. I’d bet your money.”

Serafina looked at him.

“I don’t crash,” she said.

“Everybody crashes,” said Raiden. “That’s why you need a mean engineer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina didn’t laugh at that.

She looked at him with her head on one side. Then she looked up at the column he’d been standing under. Then back at him.

“You said it was fighting the harbour,” she said.

“Terrible feng shui.”

“That’s not what you were looking at.” Serafina pointed at the top of the column, at the gold. “You were looking at the crack. There’s a crack. There. Where the gold meets the marble. You looked at it for a good while before you started shouting. I watch tyre walls for a living, I know what someone looking at a crack looks like.”

Raiden’s smile stayed where it was, but Jinx saw it stop being a smile.

“It’s cosmetic,” he said, after a moment. His voice had gone flat and plain. “The marble’s just cladding. The real column’s concrete, inside, and it’s fine. The crack’s because they put the gold on with the wrong glue in 1987 and it’s been pulling at the stone ever since. It’ll fall off one day and hit someone on the head, but it won’t bring anything down.” He looked at Serafina. “Don’t sit under it.”

Serafina Song stared at him.

Then she laughed again. The loud short one.

“Oh, you’re awful,” she said, delighted. “You’re absolutely awful. You’re the cleverest man in this room and you’ve spent an hour telling everyone their tables are unlucky.” She held out her hand to Jinx. Not to him. To Jinx. “I’m Serafina.”

“Jinx,” said Jinx, and shook it. Serafina’s hand was hard and dry and had calluses in the same places as hers.

“I want a bike,” said Serafina.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came to the garage on the Tuesday.

On her own bike, a tired old Japanese thing she’d had since she was eighteen, that coughed at the end of the street and died outside the black door. She got off it and looked at the black door, and the sign that still said TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS, and the anchor woman, who’d come out to look at her. Then she came in, and stopped, and looked at the workshop the way Raiden had the first day, slowly, all the way to the back.

“Oh,” she said. “Oh, I see.”

Jinx was on the floor by the sidecar.

She’d started it in January. A sidecar outfit. A big old bike with a frame she’d built for it, and the chair beside it, a long low boat-shaped thing in steel, with a seat and a little screen and a board that folded out over the knees. For him. So that he could come with her when she went north to the dyno shop, or to a race, or anywhere further than twenty kilometres an hour on the pale green bike would get him. So that he could sit beside her, at the same speed, and draw.

He didn’t know about it. It was under a sheet when he was home.

“Who’s that for?” said Serafina, looking at the chair.

“Nobody.”

Serafina looked at the board that folded out over the knees, and the little tray for pencils, and didn’t say anything, and Jinx liked her for it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The sidecar needed a gearbox.

It needed one with a reverse, because an outfit that heavy couldn’t be pushed backwards out of a parking space by one woman, and none of the bike gearboxes she had would do it, and the one she’d found in Germany would take four months to come. She told Serafina this, without meaning to, standing in the workshop with her arms folded, because Serafina had asked, and was standing there listening the way Raiden did, as if it mattered.

Serafina thought about it.

“I’ve got one,” she said.

“What?”

“A gearbox. Small, sequential, with a reverse. It came out of a little race car somebody built in Japan in the nineties, a tiny thing, for hill climbs. I bought the whole car for parts two years ago and never used it. It’s in a crate in my garage.” She shrugged. “It might fit. If you made it fit.”

“I’d make it fit.”

“I know you would,” said Serafina. “That’s why I’m here.”

They looked at each other across the workshop.

“I’ll pay you for it,” said Jinx.

“No,” said Serafina. “You’ll build me a bike.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She built it over the summer.

It took her four months, in between the customers and the sidecar and the dyno, which she’d stopped calling too much and started calling mine. She built it for Serafina’s body and Serafina’s riding, which she studied for two Saturdays at a car park in the industrial district, where Serafina raced for money at the street races an old woman called Granny Shum ran from a folding chair. She built it light and stiff and sharp and fast, with a frame that told you everything the road was doing through your knees, and nothing on it that didn’t need to be there. She painted it a dark gold, the colour of the gold on the bonnet of Serafina’s race car, and she didn’t put a carp on the tank, because the carp was hers.

Serafina came for it in August.

She sat on it in the workshop without starting it. Then she started it. Then she rode it once round the block, fast, and came back, and stopped outside the black door, and took her helmet off, and her face was wet.

“I can’t pay you for this,” she said.

“You did. The gearbox.”

“That’s not—” Serafina looked down at the bike. “That’s not the same. A gearbox isn’t—this is—”

“You paid me in a gearbox,” said Jinx. “I paid you in a bike. We’re even.”

Serafina wiped her face with the back of her scarred hand and laughed, wet and furious.

“A bike isn’t money,” she said. “A gearbox is a gearbox. This is—you can’t call this even. I’m going to say you owe me for that gearbox for the rest of your life, and one day I’m going to turn up at that door and ask you for something, and you’re going to say yes.”

“Maybe,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

The gearbox fitted the sidecar in the end.

She had to make a whole new mount for it, and an adaptor plate, and a linkage for the reverse that went to a lever by her left knee. It took three weeks. And on the first Sunday in September she pulled the sheet off, and wheeled it out into the street, and Raiden came down the stairs with a cup of tea and stopped dead on the step.

He looked at the outfit: the long steel chair, the seat, the little screen, the board that folded out over the knees, the tray for pencils.

He put the cup of tea down on the step slowly.

“It’s yours,” said Jinx. “Get in.”

He got in.

He didn’t say anything. He sat in the chair with his knees up and his hands on the edges of it and his face turned up to her, and she put the spare helmet on him, the right way round, and did up the strap, and got on, and started it.

They went north on the expressway at a hundred and ten, side by side, in the slow lane, with the wind in his face and the board folded out over his knees, and he drew the whole way: the bridges, the river, the flyovers, and her on the bike beside him, from below, with the sky behind her. He drew until he ran out of pages, and then he drew on his arm.

When they stopped for petrol in the north he got out of the chair and stood on the forecourt with pencil all up his left arm to the elbow, and looked at her, and she looked back at him.

“You built me a seat,” he said.

“You can’t ride.”

“You built me a seat next to you,” said Raiden. His voice wasn’t working. “Jia. You built me a seat next to you.”

He held out his arms. She walked into them, on the petrol station forecourt, in front of a man filling a lorry with diesel, and didn’t care.

chapters.title: Raiden Is Proud of Her for an Entire Week
chapters.desc: October 2022. Best in Show at the custom show in the north. He tells everyone. The doorman, the anchor woman, a bus. Everyone except his own family. Then he tells Zhao, and Zhao already knows.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d like everyone to know. I’d like a plane to write it in the sky. I’ve looked into it. It’s very expensive and the wind spoils the letters.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
The Northern Custom Show was held every October in an old aircraft hangar two hours north of the city, and she’d been going for six years, and she’d never entered.

She went to look. She went to see what the men from the big shops had built, with their sponsors and their paint booths and their teams of six. She walked round the hangar in her old jacket with her hands in her pockets and looked at every bike in it, slowly, and went home and built something better in her garage on her own, and never showed it to anyone.

“Enter,” said Raiden, in August.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because then they’ll look at it.”

He was lying on the green sofa with his feet on the arm and a sketchbook on his chest. He turned his head and looked at her, at her bench by the window, where she was filing a bracket.

“They’ll look at it,” he said, “and they’ll see what I saw on the shipyard road. And then they’ll know. And you’ll know they know.” He went back to his sketchbook. “Enter. I’ll fill the form in. You won’t have to touch it. I’ll put Jinx and the garage and nothing else.”

She went on filing the bracket.

“Put the carp,” she said. “On the form. Where it says the name of the bike. Put Carp.”

He didn’t say anything. He got up off the sofa and came across the room and kissed the back of her neck, once, over the collar of her overalls, and went and got his laptop.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went up on the Friday night in the van, with the black bike on a trailer behind it that she’d borrowed a hitch for, and Raiden in the passenger seat with his sketchbook on his knee, drawing the motorway in the dark by the light of the dashboard.

The hangar was enormous and cold and full of men.

Four hundred bikes. Stands and lights and banners, and music from somewhere, and the smell of coffee and two-stroke oil and tyre polish, and men in leather and men in branded shirts and a few women, not many, who looked at her as she wheeled the black bike in and nodded, the way she’d seen Serafina nod. She put the bike where the organisers told her, on a square of grey carpet at the far end by the doors, between a big chrome cruiser from a shop in the Coastal High-Rise and a matte green racer with a team of five standing round it in matching jackets.

She polished nothing. She didn’t put up a sign. She stood the black bike on its stand on the grey carpet with its front wheel turned slightly, the way it liked to stand, and stood back.

The team in the matching jackets looked at her. One of them laughed.

Raiden, beside her, put his hand on the small of her back and said under his breath, “That one. With the beard. I’m going to remember his face.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The judges came round at two on the Saturday.

Three of them. An old man who’d built bikes in the north for forty years and whose name she’d known since she was ten, from the magazines in her father’s office. A woman who wrote for one of those magazines. A younger man from a big shop in the south, with a clipboard.

They looked at the cruiser. They looked at the matte green racer, while the team in the jackets talked at them.

Then the old man came to the black bike.

He didn’t say anything. He walked round it once. Then he crouched down, slowly, with a hand on his knee, beside the engine, and looked at the intake. He stayed there, crouched. He reached out and ran his thumb along the third runner, where she’d filed the mouth by hand, and stopped on the little lip, exactly the place Raiden had drawn.

He looked up at her.

“Who made this?”

“I did.”

“The whole thing?”

“The frame. The swingarm. The intake. The tank, out of a scrap one. The engine’s old. I rebuilt it.”

“On your own?”

“Yes.”

The old man looked at her for a moment more. Then he looked back at the intake.

“I’ve been doing this forty-one years,” he said. “I’ve never seen anybody match runners that well by hand. Never.” He stood up, with a grunt. “What do you call it?”

“Carp,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

It won Best in Show.

They read it out at five o’clock on the Saturday, from a little stage at the end of the hangar, into a microphone that whistled. The old man read it. Best in Show: Carp. Built by Jinx. Garage near the Iron Docks. And there was a silence, because nobody in the hangar knew who that was. And then the women at the far end, the few of them, started clapping, and then the old man did, and then everyone else did, slowly, the way a crowd does when it’s working out whether it’s allowed to.

She stood by the black bike and didn’t move.

Raiden made a noise.

She’d never heard it before. It was a sort of yell, a whoop, loud, like a boy on a roller-coaster, and it went right up into the roof of the hangar, and the whole crowd turned round to see who’d made it. Then he picked her up off the floor, round the waist, in both arms, and swung her round, in front of four hundred men and the team in the matching jackets, and her boots went out and nearly kicked the chrome cruiser, and she was shouting at him to put her down, and he wouldn’t, and he was laughing, and she was—

She was laughing too.

She realised it about halfway round. She was laughing out loud in an aircraft hangar with her arms round his neck and her face in his hair, and she couldn’t stop.

When he put her down, he didn’t let go. He took her face in both hands and kissed her, hard, and the whole hangar saw it. Somebody whistled. The man with the beard said something and his friends laughed, and Raiden didn’t stop, and after a second she didn’t care, and grabbed his waistcoat and kissed him back until the women at the far end started clapping again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was proud of her for an entire week.

He told the man at the petrol station on the way home. He told the woman at the toll booth. He told the anchor woman, who said about time, and Mrs. Tong, who gave them both free noodles and put a picture of the black bike, cut out of a newspaper somebody had brought in, on the wall behind the counter next to the picture of her late husband. He told the man on the desk at the Meridian, who said the lady with the bicycle? and he said the lady with the bicycle, and the man shook his hand.

He told his firm in the south on a video call. He told the foreman who’d built the top floors, who rang him back two days later to say his brother-in-law wanted a bike built. He told Big Fok at the shipyard road on the Saturday night, who said I know, everyone knows, she’s going to be impossible now. He told a man at a bus stop. He told a whole bus. She was there for that. He got on a bus on Harbour Road, which he never did, because the pale green bike had a puncture, and before it got to the next stop he’d told the driver and an old lady with a trolley and a schoolboy, and the old lady had asked to see the picture on his phone, and said it was very nice, and asked if Jinx was single.

“No,” said Raiden. “She’s mine. I’ve asked her to marry me fifteen times.”

“And?” said the old lady.

“Not yet,” said Jinx, from the seat behind.

The old lady looked round at her.

“Say yes,” she said. “Look at him. He’s told the whole bus.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t tell his family.

She noticed it on the Wednesday. They were at the long table upstairs, eating noodles he’d made, and his phone buzzed on the table, and he looked at it, and it said Elowen. He picked it up and read the message, and smiled. She watched him start typing something long, fast, and then stop and look at it, and delete it, one letter at a time. Then he wrote something short, sent it, and put the phone face down on the table.

“What did she say?” said Jinx.

“She asked if I’m coming on Sunday. It’s my father’s birthday dinner.”

“And what did you start to say?”

He looked at her.

“I started to say, I can’t wait to tell you, the woman I love won Best in Show at the Northern Custom Show with a bike she built with her own hands, and the old man from the magazines crouched down and touched the intake, and I’ve drawn it over and over, and I want to show you the drawings.” He picked up his chopsticks. “And then I remembered it was the rule. My side and your side. So I said yes, I’ll come, what time.”

She sat there.

She’d made the rule. She’d made it on the thirty-first floor in June 2021, standing in his empty flat with her arms folded, and he’d said yes, and he’d kept it for sixteen months. He’d kept it so well she’d thought it was easy for him. He was a Lin. He had a whole family. He went to dinner on Sundays in the Walled City and came home and cooked for her and never said a word about it, and she’d thought that meant he didn’t mind.

He was looking at his noodles.

“I’m so proud of you,” he said. “I want everyone to know. I’d like a plane to write it in the sky. I’ve looked into it. It’s very expensive and the wind spoils the letters.” He was smiling a little, but not with his eyes. “I’d like my sisters to know. That’s all.”

She didn’t know what to say. She knew the rule was hers and that she wasn’t ready to break it, and she knew that she’d just watched him delete the best thing anyone had ever written about her, one letter at a time, so as not to break it either. She sat there at the long table with the noodles going cold, and felt sick.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Friday he went to the flower shop.

He went to deliver a shelf. Elowen had a row of glasses on the windowsill in the kitchen of the house on the hill that had got too long, and he’d made her a shelf for them out of old shipyard timber, and he went on the pale green bike with the shelf strapped to the board, at twenty kilometres an hour, the whole way to the old town.

Zhao was in the flower shop. He usually was, on Fridays. He sat in a chair behind the counter that Elowen didn’t let him sit in, with a newspaper, while she did the morning’s orders.

Elowen was in the back. Raiden heard her on the phone to a supplier, being cold and precise about tulips.

He put the shelf down on the counter.

Zhao looked at it over his newspaper.

Raiden looked at Zhao.

He hadn’t meant to. He’d meant to put the shelf down and say something silly and go. But he stood there in the flower shop with the tulips in their buckets on Raiden’s floor, the floor he’d put in two years ago with a steel room underneath it, and the morning sun coming in, and Zhao looking at him over the paper with his flat black eyes, and it came out.

“She won Best in Show,” he said. “At the Northern Custom Show. Last Saturday. The whole hangar. Four hundred bikes.”

Zhao looked at him for four seconds.

“Hm,” he said. “I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden didn’t move.

“How do you know?”

Zhao turned a page of his newspaper.

“Big Fok,” he said. “And the anchor woman. And the boy.” He meant Xiao Pan. “And Mrs. Tong put it on her wall.” He turned another page. “And the bus.”

“You know about the bus.”

Zhao turned another page.

“How long have you known?”

Zhao looked at him over the paper. Then he put it down, folded, on his knee.

“Since the hospital,” he said. “The jacket.”

Raiden stared at him.

“You took the jacket,” he said slowly. “You took her jacket. Off the chair. I saw you. Before Elowen turned round.”

“Hm.”

“And you’ve never told Elowen.”

Zhao looked at him for a while. Then he looked toward the back of the shop, where his wife was telling a tulip supplier exactly what she thought of him, in a voice that could have cut glass.

“Not mine to tell,” said Zhao.

He picked up the newspaper again.

Raiden stood there in the flower shop. His eyes stung, and he let them. He put his hand out on the counter, flat, beside the shelf. Zhao looked at it. Then, without putting the paper down, he put his own hand on top of it, once, heavy, and took it away.

“Tell her well done,” said Zhao, behind the paper. “From me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her that night, in the bath, with her back against his chest.

“He said well done,” he said. “From him. He’s hardly said a word to me in two years, and today two of them were well done. For you.”

She lay against him in the hot water and didn’t say anything.

“He’s known since the jacket,” said Raiden. “He never told Elowen. He said it wasn’t his to tell.”

“It isn’t.”

“I know.” He kissed her shoulder. “I’m not asking. I promise I’m not asking. I just wanted you to know that somebody in my family knows, and thinks well done, and has kept it for sixteen months because you asked me to. That’s all.”

She turned her head on his shoulder, in the water, and looked up at him.

He’d drawn her over and over since Saturday: at the bike, by the stage when they read it out, laughing in the air with her boots kicking.
