He’d got her boots and her arms and the back of her head and the line of her shoulders and the carp on her arm. He hadn’t got her face. He’d torn out the face every time and folded it small.

“Raiden,” she said.

“Mm.”

“I’m proud of you too.”

He went still in the water.

“For what?”

“For keeping it,” she said. “My rule. I know it cost you. I didn’t know until Wednesday. I’m sorry.”

He didn’t say anything. Then he wrapped both arms round her, under the water, tight, and put his face in her wet hair, and stayed there until the water went cold.

The Best in Show trophy went on the shelf over her bench, between the glass prize and the tin of washers.

chapters.title: Memes at 2 A.M.
chapters.desc: December 2022. He can’t sleep, so he sends her memes from the next pillow. She knows why before he does. Then a farm in the borderland, a freezer, eleven hours, and a light that comes on by itself.
chapters.epigraph: “You built me a freezer with the light on.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
Just after two in the morning on the twenty-eighth of December, her phone buzzed on the floor by the bed.

She opened one eye.

It was a picture of a cat. A grey cat, sitting in a cardboard box much too small for it, with its whole body spilling over the sides, and its face perfectly calm. Underneath, someone had written: me fitting into my responsibilities.

It was from Raiden.

Raiden was lying beside her. She could feel him. His shoulder was against hers, under the duvet, and his phone was lighting up his face, blue, in the dark of the long room.

The phone buzzed again.

A picture of a building. An ugly one, a tower in some other city, with every window a slightly different shape. architect: i have a vision. the vision:

Again.

A dog in a hard hat.

Again.

A drawing of a staircase that went up into a ceiling and stopped. me when i start a sentence.

She rolled over onto her side and looked at him.

He was lying on his back with the phone held up over his face in both hands, scrolling. He didn’t look at her. He sent another one. Her phone buzzed against the floor.

“Raiden.”

“Mm?”

“I’m next to you.”

“I know,” he said. “I didn’t want to wake you.” He sent another one.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lay there and watched him for a while.

He looked fine. He looked the way he always looked, mostly. A bit pale, in the blue light. His hair everywhere. But his eyes were moving too fast, back and forth over the screen, and his jaw was tight, and every time a lorry went past in the street below and its lights went across the ceiling, she felt his shoulder go hard against hers for a second, and then soft again.

She thought: he did this last year.

She hadn’t put it together, last year. They’d only been living above the garage a few months. But the last week of December, the week between Christmas, which nobody in the Docks bothered with, and New Year, which everyone did, he hadn’t slept. She’d woken at three and four in the morning and found him up, at his drawing table or at the window, or once downstairs in the workshop, with all the lights on, standing in front of the black door checking the bolts. And he’d said couldn’t sleep, too much coffee, and she’d believed him, even though he didn’t drink coffee.

And she’d found drawings that week, stacks of them. Not buildings: doors, with locks, with bolts, with light coming under them. And stairs that went up and up.

She’d thought it was work.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took the phone out of his hands.

He let her. He lay there with his hands still up where the phone had been, in the dark, and then put them down on his chest.

She put the phone face down on the floor beside hers.

“What happened in December?” she said.

He didn’t answer.

“Last year,” she said. “Same week. You didn’t sleep. You checked the door. You drew doors. Hundreds.” She looked at his face in the orange light from the street. “Now it’s every night since Christmas. What happened?”

A lorry went past below. He didn’t say anything until it had gone.

“I hadn’t noticed,” he said at last. “That it was the same week.” He gave a small laugh. “That’s ridiculous. That’s—I hadn’t noticed. Fifteen years. You’d think I’d notice.”

“Fifteen years since what?”

He turned his head on the pillow and looked at her.

“The freezer,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her.

Lying on his back in the dark, in the long room, with the cranes lit up through the five tall windows and the lorries going past on the street. He told it in a flat, steady voice, not his voice at all, as if he’d been holding it in one piece for fifteen years and was afraid that if he held it differently it would break.

“I was nine,” he said. “At the farm. In the borderland. I told you about the farm. The water tower. Uncle and Auntie. It was winter, the week before New Year. And there was fighting on the far side of the river. You could hear it at night. Guns, a long way off. Like someone hammering in another street.”

“And one night there were trucks on the road. The river road. It went right past the farm gate. And they were driving with their lights off. You could hear them coming, a long way away. Lots of them. And Uncle heard them, and he came into my room and picked me up out of bed, and carried me to the kitchen, and there was a chest freezer in the corner, a big old white one, and he took the food out of it and put it on the floor, and put me in it.”

She didn’t move.

“It wasn’t on,” said Raiden. “He’d pulled the plug. It was just cold. It still had frost on the sides. And he put a blanket in, and me on the blanket, and said don’t make a sound, whatever you hear, don’t make a sound, and don’t come out until I open it. And he shut the lid.”

He stopped for a moment.

“I was in there eleven hours,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I could hear them,” he said. “The trucks. They came along the road and they slowed down at the gate. I could hear the engines through the side of the freezer. And men’s voices. I couldn’t hear what they said. And the dogs barking. And then the trucks went on. And then more came. All night. Truck after truck.”

“I didn’t know who they were. Nobody told me why I was at the farm. Nobody ever told me anything. But I’d heard the women talking, in the village. About my father. That he was an important man in the city, and that people wanted things from him. So I lay in the freezer in the dark and I thought, they’ve come for me. I thought every truck was the one that was going to stop. And open the gate. And come into the kitchen. And open the lid.”

“So I counted.”

“I counted to keep from making a sound. One, two, three. In my head. Over and over. Every number. I got to forty thousand. I know because I couldn’t stop. When I got to a thousand I’d make a mark on my hand with my fingernail, in the dark. Forty marks. I had them on my palm for a week afterwards.”

“And in the morning, Uncle opened the lid, and it was light, and the trucks had gone. All of them. They’d just gone past. Nobody had come in. Nobody had been coming for me at all.” He was quiet for a moment. “And there was a tin of peaches on the gatepost. Somebody had left it. I never found out who. I went out into the yard in my blanket, and it was on the gatepost, by itself, in the frost. And I ate the whole tin, standing up. With my fingers.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She lay on her side and looked at him and couldn’t think of one right thing to say. She put her hand on his chest, flat, over his heart, and left it there.

His heart was going fast.

“And every December,” he said, “the last week. I don’t sleep. I hadn’t noticed it was every December. I thought it was just—I thought I was just bad at sleeping, sometimes. And I get up and check the doors.” He put his hand over hers on his chest. “And I draw doors. I didn’t know that either. Until you said.”

She thought about the doors. Hundreds of them. With light coming underneath.

And she thought about the steel room behind her tool wall.

She thought about him standing in front of it in April, showing her. A light that comes on by itself. A vent in the ceiling. A phone on the wall. A line out that doesn’t go through anyone’s exchange. You could sit in there for three days. She thought about Elowen’s shop, which she’d never been to, which had a floor he’d built with something under the tulips. About every safe room he’d ever drawn, for his family, for anyone, in the six years since he’d started. Every one of them a box you could hide in. Every one with a light, and air, and a way to call for help, and a way out.

“Oh,” she said.

He turned his head.

“Raiden,” she said. “You built me a freezer with the light on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stopped breathing. She felt his whole chest go still under her hand.

Then something gave way in him. It went the way he’d once told her a beam goes in a building: a long low creak, then a crack, then everything it had been holding up coming down.

He turned over onto his side, away from her, and put his face in the pillow, and his shoulders went.

He didn’t make much noise. He’d learned that, she thought. In the freezer. To not make a sound, whatever happened. He lay with his face in the pillow and his whole body shaking, and the sounds that came out of him were small and terrible, and she’d never heard a man cry like that. Her father had never cried. The men at the shop had never cried. She’d never known what it would sound like if someone did, properly, all the way from the bottom.

She lay against his back.

She put her arm round his chest from behind. She put her face against the back of his neck. She held on, as hard as she could, with her whole arm, the way she held a bike that wanted to go over, and didn’t let go.

“I’ve got you,” she said.

She’d never said that to anyone either.

✦ ✦ ✦

It went on.

The lorries went past. The lights went across the ceiling. Down in the street, someone was singing on their way home, badly, a New Year song, three days early. And she lay with her arm round him and held on until the shaking slowed down and stopped, and his breathing went long and uneven and then even, and his hand came up and found hers on his chest and held it.

“Sorry,” he said, into the pillow. His voice was wrecked.

“Don’t say sorry.”

“I’ve never—I haven’t—not since the—”

“I know,” she said. “It’s all right.”

He was quiet.

“I can’t sleep,” he said, after a while. “I’m sorry. I’m so tired. I can’t. Every time a truck goes past—”

She thought about it.

Then she did the only thing she could think of. She’d never been any good with words.

“Then I’ll count,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything. She felt him go still against her.

So she counted.

Out loud, low, against the back of his neck, in the dark. One. Two. Three. Slowly, with nowhere to get to. Four. Five. The way she counted turns on a bolt when she was doing it up by feel, waiting for it to seat.

“You don’t have to,” he said, at twenty-three.

“Twenty-four,” said Jinx. “Twenty-five.”

At a hundred and twelve, a lorry went past, and she felt him go hard all down his back, and she didn’t stop. A hundred and thirteen. A hundred and fourteen. And he went soft again.

At four hundred, his hand went loose on hers.

At nine hundred, his breathing changed.

At eleven hundred and something, she lost count, and started again from a thousand, because it didn’t matter, it wasn’t for getting anywhere, and he made a small sound, half asleep, that might have been a laugh.

She got to four thousand and six.

By then he’d been asleep for an hour, heavily, on his side, with her arm round him and her face against his neck. She stopped counting. She lay there in the dark and listened to him breathe, and to the lorries, and to the cranes, and didn’t sleep at all herself, and didn’t mind.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he slept until eleven.

She went downstairs at seven and opened the black door, and worked. At ten there were no three coffees on the bench, because he was upstairs asleep, and she found she missed them so much it was stupid.

At half past eleven he came down the stairs in his shorts and a jumper, with his hair flat on one side and his eyes still swollen, and stood at the bottom and looked at her.

She was under the black bike, on the creeper. She pushed herself out.

“You counted to four thousand,” he said.

“Four thousand and six.”

He came across the workshop. He didn’t say anything else. He got down on the floor beside her, on the concrete, in his shorts, and lay down on the other creeper, and pushed himself under the bike next to her, where they’d lain the first time. His shoulder was against hers, under the sump, in the orange light.

“I love you,” he said.

He’d said it before. Lots of times. In the noodle shop. On napkins. In the bath. But he’d never said it like that, lying on his back on a creeper on a cold floor, as if it had cost him something to get to and he’d carried it all the way down the stairs.

She looked at the underside of the engine.

“I know,” she said.

He gave a small laugh and put his hand on hers, on the concrete, palm to palm.

Then he turned his head on the creeper, and she turned hers, and he kissed her. His mouth was soft and tired and tasted of sleep. He kissed her as if he’d been somewhere dark all night and come back up into the light and found her there.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon she went to the tool wall, and pressed the thing behind the big spanner, and swung it out, and opened the steel door, and stood in the small concrete room with the light that came on by itself.

Then she went out to the van and got her drill.

When he came down at six with the shopping, she was still in there. She’d put a shelf up over the bench, at the height of someone lying down, and on the shelf a lamp, a proper one, warm and yellow, with a shade. You could switch it on and off with your own hand without getting up.

Beside it was a tin of peaches from Mrs. Tong’s, who’d had to go to the cash-and-carry for it.

He stood in the doorway of the room he’d built with the shopping hanging from his hands.

“In case,” said Jinx.

He put the shopping down on the floor of the workshop. He didn’t say anything at all. He came into the room and put his arms round her, from behind, in the small concrete space, with the warm lamp on and the tin of peaches on the shelf, and put his face in her neck, and stayed there.

She stood with her hands over his on her stomach and let him.

chapters.title: Ten, Walking Home Alone
chapters.desc: January 2023. How a boy of ten copied a road map onto his arm, rode under the ice in a fish truck, and knocked on his father’s door. Then, at two in the morning, she goes to the Walled City for the first time, to see the door.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody was coming. So I went to them.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
After the freezer, he talked about the farm more.

Not all at once: little things, at odd times, while he was cooking, or while she was under a bike and he was on the crate drawing. Once in the bath, out of nowhere, with his chin on her shoulder: that Auntie had kept geese, and the geese had hated him, and he’d hated them back, and there’d been one in particular, a big grey one, that used to wait for him outside the outhouse.

“Did you win?” said Jinx.

“No,” said Raiden. “Nobody ever won against that goose. It died of old age. I was there. I cried.”

She laughed into the bathwater.

And she noticed that every time he talked about the farm, now, he stopped at the same place. The morning after the freezer. The tin of peaches on the gatepost. And then he’d say and then I came home, at ten, and go on to something else. The Walled City. The long kitchen table. Ah Sim the cook. His sisters.

He never said how.

✦ ✦ ✦

She asked on a Saturday in January.

They were in the dyno room, next door, at night. She had a customer’s bike strapped down on the rolling road, a big old twin, and she was running it, over and over, and changing the jets between runs, and he was sitting on the desk with his feet on a chair watching the line on the screen climb and dip and climb.

With the fan and the engine both going, it was loud.

She shut it off. In the silence, the drum went on turning for a while by itself, slower and slower.

“How did you come home?” she said.

He looked at her.

“You always say and then I came home, at ten,” she said. “You never say how. Did your father send for you?”

He was quiet for a moment.

“No,” he said. “I walked.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat down on the edge of the dyno pit.

He didn’t come down off the desk. He sat there with his feet on the chair and his hands between his knees and told it to her the way he’d told her about the freezer: quietly, in one piece.

“After the freezer,” he said, “I stopped waiting. I’d been waiting since I could remember. For someone to come. My father, or someone from him. Every time a car came down the river road, I’d run to the gate. Every time. For nine years. And nobody ever came. And then I lay in the freezer for eleven hours thinking somebody was finally coming, and it was the wrong people, and they didn’t come either.” He gave a small shrug. “So I thought, all right. Nobody’s coming. I’ll go to them.”

“You were nine.”

“I was ten by the time I went. I waited for my birthday. I don’t know why. I think I thought you had to be ten.” He smiled a little. “There was a map in the farm kitchen. An old road map, on the wall, that Uncle used for the trucks. It had the river road, and the border town, and the main road south, and the city at the bottom, tiny. And I copied it. Onto my arm. In biro. Every night for a month, after I’d washed it off, I drew it again. Until I didn’t need it. Until I could see it with my eyes shut.”

She thought of him at her kitchen table under the bare bulb, the night after the roof of the noodle factory, drawing every street under the flyover until two in the morning. Making a map. Of every way out.

“And then I went,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d left on the first of May, in the night, with a bag of rice cakes and a bottle of water and forty in coins he’d saved, which wasn’t enough for anything.

He’d walked to the border town. It took three days, and a ride on the back of a farm cart for part of it. He’d walked along the river road in the day and slept in a culvert under it the first night, and in a barn the second, with a dog that didn’t bark, and he’d kept off the road whenever a truck came, the way he’d learned.

“How did you cross?”

“I didn’t. Not properly.” He looked at his hands. “There were trucks that went across every morning. Fish trucks. From the river. They had boxes on the back, big ones, full of ice, with the fish in. And the men at the crossing never looked in the fish. Nobody wants to put their hand in a box of ice and fish at six in the morning. So I got in one.”

She stared at him.

“In the ice,” she said.

“Under the top layer. With a sack over me. And the fish.” He almost laughed. “It was fine. It was only an hour. It wasn’t dark, there were cracks in the box. And I knew it was going to stop. I knew where it was going. That was the difference. In the freezer I didn’t know anything. In the fish truck I had a map on my arm.”

“Raiden.”

“I know,” he said. “I know. I was ten. It was stupid. I could have died of cold. I nearly did, a bit. When I got out on the other side I couldn’t feel my hands for an hour.” He turned them over now, his long clever hands, and looked at them as if he were checking they were still there. “But I got out, and the man driving it saw me get out, and he didn’t say anything. He just gave me his coat. And a ride as far as the main road.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Then a bus. Two buses. Then a lorry driver who took him a long way south and bought him noodles and didn’t ask him any questions, and dropped him at a service station on the edge of the city, where he slept in the toilets. And then he walked.

“Into the city?”

“Through it. From the north side. It took a whole day. I’d never seen it. Not since I was a baby. I didn’t know it was so big. I had the map, but the map was only the main road, and the city at the bottom was a dot, and then I was in the dot and it was the biggest thing I’d ever seen in my life.” He stopped. “I walked across the whole city looking up. All day. At the buildings. I’d never seen a building taller than the water tower. I walked past the Coastal High-Rise and I thought I was dreaming. I stood under a bridge for an hour, just looking at how it stayed up.”

“And you found the Walled City.”

“I asked. An old man at a noodle stall. He looked at me for ages and then pointed. And I went down a lane, and up some steps, and there was a door. A big old red door, with brass on it. And I knew it. I’d never seen it, and I knew it. And I knocked.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stopped.

The drum in the dyno pit had stopped turning. The fan had stopped. The room was quiet. Outside in the lane, somebody’s cat was crying.

“Who opened it?” said Jinx.

“My father.”

He was looking at the floor.

“It was eleven at night,” he said. “He opened it himself. I don’t know why. There were always people to open doors. But he opened it, and he looked down at me, on the step, in a fish man’s coat that came down to my ankles, with a map on my arm in biro and a bag with no rice cakes left in it. And he knew me. He hadn’t seen me since I was three days old. And he knew me. I saw it happen.”

“What did he say?”

“Nothing,” said Raiden. “Not for ages. Then he said, you shouldn’t be here. He said, you’ll be taken. They’ll take you. That’s why you were there.” He took a breath. “And I said, nobody came. In the freezer. Nobody came, so I came.”

He looked up at her then.

“And he sat down,” he said. “On the step. In the doorway. Lin Jian. He sat down on his own front step like his legs had gone, with me standing in front of him, and he put his face in his hands. And then he put his arms round me. And he didn’t send me back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t say anything.

She got up off the edge of the dyno pit and went and stood in front of him, where he was sitting on the desk, between his knees. She put her hands on his face. He let her. His eyes were bright.

“And then you decided to be stupid,” she said.

He laughed, surprised into it.

“That night,” he said. “Yes. In bed. In a room at the top of the house that had been mine for ten years and that I’d never been in. I lay there and I thought, he didn’t send me back. But he wanted to. He said I’d be taken. So I have to be someone nobody would want to take.” He shrugged in her hands. “So in the morning I came down to breakfast and I was the stupidest boy in the Walled City. And I’ve been him ever since.”

“You weren’t stupid.”

“No,” said Raiden. “I was ten, and I’d walked home on my own across a border in a box of fish, with a map on my arm. I was the least stupid boy in the Walled City. That’s why I had to hide it.”

She stood there between his knees with her hands on his face.

She thought about a boy in a fish man’s coat on a red step. About a big grey man sitting down on his own front step with his face in his hands. About her own father, at his desk, writing in his book under a yellow lamp, and never once coming to find her in the four years since she left. About Lin Jian, who she’d been afraid of since she was nine years old, since the black car came down the lane under the flyover. Who’d opened his own door.

“Show me,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t understand.

“The door,” said Jinx. “Show me the door.”

He went still under her hands.

“The Walled City,” he said slowly.

“Not inside. I’m not ready for inside.” She let go of his face. “But I want to see the door you knocked on. Stand where you stood.”

He looked at her.

“It’s two in the morning,” he said.

“Good. Nobody’ll be there.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went in the sidecar.

Through the empty city, across the harbour bridge, with the lights on the water and nothing else on the road, and him in the chair with the board folded down and his hands on the edges, not drawing, just looking up at the buildings going past the way he must have done when he was ten. She went slowly. She took the long way round, past the Coastal High-Rise, past the bridge he’d stood under for an hour.

The Walled City was dark and old and steep, a hill of narrow lanes and stairs and walls with houses crowded on top of each other and lamps on brackets. She’d never been there. She’d been told not to go there when she was nine, and she’d never gone, and she’d built a life around never going, and now she was riding up its lanes at two in the morning in a sidecar outfit with Lin Jian’s son beside her.

He showed her where to stop, at the bottom of some steps. She turned the engine off. The silence was enormous.

They walked up the steps together.

There was a lane at the top, narrow, between high grey walls. A lamp on a bracket. And a door.

It was red, an old faded red, nearly brown, with brass studs, and a brass knocker in the shape of a lion’s head, and a brass plate beside it with nothing written on it at all. Two stone steps up to it. A gutter beside it, and a drain.

She stood at the bottom of the steps and looked at it.

“That’s it,” said Raiden. “That’s the step he sat on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went up the two stone steps.

She stood on the top one, where a ten-year-old boy in a fish man’s coat had stood fifteen years ago at eleven at night and knocked. She looked at the lion’s head. She didn’t touch it.

She put her hand flat on the old red wood beside it instead.

It was cold. It was only a door. She’d been afraid of it since she was nine. Not this door. The idea of it. The black car, and the man in the dark coat, and her father’s hands flat on the desk. And it was only a door, red, old, with a drain beside it and a lamp over it, and somewhere behind it, asleep, a big grey man who had sat down on his own step and put his face in his hands.

She stood there with her hand on it.

Behind her, at the bottom of the steps, Raiden didn’t move.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she came down, he was crying.

Not like after the freezer. He was just standing in the lane under the lamp with his hands in his pockets and his face wet, not doing anything about it.

She stood in front of him.

“I’d like you to come in,” he said. “One day. I’d like to take you up those steps and open that door and take you in and say this is Jia. To all of them. I’d like that more than anything in the world.” He took a breath. “I’m not asking. I’m not. You said not yet, and I said it was different, and it is, and I’ll keep it. I’m only telling you what I’d like.”

“I know,” she said.

She looked at the red door, over his shoulder, at the top of the two steps.

“One day,” said Jinx.

He shut his eyes.

She’d never said that before. She’d said not yet to seventeen napkins. She’d never said one day. She heard it come out of her mouth and didn’t take it back.

He opened his eyes.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t make a joke. He took her face in his hands, in the narrow lane at the top of the steps in the Walled City, with his father’s door behind her and the lamp over their heads, and kissed her, carefully at first, as if she might change her mind, and then not carefully at all, so that she ended up with her back against the old grey wall across from the red door and her hands in his coat and his whole body against hers, and somewhere a dog barked, and a window went on, high up, and off again.

“We’ll wake him,” she said against his mouth.

“He sleeps like a rock,” said Raiden, and kissed her again. Then he pulled back, breathing hard. “Let’s go home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the way back down the steps he stopped, and took out his sketchbook, and drew the door.

It took him two minutes. The red door, the lion, the two steps, the lamp. And on the top step, small, a figure, standing, with her hand flat on the wood beside the knocker.

Not her face: her back, her shoulders, the shaved side of her hair, her hand on the door.

He drew one more line, at the bottom, and showed it to her under the lamp.

1:50. Will you marry me? (I know. Not yet. I had to.)

“Not yet,” said Jinx, and he folded it up and put it in his wallet.

But she held his hand all the way back down the steps to the sidecar, and all the way across the harbour bridge, reaching across from the handlebars with her left hand while she rode with her right, which was a terrible idea, and which she did anyway.

chapters.title: A Commission From the Syndicate
chapters.desc: June 2023. Drawings on his table for a house on the Peak, and a room inside it that nobody can get into. She finally sees what he really does, and for whom, and what it could cost. They fight. They don’t finish the fight. Then he asks her to a wedding.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody looks at me. That’s the whole point.” “I looked.” — Raiden Lin and Jinx
chapters.content:
The drawings were on his table when she came up at ten.

He wasn’t there. He’d gone out for oil, because he’d run out halfway through cooking, and the rice was on, and the window by his drafting table was open, and the drawings were moving a little at the corners in the warm air off the street. Five big sheets, pinned down with a ruler and a mug and two of her washers.

She didn’t mean to look.

She went to shut the window, and the top sheet lifted in the breeze, and she put her hand on it to hold it down, and looked.

It was a house. A big one. Old, three storeys, on a slope, with a garden in terraces going down and a view drawn in with a few lines across the top of the sheet that could only be the harbour from very high up. The Peak. She’d been to the Peak once, to deliver a bike to a collector who’d made her use the service entrance. She knew what kind of people lived up there.

The plans were detailed, every room drawn in. A long drawing room with tall windows. A library. A kitchen. Stairs. And in the middle of the house, in the middle of the second floor, a room that wasn’t on the plan at all.

You could only see it if you knew how he drew. She knew how he drew. The walls round the library were too thick. Not much. A few centimetres more than they should be, on all four sides. And on the next sheet, the section, the side view, there was a space between the library and the bedroom above it that wasn’t a floor and wasn’t a ceiling, a gap a metre high, and inside it, tiny, a note in his capitals: SEE SHEET 5. DO NOT ISSUE.

She lifted the mug and looked at sheet five.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a room.

Inside the library walls. Behind the bookcases. A room of steel, drawn in section like a box, with every layer of the walls marked. Steel plate. A layer of something she didn’t know the name of. Concrete. Steel again. A door that was part of the bookcase, with hinges drawn in detail, and a locking bar, and a note: rated. Air, from the roof, through a pipe with filters. A separate power supply. A tank of water. A line out.

It was like the room behind her tool wall, but hers was a box you could sit in for three days. This one was built for someone people would come for with more than a truck.

In the corner of the sheet, in the title box, where the architect’s name and the client’s name went, he’d written the client’s name, small.

C.S.

She knew who that was. Everyone in the city knew who that was. Everyone at the Docks said it under their breath, or not at all. Chen Si. The head of the Syndicate. The man the Walled City answered to, and the crews in the Slums answered to the Walled City, and her father’s buyers answered to the crews. The very top of all of it, sitting on the Peak, and Raiden was drawing him a room where nobody could reach him.

She stood there with her hand on the sheet.

The rice boiled over behind her on the stove.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came up the stairs with the oil and stopped in the doorway.

She hadn’t moved. She was standing at his table with sheet five under her hand and the rice hissing on the stove and her face doing whatever it was doing, and he looked at her, and at the drawings, and put the bottle of oil down on the floor slowly.

“Ah,” he said.

He went past her and turned the rice off.

“I was going to tell you,” he said, with his back to her, at the stove.

“When?”

“When it was finished.”

“Like the building.”

“Yes,” said Raiden. He turned round. “It’s a house on the Peak. It was the Song family’s house. His wife’s family. Aurelia. She grew up there. Her father’s going to lose it this year, and when it comes up at auction she’ll buy it back, and she’ll want it as it was, and Chen Si wants it safe before she ever walks in. So he asked me.”

She didn’t say anything.

“Zhao told him. Zhao told him about Elowen’s floor, the one under the tulips. And then Chen Si came to see me.” He put his hands in his pockets. “At the firm. In the south. In a suit. He waited in reception for an hour reading a magazine about kitchens until I came out. And then he said he’d like a room his wife could go into if anyone ever came for her, and he’d like her never to know it was there unless she needed it, and could I do that. And I said yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Do you know what he is?” said Jinx.

“Yes.”

“Do you know who my father’s buyers answer to? And who they answer to?” She heard her voice going up and couldn’t stop it. “He’s the top of it. Everything I got out from. Everything I’ve kept away from that black door for five years. And you’re drawing him a room.”

“I know.”

“You said you made places safe for your family.”

“Aurelia is Elowen’s friend. Chen Si is Zhao’s brother. Not by blood. They were in Block C together, when they were boys. Zhao would die for him. Zhao would die for her.” He took a breath. “That’s family. In my family, that’s family.”

“And who keeps you safe?”

He stopped.

“You’ve drawn the inside of Chen Si’s house,” said Jinx. “Every wall. Where he goes when people come for him. On your table. By an open window. Under a mug.” She picked up the mug and held it out at him, and her hand was shaking, and the cold tea in it shook. “Anyone who wants that man only has to get to you first. You’re the key. And you left it by the window.”

“Nobody knows,” said Raiden. “Nobody looks at me. That’s the whole point. That’s why I’m—”

“I looked,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

She put the mug down, too hard. Tea went on sheet four.

“I looked,” she said. “On the shipyard road. Half a second, at a hundred and ninety, and I knew you weren’t a fool. Serafina knew in an hour. The old man at the show. Mrs. Tong. Anyone who really looks knows.” She took a breath. “Nobody important’s bothered yet. One day somebody will. Somebody who wants that room. Then they come to the black door.”

She was shaking all over. She hadn’t known she would. She stood in the long room in front of the drawings with her fists closed and her whole body going, and she couldn’t make it stop.

“I’m frightened,” she said.

She’d never said that out loud in her life.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came across the room.

She put her hand up, flat on his chest, to stop him.

He stopped. Her hand was on his chest and she could feel his heart under it going as fast as hers.

“Don’t,” she said. “Don’t do the face. Don’t make a joke.”

“I’m not going to make a joke,” said Raiden.

He wasn’t. She’d never seen his face so serious, not on the back stairs of the gallery, not at his father’s door.

“I love it,” he said.

She stared at him.

“I’m not going to lie to you. Not about this. I love it. I love that room.” He put his hand over hers, on his chest. “A box nobody can open, inside a library, and nobody knows it’s there. Not the builders, not the guests, not Aurelia, not till the night she needs it. And somewhere in this city there’s a florist who went under her own tulips and shut a bolt and was safe, because of a floor I drew. That’s the best thing I’ve ever done.” His voice cracked. “I spent eleven hours in a box that wasn’t safe. That’s why I’m good at this. I’m not going to stop. I can’t.”

“I’m not asking you to stop.”

“Then what are you asking?”

She didn’t know.

She stood there with her hand on his chest and didn’t know, and that made her angrier than anything, and she grabbed a fistful of his shirt with the hand that was on his chest, and pulled.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came.

He kissed her as if he was angry too, hard, with his hands in her hair. She’d never felt that from him before. And she kissed him back the same way, and walked him backwards across the long room, not on purpose, toward the stairs, and they went down them, not on purpose either, one step at a time, banging into the wall, with his mouth on hers and her fists in his shirt.

“You left it by the window,” she said, against his mouth, on the fifth stair.

“I know.”

“Raiden.”

“I’ll get a safe,” he said. “For the drawings. A proper one. In the steel room. I’ll never leave them out again. I’ll never take them out of the firm. I’ll draw it all in my head and only put it on paper in a locked room with the light on.” He kissed her neck. “Is that what you want?”

“I want you not to be the key.”

“I can’t not be the key,” said Raiden. “Jia. I’m the key to everything I’ve ever drawn. That’s what drawing it means.” They’d got to the bottom of the stairs. Into the workshop, dark, with only the street light coming in through the gap under the roll-up door. “But I can be a key nobody can find. I’m good at that. I’ve been doing it since I was ten.”

“I found you.”

“You weren’t looking,” he said. “You nearly ran me over.”

She shoved him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He hit the bench.

Her bench. The long one under the windows, with the vice on the end. It shook. A tray of screws went over. He sat back against the edge of it, and she stood between his knees and looked at him in the street light.

“I’m still angry,” she said.

“I know. So am I.”

“What are you angry about?”

“That you’re right,” said Raiden. “That you’re always right. That you looked at sheet five for two minutes and saw the one thing I’ve been not thinking about for three months.” He put his hands on her waist. “And that you’re frightened. I hate that. I hate that I did that. I’d rather you threw a spanner at me.” He pulled her closer. “Can I tell you something you won’t like?”

“No.”

“You’re the key too,” said Raiden. “To me. Anyone who wanted me would only have to get to you. You’ve known that since the hospital. That’s why you made the rule. My side and your side. Not just because you don’t want to be owned. Because you know what being mine would make you.” He looked up at her. “So we’re both keys. And we’re both frightened, and we’re both rubbish at saying so.”

She looked down at him.

“I hate you,” she said.

“No, you don’t,” said Raiden. He stood up off the bench, lifted her, turned round and put her down on it.

“Tell me to stop and I’ll stop,” he said, with his hands on her knees and his mouth a breath from hers. “Tell me to stay and I’m not going back up those stairs till morning.”

“Stay,” she said. “Don’t you dare go up those stairs.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t finish the fight.

They tried. In the gaps. He said I’ll get the safe and she said you’ll forget and he said I never forget anything, I remember the colour of the shirt the lorry driver was wearing in 2008, and she said what colour and he said orange and she laughed, against her will, with her head back against the window and his mouth on her throat. She said you’ll tell me when you go up there and he said every time, and she said before, not after, and he stopped, and lifted his head, and said before, and meant it. The tray of screws went on the floor. Then the vice handle, which he caught with his elbow, and swore, and she laughed again.

It was rough and close and angry and then it wasn’t angry, it was just close, his forehead on hers in the dark and her hands on his back, and the bench creaking under both of them, and the street light coming in under the roll-up door in a long gold stripe across the concrete.

“We didn’t finish,” she said afterwards.

She was sitting on the bench in his shirt. He was standing between her knees with his face in her neck.

“We’ll finish tomorrow,” he said. “Or we won’t, and it’ll just get smaller.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He bought the safe that week.

A big grey one, bolted to the floor of the steel room behind the tool wall, with a code he didn’t tell her and then, on the third day, did, unasked, writing it on the back of her hand with his pencil: her birthday backwards. And he never left a drawing out again. Not one. He drew the Peak house at the firm, in the south, in a room with no windows, and on the days he went up to the Peak, he sent her a message before he left. Every time. Going up. Back by six. And at six, back.

She never answered the first one. She always answered the second.

Good.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Saturday in June he cooked fish.

He didn’t say anything during dinner. He kept looking at her across the long table and then looking at his plate. She knew the look. It was the napkin look. But there was no napkin. There was no pencil in his hand at all.

“Say it,” she said.

He put his chopsticks down.

“Elowen’s getting married,” he said.

“She’s already married.”

“Properly. Again. She and Zhao did it at a registry in 2020, on a Tuesday, in about four minutes, with nobody there. And Aurelia’s been angry about it for three years. So Aurelia’s organising a real one. In the flower shop. In September. The twenty-third. Every Lin. Every friend. My father.” He looked at his hands. “Everyone.”

She didn’t say anything.

“I’d like you to come,” he said.

There it was.

“Not to the Walled City,” said Raiden quickly. “The flower shop. In the old town. You’ve been past it. You’ve seen the window. It’s a shop. It’s just a shop, with tulips, and a floor I drew. Not the red door. Not inside. Just a room with flowers in it and my sisters and some chairs.” He looked up. “I’m asking. I’ve never asked. I’ve kept your rule for two years. I’ll keep it longer if you say no. I’ll go on my own and come home and tell you what was wrong with everyone. But I’m asking.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at him across the long table.

She thought about the red door. Her hand on it, cold, at two in the morning. One day. About Zhao behind his newspaper, in that flower shop, saying well done. About a woman she’d never met, Elowen, who had gone under her own tulips and shut a bolt and been safe. About Evangeline, the silent one, the paper twin, who Raiden talked about sometimes, in a voice that went strange. About how tired she was of being the thing he deleted one letter at a time.

About being frightened. About both of them being keys.

“What do I wear?” said Jinx.

He didn’t move.

He sat there at the long table with the fish going cold and looked at her, and she watched him understand, slowly, like a building coming out of fog.

“Whatever you want,” he said. His voice had gone. “The jacket. Anything. Your overalls. I don’t care. Jia. You’ll come?”

“I said what do I wear.”

He got up from the table so fast the chair went over.

He came round the table and pulled her up out of hers and held her so hard her feet came off the floor. And he said thank you into her hair, over and over, thank you, thank you, as if he’d been carrying something heavy a long way and had finally been allowed to put it down.

She stood in his arms in the long room and let him.

She thought: September.

She thought: I’m going to need a better dress.

chapters.title: Jinx Meets the Lin Family Properly
chapters.desc: September 2023. A flower shop, thirty people standing, a father in his funeral suit, and four sisters. “Jinx, my girlfriend, she built Xiao Pan’s bike, don’t touch her tools.” One very calm mechanic, and one very silent sister who nods.
chapters.epigraph: “You were the little girl under the bench. With the carburettor. I’ve always wondered what happened to you.” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
She bought the dress in August and didn’t wear it.

It was dark red, from the same shop in the Coastal High-Rise, the same woman, who looked at her shoulders and nodded and went into the back without being asked. It was simple and fitted her like her own skin. She tried it on at the long mirror Raiden had put in the bathroom and looked at herself in it for a while, then took it off and hung it up and didn’t look at it again for a month.

On the morning of the twenty-third she put it on at five, and then her boots, and then the old jacket with the burn on the cuff.

He was sitting on the edge of the bed in his silver waistcoat, the gear one, doing up his shoes. He looked up.

“The old one,” he said.

“It’s the one I came to the hospital in.”

He didn’t say anything for a moment. Then he stood up and came and did up the zip for her, the one that only went up if you held your breath, and she held her breath, and he kissed her forehead.

“Perfect,” he said. “You look like you might fix something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went in a taxi, because she wasn’t going to turn up to his sister’s wedding in a sidecar, and because her hands were shaking and she didn’t trust them on the bars.

He held one of them the whole way. He didn’t talk. That was how she knew he was frightened too.

The flower shop was in the old town, on a corner, with a big window full of flowers and the name over the door in plain letters: ELOWEN’S. She’d been past it a hundred times on the bike, slowly, and never stopped.

It was eight in the morning. The door was open. There was an arch over it, inside, made of old dark timber with the marks of bolts still in it, and lights strung across the ceiling, tiny ones, thousands of them, not on yet. White roses in buckets. Tulips. People.

Thirty people, standing.

She stopped on the step.

He stopped with her. He didn’t pull her. He stood beside her on the step of his sister’s shop with her hand in his, and waited, and she felt him decide something.

He let go of her hand and put his arm round her waist instead, and walked her in.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Everyone,” said Raiden.

He said it loud, in the silly voice he used at parties, and thirty heads turned round.

“This is Jinx,” he said. “My girlfriend. She built Xiao Pan’s bike. Don’t touch her tools.”

There was a silence.

She stood in the doorway with his arm round her and thirty people looking at her. She looked back. She did the thing she’d done at the gala, the one he liked: she looked at each of them until they looked away first.

Most of them did.

Not all.

There was a big grey man by the cooler, in an old black suit that was too tight across the back, with his hands clasped in front of him. He didn’t look away. He looked at her, frowning, as if he were trying to remember something. She knew who he was. She’d known since she was nine.

There was a woman by the counter in gold, beautiful, with her hair up, who looked at her from her boots to her hair and back down again, slowly, the way Jinx looked at a frame she was thinking of buying. She didn’t look away either. She gave a small smile, as if she’d found something interesting.

And there was a woman at the back of the shop, alone, by the wall, in pale blue. She was tall and still, with a face like something carved and long black hair in a knot.

She didn’t look away. She didn’t look at anyone else. She looked at Jinx across the whole length of the shop, across the buckets and the tulips and the thirty people, with no expression at all.

And then she nodded. Once.

Jinx nodded back.

She didn’t know why. She didn’t know the woman. She knew who she was, because Raiden talked about her, in the voice that went strange. Evangeline. The paper twin. The one who didn’t talk. And she stood there in the doorway of the flower shop and looked at the woman in pale blue at the back, and the woman looked at her, and something went between them, the way it went between two people at a race who both know exactly what the other’s bike is doing under them.

You too, it said. You’re the one in the room who’s watching the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao was there. In black, by the arch, with a flower in his lapel that was made of sugar. He looked at her for four seconds.

“Hm,” he said.

“Hm,” said Jinx.

Beside her, Raiden made a noise that he turned into a cough.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen got her at the cooler, twenty minutes later.

Jinx had been backed into the corner by the big glass-fronted fridge, where the roses were kept cold, by a series of people being introduced to her. A man who’d flown up from the hills with tea. A detective in a plain coat who looked at her hands. Two dogs with ribbons, who sniffed her boots and lay down on them. A young woman in a hoodie with a laptop, who said, “I’m Eliana, I’m the youngest, I’ve known about you since February 2022, you’re on a spreadsheet,” and walked off. A small fierce woman in a doctor’s lanyard who said, “Elara. I’m a surgeon. Are those burns from an exhaust? You should use silicone gel,” and then saw a tall young man in glasses across the room and forgot her completely.

And then the crowd moved, and Elowen was there.

She was in green. She was calm and sharp and beautiful, with pearls in her ears, and she looked at Jinx with eyes like Raiden’s, exactly like his, and nothing like his at all.

“How long?” said Elowen.

“Two years and four months.”

Elowen’s face didn’t change. Jinx was starting to understand that nobody’s face in this family changed unless they wanted it to.

“Two years,” said Elowen. “And he never said a word. He came to Sunday dinner every week. He brought me a shelf.” She looked across the shop at her brother, who was being hugged by the man with the tea. “I thought he was lonely. I used to worry about him. I used to lie awake.”

“He wanted to tell you,” said Jinx. “I made him not. It was my rule.”

Elowen looked at her.

“Why?”

“Because I grew up in a chop shop under the flyover,” said Jinx. “My father’s buyers bought from your father’s people. When I was nine I saw your father’s car come down the lane, and every man in the shop stood up.” She didn’t drop her eyes. “He kept it because I asked. He never once broke it.”

Elowen was quiet.

Then she turned her head and looked across the shop at her husband. Zhao was by the arch, with his hands in his pockets. He felt her looking. Jinx saw his shoulders move.

“Zhendong knew,” said Elowen. It wasn’t a question.

“Since the hospital.”

Elowen’s eyebrows went up.

“He took my jacket,” said Jinx. “Off the chair. Before you turned round.”

Elowen shut her eyes. When she opened them, there was something in them that Jinx recognised, because she’d seen it in the mirror every time Raiden bought her something she hadn’t asked for. It was fury, and love, and the fury losing.

“I’m going to kill him,” said Elowen calmly. “After the wedding.” She looked back at Jinx. “Thank you for Xiao Pan’s bike. He cried when he first rode it. He told me. He made me promise not to tell you.”

“I know,” said Jinx. “I saw.”

Elowen looked at her for a moment more. Then she reached out and, lightly, straightened the collar of the old jacket, where it had turned under at the back.

“It suits you,” she said. “Don’t let Aurelia buy you a new one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Jian found her last.

She’d gone out onto the step for air. The wedding was over: twenty seconds down an aisle four metres long, and a question about a lemon tree that she hadn’t understood and that had made Zhao Zhendong cry in front of thirty people, and Elowen too, and then everyone. The lights had come on at nine forty-one, all of them at once, and Eliana had refused to say why. There was cake. There was champagne in paper cups. There was a lot of noise.

She stood on the step with a paper cup she wasn’t drinking from and looked at the street, and the big grey man came out of the shop behind her and stood beside her.

He didn’t say anything for a while.

She’d been frightened of him since she was nine. She stood beside him on the step and waited to be frightened. He was big. Bigger than her father. Grey-haired, heavy, in a suit too tight across the back, with his hands in his pockets and his eyes red from crying at his daughter’s wedding.

“You were the little girl under the bench,” said Lin Jian.

She turned her head.

“At Old Cao’s,” he said. “Under the flyover. I went there once. In 2005, maybe 2006. About a debt. And there was a little girl under the bench in the office, on the floor, with a carburettor in pieces on a newspaper. Tiny, with a screwdriver bigger than her hand. And while I talked to her father, she put it back together. All of it. In ten minutes. I watched her.” He was quiet. “I’ve always wondered what happened to you.”

She stood still.

“I asked your father,” said Lin Jian. “When I left. I said, who’s the child? And he said mine. And I said, she’ll be better than all of us. And he laughed. I didn’t laugh.” He looked at the street. “I was right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She couldn’t say anything. She stood on the step of the flower shop with the paper cup in her hand and thought about the black car, and the man in the dark coat, and her father’s hands flat on the desk for an hour afterwards, not saying anything. And she’d thought, for eighteen years, that it was fear. That her father had sat there frightened.

Maybe it was. Maybe it was something else. She’d never asked.

“Does he eat?” said Lin Jian. “My son. He never ate, when he came home. He was so thin. The cook used to chase him round the kitchen.”

“He cooks,” said Jinx.

Lin Jian turned his head and looked at her.

“Every night,” she said. “Soup. Fish. Dumplings. He makes his own noodles with a wine bottle. He takes the bones out of my fish. He washes my overalls.” She stopped. “He eats. He eats my greens.”

The big grey man looked at her.

Then he laughed.

It was a big rusty sound, as if it hadn’t been used in years, and it went right down the street, and an old woman across the road looked out of her window. He laughed with his head back and his hands in his pockets on the step of his daughter’s shop, and then he stopped, and wiped his eyes, and looked at her again.

“Ah Sim taught him,” he said. “The cook. He used to sit on the kitchen step. Every day. He’d come home from the borderland with nothing, and the only person in the house he’d sit with was the cook.” He shook his head. “I didn’t know he’d kept it.”

“He kept everything,” said Jinx.

“Yes,” said Lin Jian. “He would.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t ask her anything else.

He didn’t ask about her father, or the shop, or the debt from 2005, or why she’d never come to the Walled City. He stood beside her on the step for a while longer, a big grey frightening man who wasn’t frightening at all, and then he went back inside, to his daughter, and his son, and the cake.

At the door he stopped.

“Come on Sunday,” he said, without turning round. “For dinner. Or don’t. Either. The door’s red. He’ll show you.”

“I’ve seen it,” said Jinx.

Lin Jian looked back at her over his shoulder.

“He showed me,” she said. “In January. At two in the morning. I stood on the step.”

Something went across his face. She didn’t know what it was. Then he nodded, once, slowly, the way Evangeline had, and went inside.

✦ ✦ ✦

The party went on all day and into the night.

It moved, at some point, from the shop to a restaurant down the street, and back to the shop, and out onto the pavement, and somebody brought a guitar. The lights stayed on. The dogs fell asleep on the doormat. Aurelia made a speech that was mostly about Elowen being wrong about everything for ten years, and Elowen made a speech back that was mostly about Aurelia, and their husbands spoiled it for both of them by standing up at the same moment and saying the same word, mine, and sitting down again.

Jinx stood at the back by the wall with her paper cup and watched it.

Evangeline was beside her. She hadn’t moved since about eleven. They hadn’t said a word to each other. They stood side by side against the wall at the back of the shop in pale blue and dark red, watching the door, and every so often Evangeline’s eyes went to the window, to the roof of the building across the street, and stayed there, and came back.

Jinx didn’t ask.

At one in the morning, Raiden found her there, and put his forehead down on her shoulder, and left it there.

“Was it all right?” he said into the jacket. “Was it terrible? Was it too much? You can tell me. You can tell me what was wrong with everyone.”

She thought about it.

“Your father laughed,” she said.

He lifted his head.

“On the step,” she said. “I told him you cook. He laughed so loud a woman across the road looked out of her window.”

Raiden stared at her.

“He doesn’t laugh,” he said. “He hasn’t laughed since—I don’t know. I don’t remember him laughing.”

“He laughed.”

He stood there in front of her, in his silver waistcoat, at one in the morning in his sister’s flower shop, with the lights on over his head, trying not to cry and not managing.

Beside her, Evangeline turned her head and looked at her brother, then at Jinx, then back at the door.

But the corner of her mouth had moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went home at three in a taxi.

He didn’t fall asleep straight away. At the first red light he turned on the back seat and kissed her, slowly, with his hand on her jaw, as if he’d been saving it all day in front of thirty people. And at the second. And at the third, until the driver said the lights are green, sir, and he said I know, and didn’t stop.

He fell asleep on her shoulder before the harbour bridge, with his mouth open, in his waistcoat, holding her hand. She looked out at the water and the city going past and thought: that was all right. They were just people. Thirty people standing in a flower shop, and a father who laughed, and a sister who nodded.

She didn’t wake him when they got to the black door. She paid the taxi and got him out, mostly asleep, and up the stairs and onto the bed in his clothes. When she took his shoes off and undid the waistcoat, he opened one eye and said, “Jia. You came,” exactly the way he’d said it on the stretcher on the Docks road, and went back to sleep.

She lay down beside him in the dark red dress and the old jacket and didn’t take either of them off.

chapters.title: Her Father Calls After Five Years
chapters.desc: November 2023. A secret car built at night for a friend, a man who comes down at two in the morning and asks nothing. Then a phone call from under the flyover, a photograph of an old camp bed, and a note on the bench.
chapters.epigraph: “Gone to see my father. Don’t come. Back tomorrow.” — a note on the bench, in biro, on the back of an invoice
chapters.content:
For five weeks that autumn she built a car at night and didn’t tell him.

It wasn’t her secret to tell. Serafina had come to the black door on the third Saturday in September with a man standing behind her in the doorway, a quiet man in a dark jacket who looked like nothing at all and who stood, she noticed at once, the way the men who’d worked for the Walled City used to stand outside her father’s shop. Serafina had said you owe me for the gearbox. And Jinx had said one order, no questions. That was her rule. She’d had it since she opened the black door. She built what you asked for and she didn’t want to know where you were going.

So she didn’t tell Raiden either.

She told him she had a big job on, a customer’s car, which was true. And every night after dinner she went downstairs and pulled the roll-up door down and turned the lights on, and Serafina came, and the quiet man, and after the first week a girl with two laptops and a soldering iron, and they worked on a grey old Toyota estate that looked like a taxi company’s reject until two or three in the morning. Then she came up the stairs and got into bed, and he turned over in his sleep and put his arm round her and didn’t ask.

On the fourth Saturday, at two in the morning, he came down.

She heard him on the stairs. She looked up from under the bonnet. Serafina froze. The quiet man didn’t move at all, which was worse.

Raiden stood at the bottom of the stairs in his shorts and a jumper with his sketchbook under his arm and looked at the car, at Serafina, at the quiet man, at the girl with the laptops in the passenger seat, who’d stopped soldering.

He didn’t say anything.

He sat down on the bottom stair and opened the sketchbook and drew the car, every bolt and spring, in fine pencil lines, the way he’d drawn her bike in 2021. It took him forty minutes. When he’d finished, he tore it out, and got up, and gave it to the quiet man, who took it and looked at it without a word.

Then he went back upstairs to bed.

In the morning he made her eggs with tomato and didn’t mention it. He never did.

She stood at the long table watching him slide the eggs onto her plate and felt something in her chest she didn’t have a word for.

“Thank you,” she said.

“For what?” said Raiden, and kissed the top of her head, and went to his drawing table.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car was finished in October.

It went under a cover in the back of the sailmaker’s, beside the dyno, where nobody looked, and it stayed there. Serafina came once a week to start it and listen to it and go away again. And Jinx pulled the roll-up door down after her every time and stood in the workshop for a while with her hand on the cover.

She had a bad feeling. She didn’t know what it was. She’d had it since the flower shop.

People had talked. That was what she thought, afterwards. Thirty people in a flower shop, and then a restaurant, and then a street, and a guitar. The Lin boy’s girlfriend. A mechanic from the Docks. Built a boy’s bike. Tattoos to the shoulders. Old Cao’s girl, from under the flyover. Lin Jian laughed on the step.

People had talked, and somebody had listened.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father rang on a Tuesday in the middle of November.

It was half past four in the afternoon. She was at the bench with a set of carburettors in pieces on a rag, and Raiden was out, in the south, at the firm, and the landline rang. The old black phone on the wall by the door that nobody ever called, because it was the number that had been on the rope company’s letterhead and nobody had changed it.

She picked it up.

“Jia,” said her father.

She stood still with the phone in her hand.

Five years and eleven days. She hadn’t heard his voice since the night she left, when he’d stood in the yard under the flyover with his hands hanging at his sides and watched her load the lathe into the van and said you’ll come back, and she’d said no, and driven away.

His voice was older, thicker, as if something had been sitting on his chest.

“How did you get this number?” she said.

“It was in the paper. Under the bike. The newspaper, at the noodle shop. Somebody brought it to the shop.” He breathed. “Best in Show. I saw it.”

She didn’t say anything.

“Jia,” said her father. “I need you to come.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her.

Badly. In pieces. With long silences in between that she could hear the flyover in. She’d always been able to hear the flyover in his silences; it was the sound of her whole childhood, the trucks going over, the concrete humming.

The Syndicate’s people didn’t come to the shop any more. Not since the spring. Something had happened, in the Walled City, at the top, and the old men who used to buy from him had stopped buying, and the protection that came with them had stopped too. And then a crew had come. A new one. From the other side of the Slums. A man called Guo.

Guo had bought his debts.

“What debts?” she said.

There was a long silence.

“The shop,” said her father. “The rent, since the spring. The parts. Some money I borrowed. In the summer. For the roof.” Another silence. “And some I lost. At cards. In the back of the place on the corner.”

She shut her eyes.

“How much?”

He told her.

It was more than he’d ever see. It wasn’t a lot for her. She could have paid it from the money in the tin under the bench, nearly. She opened her mouth to say so.

“He doesn’t want money,” said her father.

✦ ✦ ✦

Guo wanted bikes.

Twelve of them. Built from what came through the shop. Stolen parts, stolen frames, built up into whole bikes with new numbers and new papers, the kind that went out to buyers who didn’t ask. Good ones. Fast ones. The kind that only one person under the flyover had ever been able to build well enough that nobody ever caught them.

“He knows about you,” said her father. “He knows what they called you. At the shop. Somebody told him. He says if Jinx builds him twelve bikes, the debt’s gone. And if not—”

He stopped.

“If not what?”

“He’s been here,” said her father. “Every night. Him and his men. They sleep here. In the office. On your—” He stopped again. “On the camp bed. Yours. I kept it. I never took it down.”

She stood by the black door with the phone in her hand and her whole body gone cold.

“Jia,” said her father. “Please. Come. Just come and talk to him. Just once. I’m sixty-one. I can’t—they’ll take the shop. They’ll take—” His voice broke. She’d never heard it break. “Please. You’re the only one he wants.”

“No,” she said.

She put the phone down.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood there.

Then she went back to the bench and picked up the carburettor and looked at it and couldn’t remember what she’d been doing to it.

Her mobile buzzed in her pocket.

She took it out. A message from a number she didn’t know. No words, just a photograph.

It was the office at the shop. She’d have known it anywhere. The little square window with the wire in the glass. The desk where her father wrote in his book. The lamp, yellow. And under the window, against the wall, the camp bed. Hers. Green canvas, with the rusted frame and the burn on the corner where she’d put a soldering iron down when she was eleven. Somebody had been sleeping in it. The blanket was thrown back.

And on the pillow, pinned to it with a screwdriver driven through it into the canvas, there was a photograph.

Raiden.

On the step of the flower shop in the old town. In his silver waistcoat. Laughing. With his arm round a woman in an old leather jacket whose face had been scratched out of the picture with something sharp.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember sitting down.

She was on the floor with her back against the leg of the bench and the phone in her hand and the carburettor in pieces above her on the rag. She was looking at the photograph. She couldn’t stop looking at it. At the screwdriver, driven through his laughing face into the pillow she’d slept on until she was twenty-two.

Everyone he loves is something somebody else can take.

He’d said that. On the thirty-first floor, in June 2021, with his arm in plaster. I wanted to keep you out of it. I wanted you to be mine and nobody else’s business.

She’d said I can stand in front of myself.

She’d been so sure the danger was the Walled City. The Lins. Being his. That if she kept her side and his side, and never walked through the red door, she’d be safe, and so would he.

It had been her side all along. Her father, her shop, her old camp bed under the flyover. She’d walked into the flower shop in her old jacket and let thirty people see who she was, and someone from under the flyover had heard about it, and now there was a screwdriver through his face.

She was the key. He’d told her. On the bench, in June. You’re the key too. Anyone who wanted me would only have to get to you.

She hadn’t believed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got up.

She put the carburettor back together. She did it slowly, with her hands, by feel, every jet and screw and float, because her hands needed something to do and it was the only way she’d ever known to think. She put it on the shelf.

Then she went upstairs and changed into her overalls and her boots and her old jacket, and came back down, and went to the tool wall, and stood in front of it.

She didn’t open the steel room. She didn’t need anything from it.

She took down the thirteen, a set of picks, her good screwdrivers in their roll and a torque wrench, and put them in her bag, the one she’d left the shop with five years ago and never used since.

She was going to go and talk to Guo.

She was going to go on her own. On Thursday. When Raiden was in the south, at the firm, all day, the way he was every Thursday. She was going to go to the shop under the flyover where she’d learned engines before letters, and find out exactly what Guo wanted, and give it to him, or not, and come back, and he’d never have to know there’d ever been a screwdriver through his face.

I wanted to keep you out of it.

Standing in her workshop in front of the tool wall with her bag on her shoulder, she thought of the linen room, and the service lift, and go before they see you. She’d thought he was ashamed. He’d been doing this: standing between someone he loved and the people who’d use them, and deciding, alone, that he’d rather go out the back than let them see.

She’d hated him for it, for three weeks, in 2021.

She was going to do it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home at seven with the shopping.

She’d put the bag under the bench. She’d put the phone in a drawer. She was at the stove when he came up the stairs, which never happened, frying eggs, badly.

He stopped at the top of the stairs.

“You’re cooking,” he said.

“Eggs.”

He put the shopping down. He came and stood beside her and looked into the pan, at the eggs, which were burnt at the edges and raw in the middle.

“Jia,” he said. “What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

He didn’t say anything.

She could feel him looking at her the way he looked at buildings, at a crack where gold met marble, and she knew he could see something. She’d never been able to hide anything from him; she’d never tried. She stood there with the spatula in her hand and her face doing nothing at all and knew that he was seeing her do exactly what he’d done on the gallery stairs, and at the hospital, and on the morning of the Docks road, and every day for thirteen years before he met her.

He didn’t ask.

He took the spatula out of her hand and turned off the gas, and put the eggs in the bin. And then he put his arms round her from behind, at the stove, and his chin on her shoulder, and held on.

“I’m here,” he said. “Whatever it is. When you want. Or never.”

She stood in his arms and didn’t tell him.

It was the worst thing she’d ever done.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday he went to the firm at eight.

She stood on the step and watched the taxi go up the street. She’d kissed him goodbye at the door. She’d kissed him so long he’d said what’s that for and she’d said nothing and he’d looked at her, and then got in the taxi, and turned round in the back seat to look at her through the rear window until it went round the corner.

She went back inside.

She’d made him promise, in June. On the bench. You’ll tell me before you go up there. Before, not after. And he’d said before, and meant it, and he’d done it every single time. Going up. Back by six.

She took an invoice off the pile on the bench, and turned it over, and found a biro.

She wrote it in capitals, because her handwriting was bad.

GONE TO SEE MY FATHER. DON’T COME. BACK TOMORROW. J.

She put it on the bench, under the thirteen’s empty hook, where he’d see it the moment he came in.

Then she put the bag on her shoulder and went out to the black bike and rode north, toward the flyovers, at exactly the speed limit, the whole way.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home at half past four.

He’d left the firm early. He didn’t know why. He’d sat at his desk in the south all morning drawing a staircase and getting the risers wrong, and at two o’clock he’d put his pencil down and thought, I have to go home, and got a taxi.

The roll-up door was down. The black bike was gone.

He went in through the side door. The workshop was dark and cold and tidy. Too tidy. She never left it tidy.

He saw the note.

He stood in front of the bench and read it, in the grey light from the side door. GONE TO SEE MY FATHER. DON’T COME. BACK TOMORROW. J.

He read it three times.

He looked up at the tool wall. At the empty hook between the twelve and the fourteen.

He thought about her at the stove on Tuesday, burning eggs, with her face doing nothing at all. About the way she’d kissed him at the door that morning. About a roof across the road from a shop under the flyover, in August 2021, and her sitting on the edge of it with her boots over the drop, saying something happened, when I was seventeen. I’m not telling you that one. And her father in the little square window with the wire in the glass, writing in his book. He didn’t stop it. I can see it from here.

He didn’t sit down. He didn’t ring anyone.

He went upstairs, to his drawing table by the window, and opened the long flat drawer at the bottom that he never opened, and took out a roll of paper, and unrolled it on the table, and weighted the corners with her washers.

It was the map.

The one he’d drawn on the night of the roof, in August 2021, at her kitchen table under the bare bulb, until two in the morning. Every street under the flyovers, every lane and alley and fire escape and gap in a fence. And on top of it, added over two years of spare evenings she’d never known about, everything else: the plans of every building in the Slums of the Industry that the city archive had ever filed, which was most of them. The walls, the stairs, the drains under the lanes, which roofs joined and which didn’t.

And at the end of a lane under the lowest flyover, a long low building with three roll-up doors and a little square window in the side.

He looked at it.

Don’t come.

Not this time, he thought.

He rolled it up, and put it inside his jacket, and went down the stairs two at a time.

chapters.title: The Men Who Own Her Father
chapters.desc: Under the flyover, a polite man with reading glasses, a debt in stolen bikes, and a dead brother’s motorbike that hasn’t run in nine years. Then the useless Lin boy wanders in through the yard with a bag of dumplings, completely lost, with a floor plan in his jacket.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m terribly sorry. I think I’m lost. Is this the right flyover?” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
Nothing had changed under the flyover except her father.

The lane was the same: the pillars going down into the ground, the orange lights that never went off because the sun never got in, the three roll-up doors, all up, and the sign, CAO MOTOR REPAIR, and the bikes on the pavement outside. The noise of the trucks overhead, which you stopped hearing after a day and started hearing again the moment you’d been away.

He was standing in the middle door.

He’d seen the bike coming down the lane. He was standing in the doorway with his hands hanging at his sides, the way he’d stood in the yard the night she left, and she stopped the bike in front of him and turned it off and took her helmet off and looked at him.

He was old.

That was all she could think. Five years, and he’d got old. His hair had gone from grey to white. His shoulders had come forward. His big hands, which she remembered on everything, on every engine, on her head once, when she was small, were thick and spotted and shook a little at his sides. He looked at her, and his mouth worked, and he said, “Jia,” the way he’d said it on the phone.

“Where is he?” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Guo was in the office.

In her father’s chair, at her father’s desk, under the little square window with the wire in the glass. A thin man, in his fifties, in a grey shirt buttoned to the neck and a pair of reading glasses, drinking tea out of one of her father’s chipped cups. He looked like an accountant. He looked like the man who came on a scooter for the rent.

There were two men behind him. One big, with a scar through his eyebrow, standing by the door. One small, sitting on her camp bed with his boots on the green canvas, by the soldering-iron burn.

Guo put down the cup.

“Miss Cao,” he said. “Or Jinx. Which do you prefer?”

She didn’t answer.

“Jinx, then.” He smiled. It was a nice smile. “Sit down. Have some tea. Your father’s tea is terrible, but it’s hot.”

“I’ll stand.”

“As you like.” He folded his hands on the desk. “I’m so glad you came. Your father was worried you wouldn’t. I told him not to be. I said, a woman who builds a bike for a boy with burnt hands and doesn’t charge him isn’t going to let her own father lose his shop. That’s what I heard about you. That you’re good to people.” He looked at her over his glasses. “It’s a weakness, you know. In business.”

She looked at the man on her camp bed.

“Get off that,” she said.

The man looked at Guo. Guo made a small movement with one finger. The man got up and stood by the wall.

“There,” said Guo. “We can be civilised.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He wanted what her father had said. Twelve bikes. From what came through the yard. Built well enough that they’d never be traced.

“And then?” she said.

“And then twelve more,” said Guo, pleasantly. “I won’t lie to you. There’s a great deal of money in this, if it’s done properly. And nobody’s done it properly under this flyover since you left. Your father’s very good, but he’s old, and his hands shake, and the last three bikes he built for me were found by the police in a week.” He took his glasses off and polished them on his shirt. “You were bad luck for the police. That’s what they told me. Every bike you touched got away clean. I’d like some of that luck.”

“I don’t do that any more.”

“I know. You build beautiful bikes for rich men in a garage near the Docks. I saw it in the newspaper. Best in Show.” He put the glasses back on. “And you have a boyfriend. A rich one. With a famous father. I saw that too.” He reached into his shirt pocket and took out a photograph and put it on the desk between them, face up.

The flower shop. The step. Raiden laughing, in his silver waistcoat. Her face scratched out.

“Such a happy boy,” said Guo. “Everybody says so. Not very bright, they say. But happy.”

She stood in her father’s office, where she’d slept on a camp bed until she was twenty-two, and looked at the photograph, and didn’t move. She’d learned that at the shop too. Before reading. The men who moved first were the men who lost.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I won’t build you twelve bikes,” she said.

Guo looked at her.

“I’ll build you one,” said Jinx. “Tonight. Something nobody else can. And when it’s done, the debt’s gone. My father’s free. You never come back to this shop. And you never, ever say his name.” She put her finger on the photograph, on Raiden’s laughing face. “Or look at this again.”

There was a silence.

The man with the scar shifted his weight by the door. Out in the yard, somebody dropped a spanner.

Guo looked at her for a while over his glasses. Then he smiled. A different smile. Interested.

“One bike,” he said.

“One.”

“Something nobody else can.” He thought about it. Then he got up, slowly, and came round the desk, and went past her, close, smelling of tea and soap. “Come with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a bike in the back of the yard.

Under a tarpaulin. In the corner by the wall, where the scrap went, where she’d never been allowed to go as a child because of the rats. Guo pulled the tarpaulin off himself, and stood back, and she looked at it, and her stomach went over.

It was a Kawasaki. An old one. A 750, from the seventies, a two-stroke triple, three cylinders side by side, with three chrome exhaust pipes coming out of the back like the barrels of a gun. One of the fastest, most dangerous bikes anyone had ever built. They’d called it a widowmaker, when it was new. It was blue, or had been. It was covered in dust and rust and pigeon droppings, and the tyres were flat and split, and there was a dead leaf in the air box.

“My brother’s,” said Guo.

His voice had changed a little.

“He bought it in 1989,” he said. “He rode it for twenty years. He loved it more than his wife. Then he died. Not on it. In a hospital, of something boring, in 2014. And it’s been sitting here ever since. Nine years. Your father said he’d fix it, in 2015, for nothing, as a favour, and he put it in the corner and never touched it.” He looked at her. “The engine’s seized. It’s been seized since 2016.
