Every mechanic I’ve taken it to says it’s finished. The pistons are rusted into the barrels. They say I’d need a new engine, and there aren’t any, and I’d be better off selling it for parts.”

He put his hand on the tank, lightly, on the dust.

“Make it run,” said Guo. “By morning. By six. If I can start it and ride it once round this yard, the debt’s gone. Your father’s free. I’ll go away and you’ll never see me again.” He took his hand off the tank. “If not, you build me twelve. And then twelve more. And I keep the photograph.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She crouched down by the engine.

She didn’t touch it. She looked at the three barrels, their cooling fins rusty and packed with dirt, and the heads, and the three carburettors behind them, crusted green. The ignition cover, the oil pump, the flat tyres. The chain had rusted solid in a curve, like something fossilised.

She thought about how long it would take to do it properly. A week. Two. In a clean workshop, with the right parts, and the dyno, and nobody watching.

She thought about the photograph with the screwdriver through it.

“Have you got parts?” she said.

“My brother kept everything. There’s a box.” Guo nodded at the office. “Rings. Gaskets. Seals. Plugs. He bought them in 2013, for a rebuild he never did.”

“I’ll need my father’s tools. And the light. And nobody in the yard.”

“You’ll have Dou,” said Guo. The man with the scar. “He’ll be by the door. All night. In case you have any ideas about leaving.” He smiled, and went back toward the office. “Six o’clock, Miss Jinx. I’ll bring tea.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She started at three in the afternoon.

She dragged the bike out into the middle of the yard under the big lamp, on its wheels, which were flat, with the rims scraping. She put it on a stand. She got her father’s tools from the shop, his big tool chest with the red drawers, which hadn’t changed either, every tool in the same drawer it had been in when she was five. Her father stood in the doorway of the shop and watched her and didn’t come out.

She took the heads off.

All three. It took an hour, because the nuts were rusted and she had to heat them with the torch, one at a time, and tap them, and wait. And under the heads, the tops of the pistons, in the barrels, brown and rough and fused. She put a wooden block on the first one and hit it with a mallet, gently. Nothing. Harder. Nothing.

She soaked them. She filled the tops of all three barrels with penetrating oil and left it to go down past the rings, into the rust, and went and sat on an oil drum in the yard and looked at the bike while it worked.

Dou stood by the door with his arms folded and watched her.

At six, she heated the first barrel. Not too much. Too much and the aluminium would go. Just enough that the barrel grew and the piston didn’t, and there was a gap, a hair’s width. She put the wooden block on the piston and hit it, once, hard, and it moved.

A millimetre. She felt it in the mallet before she saw it.

She sat back on her heels in the yard under the lamp and breathed.

✦ ✦ ✦

By nine she had the barrels off.

All three. She’d freed every piston, one by one, with heat and wood and patience, and slid the barrels up off them, and there they were, three pistons on their rods, sitting on the crank, rusted, scored, ugly. And the bores, inside the barrels, brown with rust, but not cracked. She held each one up to the lamp and looked through it and turned it and looked again.

She could hone them. She could clean them and hone them and put new rings on the pistons from the dead brother’s box, and if the crank seals were all right, and the crank was all right, and the ignition was all right, and the three carburettors would clean up, and the oil pump would pump—

That was a lot of ifs.

She put the first barrel in the vice and started to hone it.

It was dark under the flyover. It was always dark. But it got darker. The orange lights on the pillars buzzed. The trucks went over. Her father had gone inside, into the office, and she could see him through the little square window, at his desk, with the lamp on, not writing anything. Just sitting. Guo had gone somewhere. The small man had gone with him. Dou stood by the door.

She honed the first bore and held it up to the light and it was clean. Grey. Cross-hatched, the way it should be. She put it down carefully on a clean rag.

At ten, she started the second one, and heard a voice in the lane.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a cheerful voice.

It was coming down the lane from the far end, by the noodle factory, loud, uncertain, the voice of a man who’d taken several wrong turnings and was trying to make the best of it.

“Hello?” it said. “Hello? Sorry. Excuse me. Is this—is this the right flyover? There are rather a lot of them. I’ve been under three.”

Her hands stopped on the hone.

Dou turned round in the doorway.

And round the corner of the yard, past the scrap heap, from the one direction nobody came from, where there was no gate and no lane and only a gap behind the heap between the wall and the pillar that she’d squeezed through every day of her childhood and had thought nobody else in the world knew about, came Raiden.

In his good grey trousers. In the clean brown shoes, which weren’t clean any more. With his hair everywhere and a smear of something on his cheek and a paper bag in one hand that said Mrs. Tong’s on the side.

He stopped in the middle of the yard under the lamp and looked round, at the bikes, at the pillars, at the scrap, with his mouth open, as if he’d wandered into a cathedral.

“Oh,” he said. “Oh, there you are.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dou had a knife.

She saw it come out of his jacket, short, and turn in his hand, and she was on her feet with the hone still in her fist. Raiden looked at Dou and the knife and smiled the silly smile he wore for rooms full of strangers, enormous and bright and stupid.

“Oh, hello,” he said. “I’m so sorry. I’m the boyfriend. I’m lost. Well, I’m not lost now, I’ve found her, but I was lost. I got the bus. Two buses. I’ve never been on two buses.” He held up the paper bag. “I brought dumplings. She didn’t have dinner. She never has dinner when she’s working. Would you like one? They’re pork.”

Dou looked at him.

He looked at the paper bag, the brown shoes, the waistcoat under the jacket, the face. Jinx watched him look, and watched him decide, the way everyone always decided, in about two seconds: the useless one. The happy one. Not very bright.

The knife went down. Not away. Down.

“How did you get in?” said Dou.

“Through there,” said Raiden, pointing vaguely behind him at the scrap heap. “There’s a sort of—gap. I think a cat showed me. There was a cat.” He beamed. “Is she in trouble? She left a note. She said don’t come. But she always says that. She said it about the dumplings.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Guo came out of the office.

He’d heard. He came out into the yard drying his hands on a handkerchief and stood in the doorway and looked at Raiden standing under the lamp with his paper bag, and Jinx saw his face, and saw him understand who it was, and saw him smile.

“Mr. Lin,” said Guo.

“Hello!” said Raiden. “Do I know you? I’m terribly sorry. I meet so many people. Was it a party? I’m awful with faces.”

“We haven’t met,” said Guo. He came across the yard. He looked at Raiden from very close, the way he’d looked at Jinx in the office, over his glasses. “But I’ve seen your photograph.”

“Oh, the newspaper?” said Raiden. “That was her, really. I was just holding the trophy.”

Guo laughed.

It was a real laugh. Delighted. He looked at Raiden, and then at Jinx, with the hone in her fist by the vice, and back at Raiden, and laughed again, and put the handkerchief in his pocket.

“Well,” he said. “Well, well. You came all this way. On two buses. To bring your girlfriend dumplings.” He shook his head. “You’re very welcome, Mr. Lin. Please. Stay. Stay as long as you like.” He turned to Dou. “Get Mr. Lin a chair. He’s our guest.”

He went back to the office. At the door, he looked back at Jinx over his shoulder, and she knew what the look meant.

Now I’ve got both of you.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden sat down on the oil drum.

He put the paper bag down beside her on the bench, by the vice, and took out a carton, and took the lid off, and put chopsticks beside it, split, and the little packet of chilli oil, opened. He did it neatly and quickly, the way he had on the first day in her garage.

Dou went back to the door with the knife, and stood there.

She looked down at Raiden.

“I said don’t come,” she said. Her voice was low and shaking. She didn’t know if it was fury. “I wrote it. In capitals.”

“I know,” said Raiden. He didn’t look up from the carton. He was smiling his silly smile still, for Dou, by the door. But his voice, low, just for her, wasn’t silly at all. “You also wrote it on the back of an invoice for a clutch you haven’t charged for. And you left the thirteen’s hook empty. And you burned eggs on Tuesday.” He held out the chopsticks. “Have something. You’ll need your hands.”

She took them.

She didn’t eat.

“How did you find the gap?” she whispered. “Behind the heap. I used it to get to school. Nobody knows about that.”

“I do,” said Raiden. “I’ve known for two years. It’s on the archive drawings from 1974. There was a drain there, and they filled it in, and the wall settled, and the pillar didn’t.” He looked up at her, finally, just for a second. His eyes were steady. “I told you. I made a map. Of every way out.”

She stood there with the chopsticks in her hand.

“Every way in, too,” he said. “It’s the same map.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She ate four dumplings standing up, fast, without tasting them.

Then she wiped her hands on her overalls and put the second barrel back in the vice and picked up the hone.

He got up off the oil drum. He went to her father’s tool chest, the red one, and opened the top drawer, and took out the big rubber torch, the one that had been in that drawer since before she was born, and switched it on, and came and stood beside her at the vice and held it, steady, exactly where she needed it, on the inside of the bore.

She hadn’t told him where. He’d watched her for two and a half years.

“Is it going to run?” he said, under the noise of the trucks.

She looked at the bore in the light.

“I don’t know,” said Jinx.

“All right,” said Raiden. “Then I’ll hold the torch until you do.”

chapters.title: She Builds Her Way Out
chapters.desc: One night, one engine, three cylinders that haven’t moved in seven years. He holds the torch. Her father comes out of the office at three in the morning. At 5:40 the widowmaker coughs.
chapters.epigraph: “Two-strokes don’t forgive. They either run or they don’t. I like that about them. I like it about people too.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
By midnight she had all three bores honed.

They sat on the clean rag on the bench in a row, grey and cross-hatched under the torch, and she looked at them with her hands flat on the bench on either side. Then she picked up the first piston.

The rings were rusted into their grooves. She’d known they would be. She broke them out with a pick, in pieces, brown flakes of steel, and cleaned the grooves with a broken bit of old ring the way her father had taught her when she was six, scraping the carbon out of each one until the metal shone. Three pistons. Two grooves each. It took an hour. Raiden held the torch the whole time without moving it once.

“Your arm,” she said, at the end.

“It’s fine,” said Raiden. “Keep going.”

She put the new rings on from the dead brother’s box. They were wrapped in oiled paper, from 2013, and when she unwrapped them they were perfect. Bright. Ten years in a box in an office under a flyover, waiting for a man who’d died. She held one up to the light and something went through her that she didn’t have time for.

“He was going to do it,” she said. “The brother. He bought all this. He was going to rebuild it himself.”

“And then he got ill.”

“Yes.” She fitted the ring. “Then my father said he’d do it, and put it in the corner.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At one in the morning she checked the crank seals.

They were the thing that would kill it. She knew that. On a two-stroke the crankcase was part of the engine, it pulled the fuel in and pushed it up into the cylinders, and if a seal on the crank had gone, the case would suck air, and the engine would run lean and hot and seize again in a minute, or never start at all. And there was no way to change a crank seal on a triple without splitting the cases. Which was a day’s work. Which she didn’t have.

She sealed the ports. She pumped air into the crankcase through a fitting she made out of a spark plug body and a bicycle valve, with a hand pump from her father’s chest, and watched the gauge.

It held.

Not perfectly. It dropped, slowly. She sprayed soapy water on the seals, one by one, with the torch on them, and watched for bubbles. She did it three times, one crankcase at a time, because a triple was really three engines sharing a crank. The left held. The middle held, which meant the inner seals, the ones she couldn’t see, were good. The right one dropped. She sprayed the end seal by the ignition cover and there it was, a small froth, like someone breathing out.

She sat back on her heels.

“That’s bad?” said Raiden.

“It’s a bit bad.”

“How bad?”

“It might run,” said Jinx. “It might run for an hour. It might not start. It might start and seize and throw a rod through the case and take my leg off.” She looked at the seal. “I could put sealant round it. From the outside. It’s not a fix. It’s a lie. It’ll hold for a day.”

“We only need a morning,” said Raiden.

She looked up at him. He was crouched beside her with the torch, in his ruined trousers, with grease on his face and pencil on his fingers. He looked tired and calm.

“Lie to it,” he said. “Just this once. We’ll fix it properly after.”

She lied to it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning she put the barrels back on.

At half past two, the heads. She torqued them down in the right order, a little at a time, in a cross, the way the book said, with her own torque wrench from her bag. He held the torch. Dou watched from the door. The trucks went over. In the little square window, the lamp was still on, and her father was still at the desk, not writing.

At three she started on the carburettors.

Three of them, crusted green inside, with jets blocked solid and floats stuck to their pins. She took them apart on a rag on the bench, every tiny piece, and laid them out in rows, three rows, so they couldn’t get mixed up. She soaked them in a tin of cleaner from her father’s shelf.

While they soaked, she straightened up from the bench and her back cracked, loud, and she shut her eyes. When she opened them he’d put the torch down on the vice and was standing right in front of her. He took her face in his hands, black and all, and kissed her once, hard and quick, in the yard under the lamp, with Dou watching from the door.

“For luck,” he said. “Don’t tell me luck isn’t real. I know what they call you.”

She looked at him. Then she pulled him back by the collar and kissed him again, longer, and let him go.

“I need the light back,” she said.

He picked up the torch. She blew every jet out with the airline, and held each one up to the lamp to see the light come through.

She was at the second one when the office door opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came out into the yard.

He walked slowly. He stopped at the edge of the light from the big lamp. Dou looked at him and didn’t move. Her father didn’t look at Dou. He looked at the bike, with its heads back on and its barrels clean, and at the bench, with the three rows of tiny parts on the rag, laid out exactly the way he’d taught her, smallest at the top.

And at Raiden, holding the torch.

“Who’s this?” he said.

He said it to her. Not to Raiden. As if Raiden were a part on the bench.

“Raiden,” she said. She didn’t look up from the jet. “Lin Jian’s son.”

Her father went still.

She felt it. She knew what he was seeing. A black car coming down the lane. A big man in a dark coat getting out, and going into the office, and coming out again ten minutes later. The men standing up. His own hands flat on the desk for an hour.

“I’ve heard,” said her father slowly. “About him.”

“Everybody has,” said Raiden cheerfully, in his party voice. “It’s mostly true. I’m hopeless. I’ve never fixed anything. I’ve been holding this torch for five hours and I don’t know what any of it does.” He beamed at her father. “How do you do, sir. You’ve got a wonderful tool chest. Every drawer’s in order. I could tell exactly where she learned it.”

Her father looked at him.

Then he looked at the red tool chest, with its drawers.

Then he came across the yard, slowly, an old man with spotted hands that shook, and stood at the bench beside her and looked down at the three rows of tiny parts.

“Middle jet’s the wrong size,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stopped.

She looked at the middle jet. She picked it up and held it to the lamp and read the number stamped on it, small.

He was right. It was a size up. Somebody, at some point, maybe the brother, had put the wrong one in the middle carb. If she’d built it like that, the middle cylinder would have run rich, and fouled its plug, and coughed, and she’d have spent an hour at five in the morning trying to find out why.

“There’s a box,” said her father. “Of jets. In the third drawer. At the back. Left side. In a tobacco tin.”

She looked at him.

He didn’t look at her. He looked at the jet in her fingers.

She went to the red chest. Third drawer. At the back. On the left. A tobacco tin, the same one, with a picture of a ship on the lid, that had been there when she was five. She opened it. Jets, hundreds, in little paper twists, every one labelled in his slow careful handwriting.

She found the right size and came back.

He was still standing at the bench. He’d picked up the float from the third carb. He was turning it in his fingers, the way she turned a bolt.

“This is stuck,” he said. “The pin’s bent. You’ll want to straighten it, not change it. The new ones are rubbish.” He put it down. “Like I showed you.”

“I know,” she said.

“I know you know,” said her father.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t stay.

He stood there for another minute, watching her fit the right jet. Then he turned and went back across the yard to the office, slowly, and at the door he stopped, and looked back, not at her, at Raiden, holding the torch.

“You’ve been holding that five hours,” he said.

“Five hours and twelve minutes,” said Raiden.

Her father looked at him a moment longer.

Then he went inside, and shut the door, and through the little square window she saw him sit down at the desk, under the lamp, and put his face in his hands.

She looked down at the carburettor.

Raiden didn’t say anything. He moved the torch an inch, to where she was about to need it, and kept it there.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past four the carbs were on.

At five she did the ignition. No points on this one: an early electronic box under the tank that nobody under the flyover had ever trusted. She cleaned every connector, checked the three pickups, and set the timing with a dial gauge in the plug hole, one cylinder at a time, three times, by the book. She put in new plugs from the box. She filled the oil tank with two-stroke oil from her father’s shelf, and bled the pump, and watched the oil come through the little clear lines to each cylinder, slowly, like something waking up.

She put the battery from her own bike on it, on leads, because the dead brother’s battery had been dead since 2014.

She put fresh fuel in the tank from the can.

She put new tubes in the tyres, which were rotten, and pumped them up, and they held, just.

At twenty past five she stood back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The sky under the flyover didn’t change at dawn. It never had. There was no sky. But the trucks overhead changed: the night ones, the big long-distance ones, gave way to the early ones, the vans and the buses, and the noise got higher and busier, and somewhere at the end of the lane a woman was putting up the shutter of a breakfast stall.

Guo came out of the office at half past five with a cup of tea.

The small man came behind him. Dou straightened up by the door. Her father came out last, and stood in the office doorway with his hands at his sides, the way he’d stood the night she left.

Guo looked at the bike.

It didn’t look like much. It still had the rust and the dust and the pigeon droppings. She hadn’t touched the outside of it. The tank was still dull. The chrome on the three exhaust pipes was still pitted brown. It looked exactly like a bike that had been in a corner under a tarpaulin for nine years.

“Well,” said Guo. He sipped his tea. “Well, Miss Jinx.”

She didn’t say anything.

She put the choke on. All three. She turned the fuel on, and waited, counting, while the bowls filled. She turned the key. A light came on, on the dash, red, for the first time since 2014, and Guo’s face moved, slightly.

She put her boot on the kick-start.

Behind her, she felt Raiden. He’d put the torch down. He was standing a step back, out of her way, the way he’d stood by the wall in the gallery.

She kicked it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nothing.

A cough. A sound like an old man clearing his throat in another room. Nothing.

She kicked it again.

A cough. Two. A puff of blue smoke out of the left pipe. Nothing.

Guo drank his tea.

She stood with her boot on the kick-start and breathed, and listened, not to the engine, which wasn’t doing anything, but to what it had done. Two coughs. Left pipe only. Left cylinder firing, a little. The other two not.

Rich. They were flooding. The choke was on too long on a warm morning and the middle and right ones were wet.

She took the choke off the middle and right. She held the throttle wide open, which you weren’t supposed to do, to clear them. She kicked it four times, hard, with nothing, the old engine turning over and over with its pistons moving in their new rings for the first time in seven years.

Then she let the throttle go, and kicked it once more.

✦ ✦ ✦

It coughed.

And coughed. And caught. Left. Then middle. Then right, a beat behind, and then all three at once, in a sound she’d only ever heard on old videos, a high furious ringing crackle like a chainsaw full of bees, and a cloud of blue smoke came out of all three pipes and rolled across the yard under the lamp and over Guo and his tea, and the whole bike shook on its stand like an animal that had been asleep for nine years and had just remembered what it was.

It was the loudest thing she’d ever heard under the flyover.

The breakfast woman at the end of the lane dropped her shutter.

She held the throttle steady, just above idle, and listened. Left, middle, right. Even. Hot. Rough, a bit. A bit lean on the right. The lie round the seal, holding. Holding. The oil coming through. The smoke thinning, from blue to grey to nearly nothing.

It was running.

It was five forty in the morning and it was running.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t turn round.

She kept her hand on the throttle and her eyes on the engine and listened to it, every beat, the way her father had taught her, and she heard Guo put his teacup down on the step behind her, carefully, and come across the yard, and stop beside the bike.

He didn’t say anything.

He stood in the smoke looking at his brother’s motorbike with its three pipes rattling, and his face went young, all at once, as if it was 1989 and somebody had just handed him the keys.

He put his hand on the tank, on the dust, where his brother’s hand would have gone.

She took her hand off the throttle. She stepped back.

“Once round the yard,” she said. “Gently. The right seal’s held together with sealant. It’ll last a morning. Then you get the cases split and do it properly. Not my father. Someone with a clean workshop.”

Guo looked at her.

Then he got on.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rode it once round the yard.

Slowly, in first, with the three pipes crackling and the smoke going up under the flyover, past the scrap heap and the pillars and her father in the office doorway and Dou by the door. Once round. And then again. And then he stopped it in front of her and sat there with the engine running and his hands on the bars and didn’t say anything.

Then he turned it off.

The quiet afterwards rang in her ears. The trucks went over. Somewhere, the breakfast woman put her shutter back up.

Guo got off. He stood beside the bike with one hand on the seat.

“That was very good, Miss Jinx,” he said.

Behind her, she felt Raiden breathe out.

And she thought it was over. She thought, for a second, standing in the yard at a quarter to six with the smell of two-stroke smoke in her hair and her hands black to the wrist, that it was over, that she’d built her way out, the way she’d built her way out of everything her whole life, with her hands, alone.

Then Guo smiled.

“So good,” he said, “that I don’t think I can let you go.”

chapters.title: Raiden Stops Playing Dumb
chapters.desc: Quarter to six in the morning under the flyover. A deal broken, a knife, and the useless Lin boy steps in front of her and stops pretending. Then a black car at the end of the lane, and a brother-in-law who owes him one.
chapters.epigraph: “I know every building in this district. I know yours. You added two floors in 2019 on a frame drawn for four. Shall I tell you which beam?” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
“We had a deal,” said Jinx.

“We did,” said Guo. “And you kept it. Beautifully. The debt’s gone. I’m a man of my word.” He took his hand off the seat of his brother’s bike. “But you see, I didn’t know, last night. I didn’t know what you were. I thought you were a good mechanic. Now I know you’re the only person in this city who could have done that, in one night, under a flyover, with an old man’s tools.” He smiled. “I’d be a fool to let that go back to the Docks and fix rich men’s bikes. Wouldn’t I?”

Dou had come away from the door.

He was walking across the yard, not fast. The knife was out again. The small man was behind him.

“You’ll work for me,” said Guo. “Not twelve bikes. As long as I need you. You’ll have a good wage. Better than the Docks. And your father keeps his shop, and Mr. Lin keeps his face.” He looked past her at Raiden. “His very happy face.”

She didn’t move.

She was thinking about the gap behind the scrap heap. About the bike. About the thirteen in her bag on the bench, three metres away. About Dou’s knife, and the small man, and her father in the office doorway, and how fast she could—

Raiden stepped in front of her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t do it fast. He did it the way he did everything in a room, easily, as if he’d just thought of somewhere better to stand. One step sideways, so that he was between her and Dou, and between her and Guo, with his back to her and his hands in the pockets of his ruined grey trousers.

She heard him breathe in.

And then he stopped being stupid.

She felt it happen. She was standing right behind him, close enough to touch him, and she felt it go out of him, all of it, the gallery and the silly smile and the voice, the way a whole engine changes note when the cam comes on. His shoulders came down and his head came up, and he went completely still, the way he had on the back stairs of the gallery.

“Mr. Guo,” he said.

It was the voice he used for builders, low and flat and plain.

Guo looked at him.

“You’ve got a building on Sandpit Lane,” said Raiden. “Number forty. Six storeys. Grey tiles on the front. A sign on the ground floor that says Guo Trading, and a gold cat in the window that waves.” He didn’t take his hands out of his pockets. “It was built in 1981, for four storeys. The drawings are in the city archive, sheet nine of eleven. I’ve read them. The frame was drawn for four. Somebody put two more on top of it in 2019, without a permit, in about six weeks, with concrete from a lorry that didn’t have a name on the side.”

Guo didn’t move.

“And on the third floor,” said Raiden, “on the north side, by the stairs, there’s a beam that carries everything above it. A transfer beam. It’s the only one. And it’s cracked. I walked past last summer and saw it from the street, through the window by the stairwell. A diagonal crack, about a metre long, going from the bottom edge toward the support. That’s shear. That’s a beam telling you it’s had enough.” He paused. “It’ll hold for a while. A year. Maybe two. Then one day it won’t, and the top three floors come down into the bottom three, and everybody in them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The yard was quiet.

Dou had stopped walking. He was looking at Guo. The small man was looking at Dou.

“You’re lying,” said Guo.

“I don’t lie about buildings,” said Raiden. “I lie about everything else. Never about buildings.” He took one hand out of his pocket. In it was his phone. “I took a photograph. Last summer. It’s the clearest crack I’ve ever seen. I’ve got the archive drawings too. And I’ve got the number of a woman at the Buildings Department who owes me a favour, because I once told her the car park under the new courthouse was about to fall down, and it was. One message. One photograph. She’ll have Sandpit Lane closed and everybody out of it by lunchtime, and inspectors in every room, and every drawer opened.”

He put the phone back in his pocket.

“I’m not going to send it,” he said. “Not today. Today, you’re going to say the debt’s gone, which you’ve already said, because you’re a man of your word. And you’re going to say she’s going home. And then you’re going to go to Sandpit Lane and get your third floor propped before somebody dies in it.” He tipped his head a little. “That one’s free. I’d tell you that whatever you did. I don’t like buildings falling on people.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Guo stared at him.

She watched his face. She’d never seen a face work so hard to stay still. She watched him look at Raiden, at the grease on his cheek and the pencil on his fingers and the ruined shoes, and try to put it back together into the happy boy from the photograph, the one with the waistcoat, the useless one. And fail. And try again. And fail.

“You’re Lin Jian’s son,” said Guo slowly.

“Yes.”

“They say you’re a fool.”

“They do,” said Raiden. “I worked very hard on it.”

“Your father—”

“My father’s got nothing to do with this,” said Raiden. “My father’s asleep in the Walled City. He doesn’t know I’m here. Nobody in my family knows I’m here.” He paused. “Well. One does.”

And at the end of the lane, under the lowest flyover, an engine stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard it. They all heard it.

It wasn’t a lorry or a van. It was something heavy that idled like a cat, and then stopped, and a door opened and closed. Then another, and another further away, at the other end of the lane. Then footsteps, not hurrying.

Dou turned round.

The small man turned round.

Guo didn’t. Guo was still looking at Raiden.

“I rang him from the second bus,” said Raiden. “Last night. At about nine. Before I came through the gap. I said I’m going under the Cao flyover, and if I don’t ring you by six, come.” He looked at his watch. “It’s five fifty-one. He’s early. He’s always early.”

Zhao Zhendong came round the corner of the yard.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came through the front. Through the middle roll-up door, past her father in the office doorway, who stood back to let him pass without being asked. In his black coat, hands in his pockets, alone.

He didn’t need anyone with him. There were men at both ends of the lane. She’d heard the doors. But he came into the yard alone, and stopped under the lamp, in the last of the two-stroke smoke, and looked round: at the bike, at Dou with the knife, at the small man, at Guo, at Raiden standing in front of her with his hands in his pockets, and at her.

He looked at each of them for four seconds. It took a long time. Nobody moved while he did it, not even the breakfast woman at the end of the lane, who’d come out to see what the cars were and gone very quickly back inside.

Then he looked at Guo again.

“Hm,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

For a while that was all. He stood in the yard with his hands in his pockets and looked at Guo, and Guo looked back, and Jinx watched the colour go out of Guo’s face, slowly, from the top down, like oil draining out of a sump.

Guo knew who he was. Everybody under the flyover knew who he was. Everybody in the city.

“Mr. Zhao,” said Guo. His voice had gone thin. “I didn’t know—I wasn’t aware this was—”

“She’s family,” said Zhao.

Flat, the way he said everything.

Guo’s mouth moved.

“Her father’s shop,” said Zhao. He didn’t look at the shop. “Clean.”

“Yes,” said Guo. “Yes, of course. The debt’s—it’s gone. I said so. I’m a man of my—”

“Your building,” said Zhao.

Guo stopped.

“Prop it,” said Zhao. “Today.”

He turned round, then, and looked at Raiden, and at Jinx behind him. Something happened at the corner of his mouth that on anybody else would have been nothing, and on Zhao Zhendong was very nearly a smile.

“That’s the floor paid for,” he said to Raiden. “We’re even.”

And he walked out of the yard the way he’d come in, past her father, through the middle door, and up the lane. She heard car doors at both ends of the lane, and engines, going away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Guo left five minutes later.

He didn’t say anything. He wheeled his brother’s bike out of the yard himself, by hand, because he didn’t want to start it again under the flyover, not now. Dou and the small man went with him. Dou had put the knife away. At the corner of the yard, by the scrap heap, Guo stopped, and looked back.

Not at Raiden. At her.

“It runs,” he said. “It really runs.”

“Get the cases split,” said Jinx. “Properly. Someone with a clean workshop.”

He looked at her a moment longer. Then he went.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t move.

Neither did Raiden. He stood in front of her, with his back to her, with his hands in his pockets, in the middle of the empty yard under the lamp, and the trucks went over, and the breakfast woman’s shutter went up at the end of the lane.

Then she saw his hands.

He’d taken them out of his pockets. They were hanging at his sides. And they were shaking, badly. The long clever hands that had held the torch without moving from ten at night till twenty past five were shaking so hard she could see it from behind.

She put her arms round his chest from behind, the way she had the night of the freezer. She put her face against his back, between his shoulder blades, and held on.

He made a sound.

“I’ve never done that,” he said. “In front of anyone. Since I was ten. Never.” His voice was going everywhere. “I’ve never once taken it off. Not at the gallery. Not at the gala. Not for Chen Si. Not for my father. I didn’t know if I could. I didn’t know if there was anyone under it any more.”

“There was,” she said into his back.

“I was so frightened,” said Raiden. “I was so frightened. I’ve been frightened since Tuesday. Since the eggs. I knew. I didn’t know what, but I knew. And then I read the note and I thought, she’s done it. She’s done what I did at the hospital. She’s gone out the back so they won’t see me.” He put his shaking hands over hers on his chest. “And I hated it. I hated it so much. I understood why you hated me, in 2021. For three weeks. I understood all of it before I’d finished reading it, standing at the bench.”

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“Don’t be.” He turned round in her arms. His face was wet. “Don’t you dare be sorry. You built a dead man’s bike in a night under a flyover with a seal held on with lies. I’ve never seen anything like it in my life. I’m going to draw it for the rest of my life. I’m going to draw your hands on that kick-start until I die.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She kissed him in the yard, under the lamp, in front of the office window, where her father was standing, she knew, behind the wire glass, watching. She didn’t care. She took his wet face in her black hands and kissed him the way she’d wanted to since ten o’clock last night when he came round the scrap heap with a bag of dumplings, completely lost, with a map of every way in and every way out folded inside his jacket.

He kissed her back like he was drowning.

His hands came up into her hair. They were still shaking. He held her face, and her neck, and pulled her in so hard her boots came off the ground, and she tasted salt and two-stroke smoke and the chilli oil from the dumplings, and she didn’t stop, and he didn’t, until somebody in a truck going over the flyover above them leaned on his horn, long and loud, for no reason at all.

They stopped, foreheads together, breathing.

“You came through the gap,” she said.

“I know about all the gaps,” said Raiden. “I told you. I’m the key.” He laughed, a broken one. “You said I left it by the window. I didn’t leave this by the window. I’ve been carrying this one round for two years. Just in case you ever went down the lane.”

She stood there with her forehead on his and her hands on his face.

“Take me home,” she said.

“You’re driving,” said Raiden. “I don’t drive. You know I don’t drive.”

She laughed. Out loud, in the yard, under the flyover, at six in the morning, with her arms round his neck. And he laughed too, helplessly, and held her up off the ground, and spun her round once, the way he had in the hangar in the north, and her boots knocked over her father’s oil drum, and it rolled across the yard, and neither of them went after it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father was in the office doorway when they went to the bike.

He hadn’t moved. He was standing with his hands at his sides, the way he always stood. He looked at her, at Raiden, at the empty corner where the bike had been.

She stopped in front of him.

She didn’t know what to say. She stood in front of her father in the yard where she’d grown up and didn’t have a single word.

He didn’t either. He looked at her, and his mouth worked, the way it had in the lane when she arrived.

“The middle jet,” he said at last. His voice was low. “You’d have found it.”

“Eventually.”

“You’d have found it,” said her father. He looked down at his hands. “You always found it.”

Then he turned round and went back into the office and shut the door.

She stood there.

Raiden didn’t say anything. He put his hand on the small of her back, the way he had in the ballroom of the Harbour Hotel, and left it there, and waited.

After a while she turned round, and put her helmet on him, the right way round, and did up the strap.

chapters.title: Her Father Says Sorry
chapters.desc: Winter 2023 to 2024. An old man at the black door for the first time, saying it badly. Then the red door, a Saturday dinner, a favour from Lin Jian that she refuses in his own kitchen, and fireworks over the Walled City at New Year.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody has said no to me in my own kitchen since 1987. Sit down. Eat. You’re family.” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
Her father came to the black door on the second Saturday in December.

She didn’t hear him. She was under a bike. The anchor woman came across the street and stood in the doorway and said, “There’s an old man on your step. He’s been there twenty minutes. He won’t knock.”

She pushed herself out on the creeper.

He was sitting on the step with his back to the door, on the cold stone, in an old brown coat she remembered, looking at the rope shops and the chandlers and Mrs. Tong’s sign. His hands were between his knees.

She stood in the doorway behind him.

“You can come in,” she said.

He didn’t get up.

“I’ve never been here,” he said. He was looking at the street, not at her. “Five years. I knew where it was. The whole time. I used to ride past. On the bus. I never got off.”

She didn’t say anything.

She sat down beside him on the step.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat there without talking.

A container ship sounded in the basin. Mrs. Tong came out of her shop, saw them, and went back in very fast. Upstairs, through the open window of the long room, she could hear Raiden at the stove, singing something badly, the way he did when he thought nobody was listening.

“I should have stopped him,” said her father.

She went still.

“The man,” he said. “In your room. When you were seventeen. The buyer’s man.” His hands were tight between his knees. “I heard. I was in the yard. I heard you shout. And I didn’t come. I stood in the yard and I didn’t come, because he was the buyer’s man, and the buyer was the only one who still bought from me, and I thought—” He stopped. “I don’t know what I thought. And then you came out with the tyre iron, and his hand. And I told you to say sorry to him.”

She didn’t move.

“I told you to say sorry,” said her father. “To him. I’ve thought about it every night. Ten years. Never said it to anyone.” He breathed. “I’m sorry. Jia. I should have come. With a spanner. Broken his other hand. I was a coward. Your whole life. And you were never a coward, not even at five, and I let them call you a name for it and I was proud.” His voice went. “Proud of the wrong thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t forgive him.

Not then. She didn’t know how. She sat on the step beside him with her hands black from the bike and her whole chest tight and didn’t say it’s all right, because it wasn’t, and she’d never said anything to him she didn’t mean.

But she didn’t get up either.

“You found the jet,” she said, after a while.

He looked at her.

“The middle one. I’d have spent an hour on it. You saw it from across the yard.” She looked at the street. “Nobody else could have done that.”

He put his face in his hands.

She sat there. And after a while, without looking at him, without deciding to, she put her hand on his back, on the old brown coat, between his shoulders, and left it there.

Upstairs, Raiden had stopped singing.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came to dinner. Her father.

Raiden had cooked fish, and he cooked another one without being asked, and laid a third place at the long table, and pulled out a chair, and her father sat in it as if he were waiting to be called in to see a doctor. He looked round the long room: the five tall windows, the bath through the door, the drafting table and her bench with its vice, the shelf with the glass prize and the Best in Show and the tin of washers.

“You own this,” he said.

“Yes.”

“The whole building?”

“And next door,” said Jinx. “He bought it. In my name.”

Her father looked at Raiden across the table.

Raiden was taking the bones out of her fish with his chopsticks, the way he always did, without looking. He felt the look and glanced up. He didn’t do the silly face; he’d stopped doing it at the long table since the flyover. He just looked back.

“The land under the shop,” said Raiden. “Under the flyover. Who owns it?”

Her father blinked.

“I do. My father bought it. In 1969.”

“There’s a man I know,” said Raiden. “A developer. A decent one, which is rare. He’s been trying to buy land under the north flyovers for three years, for a depot. He’ll pay a fair price. More than fair, if I ask him. Enough for a flat on the sea side with a balcony, and whatever you want on it, and no more rent and no more buyers and no more Guo.” He went back to her fish. “If you want. It’s your land. You can say no.”

Her father looked at him.

“Pigeons,” he said.

Raiden looked up.

“I always wanted pigeons,” said her father. “Racing ones. On a roof. My father had them.” He looked down at his plate. “I never had a roof.”

“The flat’s got a roof,” said Raiden. “I’ll make sure.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The land sold in January.

The developer paid twice what it was worth, because Raiden asked him to, and Raiden paid him back the difference in drawings, which she only found out about later. Her father bought a flat on the sea side, in a low old block with a flat roof and a view of the water, and Raiden drew him a pigeon loft for the roof, and Jinx built it, in steel and timber, in three Saturdays, with her father passing her the screws in the right order without being asked.

He had twelve pigeons by February. He named them after engines.

He rang her on Sundays now. Just to say what the pigeons had done. She didn’t say much back. She listened. That was new too.

✦ ✦ ✦

The red door opened on a Saturday in January.

Not at two in the morning. At six in the evening, with the lamp on over it and the lion’s head knocker polished, and Raiden beside her on the step, holding a box of pastries and her hand, and not saying anything, because he couldn’t.

Lin Jian opened it himself.

He looked at her on the step, in her old black leather jacket. He looked at their hands.

“You came,” he said.

“I said one day.”

“Yes,” said Lin Jian. “He told me.” He stood back. “Come in.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was tall and old and full of stairs.

Every sound carried. A long kitchen table in a long kitchen, with a fire at one end, and eleven chairs that didn’t match. Elowen and Zhao. Evangeline, at the end of the table, in grey, beside a man so big he made the chair look like a toy, who stood up when Jinx came in and nearly hit his head on the lamp and said, “You’re Jinx. You built Xiao Pan’s bike. Elowen told me. Can I ask you about the intake on that black one? Elowen showed me the picture from the newspaper. Four runners, equal length, by hand? How did you match them?” and talked to her about intakes for twenty minutes without stopping while Evangeline watched him with her face doing nothing at all, and Jinx liked him at once.

Elara, late, from the hospital, in scrubs under her coat. Eliana, with a laptop, who said, “Spreadsheet’s updated,” and didn’t explain.

And the cook.

Ah Sim was eighty and the size of a child and she came out of the kitchen door at the end of the room with a ladle in her hand and looked at Jinx from her boots to her hair and back down again, slowly, then at Raiden, then at Jinx again.

“He’s fat,” she said.

“He cooks,” said Jinx.

Ah Sim looked at her. Then she pointed the ladle at the chair beside Raiden’s.

“Sit down and eat,” she said. “You’re too thin too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was after dinner that Lin Jian asked.

The others had gone up to the long room on the second floor, where there was a fire, and somebody had found a bottle of something, and she could hear Elowen and Raiden arguing about a shelf. Jinx had stayed in the kitchen. She didn’t know why. She was drying dishes with Ah Sim, who hadn’t asked her to and had handed her a cloth.

Lin Jian came back down the stairs and stood in the doorway.

Ah Sim looked at him. Then she put down the ladle and went out of the kitchen without a word.

“I need a bike,” said Lin Jian.

Jinx put down the cloth.

“Not for me,” he said. “For a job. In the spring. Some cargo that has to move from one place to another very fast, in a part of the city where vans get stopped. A bike that doesn’t look like anything. That can carry a case. That nobody can catch.” He looked at her. “Your father used to say nobody could catch yours.”

She looked at him.

She thought about the black car coming down the lane under the flyover. About her father’s hands on the desk. About Guo saying I’d like some of that luck. About twelve bikes, and twelve more.

“No,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Jian didn’t move.

“I don’t build for that,” said Jinx. “Not for Guo. Not for my father’s buyers. Not for you. I got out. I’m not going back in because the man asking has a nicer kitchen.” She picked the cloth up again, because her hands needed something. “I’ll build you a bike to ride. Any bike. For nothing. Never one for a job.”

The kitchen was quiet.

The fire popped. Upstairs, Raiden laughed at something.

Lin Jian looked at her. She’d been afraid of him since she was nine. She stood in his kitchen with a tea towel in her hands and found she wasn’t, not even a bit.

Then he laughed.

It was the big rusty laugh from the step of the flower shop, and it went right up the stairs, and upstairs the arguing stopped, and somebody said what was that?

“Nobody has said no to me in my own kitchen,” said Lin Jian, “since 1987. Ah Sim said it. About a fish.” He wiped his eyes. “Good. Good. That’s good.” He came into the kitchen and took a dish off the rack and picked up a second cloth from the rail and started drying it, badly, beside her. “He’ll need someone who says no. He’s never had anyone who says no to him. His sisters let him do whatever he likes because he’s the boy. I sent him away and then let him do whatever he liked because I’d sent him away.” He put the dish down. “You say no.”

“All the time.”

“Good,” said Lin Jian again. “Then sit down at my table any time you like. You’re family. You were family when you were under that bench with the carburettor. I just didn’t know whose.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell Raiden about the bike.

She told him about the dishes. On the way home, in the taxi, with his head on her shoulder. Your father dried a plate. Badly. And he lifted his head and stared at her and said my father has never dried a plate in his life, and she said he did tonight, and he laughed so hard the taxi driver looked round.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunar New Year was the tenth of February.

They went to the Walled City on the eve, the whole family, every Lin and everyone they’d married or were going to, and some people they hadn’t, and one who only ever came for New Year and always lost. Aurelia Chen, in gold, with her husband, who played mahjong at the long table until two in the morning while Elowen watched and Evangeline beat her, hand after hand, without a word.

Jinx had painted her nails black for it. At the bench, with the vice holding the bottle. When Aurelia looked up from her tiles at two in the morning, furious, and said, “Jia. Sit in. Save me,” Jinx held up her hands from the sofa.

“Not with these,” she said. “They’re still wet.”

Raiden, across the table, put his face in his hands and shook.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight they went up on the roof.

Everybody did. The house had a flat roof with a wall round it and pots of dead geraniums that Ah Sim refused to throw away, and from it you could see the whole Walled City going down the hill in lanes and stairs, and the harbour, and the whole city across it, waiting.

The fireworks started at the stroke of twelve. All at once. From the harbour, from the Coastal High-Rise, from every roof in the Walled City. Red and gold and white, going up and up and breaking over the water, and the noise of them coming back off the hill like a war.

She stood at the wall at the corner of the roof.

He came and stood behind her. He put his arms round her, from behind, round her waist, and his chin on her shoulder, the way he had on the roof of the noodle factory, the night she’d said I’m never going to be owned again.

“Happy New Year,” he said into her ear.

She turned round in his arms.

She didn’t say anything. She looked at him in the light of the fireworks, red and gold, going over his face. And she kissed him.

Not hard, the way she had in the yard or on the bench. Slowly, with her hands on his face, on the roof of his father’s house, in front of his whole family, at midnight, with the sky breaking open over the harbour and the noise coming back off the hill. She kissed him like she had all the time in the world, which she’d never once felt in her life, and he went completely still in her arms and then kissed her back the same way, as if he’d been waiting three years for her to do it in exactly this place.

Behind them, somebody whistled. Eliana. Somebody else said finally. Elowen. And somebody said hm.

She didn’t stop.

When she did, he had his forehead against hers and his eyes shut.

“In front of everyone,” he said.

“Yes.”

“On my father’s roof.”

“Yes.”

He opened his eyes.

He reached into his jacket, and she knew what he was reaching for, and her breath caught the way it had at Mrs. Tong’s in September 2021.

He took out his wallet and opened it. Behind the cards, in the soft old brown wallet, there was a fat wad of folded paper. Napkins. Receipts. The back of a dyno manual. Thirty of them.

He didn’t take one out. He just showed her, in the light of the fireworks.

Then he put it back.

“Not tonight,” he said. “Tonight’s yours. I just wanted you to see I’ve kept them all.”

She looked at him.

“Ask me in March,” said Jinx.

He went white.

She turned round in his arms, and leaned back against him, and watched the fireworks, and didn’t say anything else at all, and felt his heart going against her back so hard she thought it would come through.

chapters.title: She Lets Him In
chapters.desc: March 2024. The thing that happened when she was seventeen, a steel box she’s had since she left, and the code to it. Then the thirty-first napkin, two creepers under a bike, to scale. Then a registry office on a Thursday, and a bike show in the north, in their good clothes.
chapters.epigraph: “Oh-three-one-one. The day I left. It’s the code to everything I own that’s mine.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
She told him on the ninth of March, at two in the morning, in the bath.

She hadn’t planned to. She’d thought about it for three years. Since the roof of the noodle factory, in August 2021, when she’d sat with her boots over the drop and said I’m not telling you that one. She’d thought about how she’d do it. Where. She’d thought it would be somewhere hard and bright, the workshop, with the lights on, standing up, so she could walk away if she needed to.

It was the bath. With her back against his chest and the water going cool and the cranes lit up through the window next door. And it came out of her the way the triple had caught under the flyover, a cough and then another and then all at once.

“I was seventeen,” she said.

He went still behind her in the water.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I slept in the office,” she said. “On the camp bed. Under the window. I always had. My father slept in the room behind the shop, and there was a door between, and he didn’t lock it. Nobody locked anything.”

“The buyer’s men used to come at night sometimes. To look at what was ready. To take it away. Usually my father dealt with them in the yard. But one night one of them came into the office.”

She was looking at the window.

“I woke up. He was standing by the bed. He’d been drinking. I could smell it. He’d come in to look at me.” She breathed. “He said something. I won’t tell you what. And he put his hand on the blanket. On my leg.”

Raiden’s arms, round her, had gone like iron.

“There was a tyre iron,” said Jinx. “Under the bed. There was always one under the bed. I don’t know why. I think I’d put it there when I was twelve, when they started calling me Jinx and looking at me differently. I don’t remember putting it there. I just knew it was there.”

“I broke his hand with it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She felt him breathe out behind her. A long one, shaking.

“Two bones,” she said. “I heard them go. He screamed. He went out into the yard screaming, holding it. And my father came out of the back room. He’d been awake. He’d heard me shout before. He’d heard me, and he hadn’t come.” She stopped. “And he looked at the man with his hand, and at me in the office door with the tyre iron, and he told me to say sorry.”

Raiden didn’t say anything. She could feel his heart against her back, going hard and fast and furious.

“I didn’t,” she said. “I didn’t say sorry. I went back in the office and shut the door and sat on the camp bed with the tyre iron across my knees until morning. And the next night I put a spanner under my pillow. A thirteen. And I slept with it there for five years. Every night. Until I’d saved enough for the van and the lathe and the first three months’ rent on the black door.” She looked at the cranes. “The thirteen on the wall is the same one. The one I threw at you. That’s why it’s worn.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything for a while.

She’d thought he’d talk. He always talked. She’d thought he’d say something about her father, or the man, or the buyer, the way he had on the roof of the noodle factory: he didn’t stop it, I can see it from here.

He didn’t.

He held her. In the water, with both arms, round her chest and her waist, so tight she could feel every breath he took, and every breath was shaking. And after a while she felt his face against her shoulder, against the top of the carp, and it was wet, and it wasn’t the bath.

“Thank you,” he said, at last. His voice was wrecked. “For telling me.”

“You never asked.”

“I never will,” said Raiden. “I’ll never ask you anything you don’t want to give me. You can tell me everything or nothing, for the rest of our lives.” He breathed. “But I’m glad you did. God, I’m glad.”

She turned round in the water.

Water went over the side. She didn’t care. She knelt up in the bath and took his face in her hands, the way she always did, and looked at him, and he looked back, with his eyes red and his face wet, not doing anything about it.

“There’s more,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him downstairs.

In towels. At half past two in the morning. Through the workshop, dark, to the back, past the tool wall, past the steel room he’d built behind it, to the corner by the lathe, where there was a cabinet.

He’d seen it. He’d seen it every day for three years. A steel cabinet, grey, old, waist-high, bolted to the floor, with a keypad on the front. It had been there before him. She’d brought it from the shop under the flyover in the back of the van on the night she left, and bolted it down on the first day, before the lathe, before anything. He’d never asked what was in it. He’d never touched it.

“Nobody’s ever opened this but me,” said Jinx.

She typed in four numbers.

Oh. Three. One. One.

“The day I left,” she said. “The third of November. 2018. It’s the code to everything I own that’s mine. The bank. The phone. This.”

The cabinet opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

There wasn’t much in it.

A tyre iron. Old. Black. With a bend in it, near the end, where it had hit something hard.

A drawing. Crayon, on the back of a parts invoice from 2002, folded and unfolded so many times it was soft as cloth. A motorbike, drawn by a child, badly, with every part labelled anyway, in letters that went backwards, and the wheels too small, and the engine drawn in enormous detail, every fin on every cylinder.

A photograph. A woman in a red dress, from behind, walking away down a lane under a flyover. Blurred. Taken by someone who hadn’t been ready.

And a set of keys. On a ring. Old ones, for a padlock and two doors.

“The shop,” she said. “Under the flyover. I never gave them back. I thought one day I might need to go back in.” She looked at them. “I don’t need them any more.”

He didn’t say anything.

He knelt down on the concrete in his towel and looked into the cabinet: the tyre iron, the crayon bike with its backwards letters, the woman in the red dress walking away.

“That’s your mother,” he said.

“I think so. My father never said. I found it in his desk when I was ten and I took it.”

He looked at it for a while.

Then he looked at the crayon bike, and slowly started to smile.

“You drew the engine,” he said. “When you were six. You drew every fin.”

“I was five.”

“You were five,” said Raiden. “And you drew every fin on every cylinder, and you got the wheels wrong, and you didn’t care, because the engine was what mattered.” He looked up at her. “That’s the best drawing I’ve ever seen. I mean it. I’ve seen the drawings in the museum in the Coastal High-Rise that cost more than this building. That’s better.”

“It’s terrible.”

“It’s the truth,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

She shut the cabinet.

She stood in front of it, in her towel, in the dark workshop, with her hand flat on the cold steel top.

“You told me about the freezer,” she said. “And the fish truck. And the step. You gave me every door in your life. I’ve never given you one.” She looked at him. “That’s the code. Oh-three-one-one. For the cabinet. For the bank. For everything. You can have it. I don’t care what you do with it. I just want you to have it.”

He knelt on the floor and looked up at her, and started to laugh, quietly, with his face wet.

“Sorry,” he said. “It’s just—that first day under the black bike, before you told me your name, I lay there thinking, I can get into any vault in this city and I can’t get into her. I never said it out loud. It was too stupid, even for me.” He wiped his face. “And you’ve just handed me the code.”

She stood there.

Then she held out her hand, and he took it, and she pulled him up off the floor, and he came up into her arms, both of them in towels in the dark workshop at three in the morning, and she kissed him.

He kissed her back slowly.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drew it at the long table at half past three.

He didn’t ask if he could. He went upstairs with her and sat down at the table under the lamp, in his towel, and took out his pencil and his ruler and a paper napkin from the drawer where he kept them, because he kept them now, a stack, for exactly this.

She sat across the table and watched him.

He drew slowly and carefully. She couldn’t see what it was, and she didn’t try, and her heart was going harder than it had at the kick-start under the flyover.

When he’d finished, he put the pencil down. He didn’t slide it across. He picked it up and came round the table and knelt down beside her chair, on the wide pale boards, and held it up for her.

This time it wasn’t a house. It was the black bike, from below, As if you were lying on the floor underneath it, looking up at the engine, lit orange by a work light. And two creepers, side by side, on the concrete. And on the creepers, two tiny people lying on their backs with their shoulders touching. And one hand, on the concrete, between them, palm up. And another one on top of it.

At the bottom, the scale bar.

1:10.

And under it:

Will you marry me? (The first place I ever asked you anything. 31.)

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at it.

She looked at it for so long that he started to shake, kneeling there on the floor beside her chair in his towel, holding it up.

She thought about the black car coming down the lane, and her father’s hands flat on the desk, and Lin, from the Walled City, don’t ever go there. She thought about the red door, and her hand on it, and Lin Jian drying a dish badly beside her in his kitchen, saying you say no. Good. About Zhao in the yard saying she’s family. About Elowen straightening her collar. About Evangeline nodding, once, across the whole length of a flower shop. About her father on the step of the black door, saying I was proud of the wrong thing.

About thirty napkins in a wallet, carried against his chest for two and a half years.

She’d said ask me when I can say yes without walking into your father’s house.

She’d walked into his father’s house. She’d said no to his father in his own kitchen. And nobody had owned her. Not for one second.

“Yes,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t move.

He knelt there holding the napkin up, and she watched it go into him, the way she’d watched not yet go into him at Mrs. Tong’s in September 2021, all the way down.

“Say it again,” he said. “I’m sorry. I’ve heard not yet thirty times. I need to—say it again.”

“Yes.”

“Yes?”

“Yes, Raiden,” said Jinx. “Yes. Yes. Get up off the floor, you idiot.”

He didn’t get up. He put his face down on her knees and cried.

He cried the way he had after the freezer, from the bottom, kneeling on the floor of the long room in his towel with the napkin in his fist and his face in her lap. It was the same sound she’d heard once before, in the dark, in December. But there was no grief in it this time.

She put her hands in his hair.

She bent down over him, and put her face against the back of his neck, and held on.

When he lifted his head at last his face was a mess and he didn’t care. He stood up and pulled her up out of the chair with him and kissed her, not slowly, with the napkin still crushed in one fist and his other hand at the knot of her towel.

“I want you,” he said against her mouth. “Now. Can I?”

“You’ve got a napkin in your hand.”

He put it down on the table, flat, and smoothed it once, carefully, and came back to her, and she said yes before he could ask again.

He walked her backwards to the bed with his mouth on hers, and the towels went somewhere, and it was clumsy and wet-haired and laughing, and then it wasn’t laughing. He kissed the carp and the inside of her wrist and the hollow of her throat, and said yes back to her, over and over, against her skin, as if he was trying the word out. She always took charge. Tonight she let him, and he took his time, and when she said his name it came out of her in a voice she’d never heard herself use.

✦ ✦ ✦

They married on the fourth of April, a Thursday, at the registry office in the old town, at ten in the morning.

She’d said small. He’d said how small. She’d said three people. And he’d looked at her and then said Elowen, Zhao, and Eliana, because Eliana will find out anyway and she’ll never forgive us, and she’d said fine.

So it was three. Elowen in green, with her hand over her mouth from the moment they came in. Zhao in black, standing at the back with his arms folded, who said hm when the registrar asked if anyone had any objection, and the registrar looked at him and went on very quickly. Eliana in a hoodie, filming it on her phone, who said for the spreadsheet.

He wore the silver waistcoat with the gears.

She wore the dark red dress, from the flower shop, and her boots, and her black leather jacket, with the burn on the cuff.

When the registrar asked him if he took her, he said yes so loudly that a man waiting outside in the corridor looked in. When the registrar asked her, she said yes the way she said everything, flat and exact, and Raiden made a sound like someone had hit him, and Zhao, at the back, put his hand over his eyes for a moment.

The ring was steel. Plain. A band he’d had made by Aurelia’s goldsmith, Enzo, out of a piece of stainless from her own bench, an offcut from the intake on the black bike, because she’d said gold was soft and rings got caught in engines. She put it on a chain round her neck as soon as they got outside, under her dress, against her skin.

He kissed her on the steps of the registry office.

In front of Elowen and Zhao and Eliana and a woman with a pushchair and two pigeons. He kissed her like he’d been waiting three years, which he had, with his hands in her hair and her back against the registry office door, until Eliana said I’m still filming and Elowen said stop filming and Zhao looked at the sky, and nobody stopped anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then they went to the bike show.

The spring one in the north, two hours up the motorway in her van, straight from the registry, in their good clothes, without changing, with the dark red dress and the silver waistcoat and a box of pastries from Mrs. Tong’s on the dashboard that Mrs. Tong had given them at seven in the morning, crying, without being told why.

He drew the whole way.

She drove with one hand on the wheel and the other, most of the time, on his knee.

At the show, they walked round the hangar for three hours, her in her red dress and her boots and her leather jacket, him in his silver waistcoat with pencil on his fingers, and looked at every bike in it. The old man from the magazines was there. He looked at her dress. He looked at the steel ring on its chain, which had come out of the neck of the dress while she bent over a gearbox. He looked at Raiden, beside her, holding her hand.

“Well,” said the old man.

“Today,” said Raiden, before she could stop him. “This morning. Ten o’clock. At the registry. She said yes on the thirty-first napkin.”

The old man looked at Jinx.

“Congratulations,” he said. “Best in show.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden told everyone for a month.

The man at the petrol station on the way home. The toll booth. The anchor woman, who said about time again, and then went into her shop and came out with an anchor, a small brass one, and gave it to him, and went back in. The man on the desk at the Meridian. His firm in the south. A whole bus. Mrs. Tong, who already knew, and put a second picture on the wall behind the counter, beside the bike and her husband: a photograph Eliana had sent her of the registry office steps, with the two of them kissing against the door and a pigeon in the corner.

Jinx told nobody at all.

She went back to work on the Friday. She opened the black door at seven. She did a clutch and two sets of brakes and a carb rebuild and argued on the phone with a collector who wanted his tank painted gold.

And every so often, under a bike, in the dark, she put her hand up to her chest, to the steel ring on its chain under her overalls. She held it for a second, and let go.

He saw her do it from the crate on the Monday. He put his pencil down and watched her across the workshop until she looked up and caught him at it.

chapters.title: The Masterpiece He Could Never Draw
chapters.desc: May 2024. A friend comes back from the mountains with a hole in her husband. She pulls the roll-up door down and turns the radio up, and he sits on the pavement outside it. Then two in the morning, the bench, and for the first time in three years he gets her face.
chapters.epigraph: “I couldn’t draw you because you never let your face do anything. Tonight it did. That’s all it was. Three years.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
For six weeks she didn’t know if Serafina was alive.

She knew some things. She knew that on the thirteenth of April, a Saturday, nine days after the registry, she’d stood at the end of a car wash on the Docks road in her helmet with the grey Toyota running, and Serafina had come in fast in her red car with the quiet man beside her and blood on the passenger window. She knew she’d taken the red car and driven it away in reverse, laughing inside her helmet, because that was what she’d been asked to do. She knew the grey car had gone the other way, toward the mountains, and nobody had come back.

That was all she knew. One order. No questions.

She went to work every day. She did clutches and brakes and carb rebuilds. She went home up the stairs at nine and he had dinner ready and she ate it and didn’t taste it. She slept, mostly. Some nights she didn’t. Some nights she went down to the sailmaker’s at three in the morning and sat in the dark beside the empty space under the cover where the grey car had been, and didn’t do anything.

He never asked. He came down sometimes and sat with her. He didn’t say anything either.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the twenty-eighth of May, a Tuesday, at six in the evening, the grey car came down the street.

She heard it before she saw it. She knew that engine. She’d rebuilt it. It was coming down from the top of the street slowly, too slowly, with a sound in the exhaust that hadn’t been there in April, a rattle, like something loose. She was in the doorway of the black door before it stopped.

It had a hole in the back window, just one, small and round, with the glass crazed white round it.

Serafina got out of the driver’s side.

She was very thin, and brown, as if she’d been somewhere with a lot of sun and not enough food, and her hair was longer, and there was something in her face that hadn’t been there in April. She stood by the car and looked at Jinx in the black doorway.

And the quiet man got out of the passenger side, slowly, with his arm in a sling made out of a stranger’s shirt.

Jinx looked at the sling, and at the way he stood, carefully, with his weight off one side. Then at the hole in the back window.

In September, when they’d first wheeled the car in, she’d told him the one thing she wanted back from it: you never bring it back with a hole in it. She’d said it to his face.

She walked straight into Serafina and held on, hard, with both arms, with her face in Serafina’s too-long hair, which smelled of woodsmoke and mountains. She held on so hard that Serafina made a sound. Then she let go, turned round, and hit the quiet man on his good arm, hard, with her fist.

He let her.

Then she went inside and pulled the roll-up door down behind her with a crash that shook the whole street.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood in the dark workshop.

She went to the radio on the shelf by the bench, the old one with the dial, and turned it on, to the station that only played old songs, and turned it all the way up. A woman singing about a train. So loud the shelf shook.

And she cried.

She hadn’t cried since the shop. Since she was eight. She’d sat in her van in 2021 with the radio on when he bought her the building, and she hadn’t cried then, she’d just sat there. She hadn’t cried when Guo pinned his face to her pillow. She hadn’t cried in the bath when she told him about the tyre iron.

She stood in the dark in her workshop with her back against the inside of the roll-up door and the radio so loud she couldn’t hear herself, and she cried so hard she slid down the door onto the concrete and sat there with her knees up and her face in her arms and couldn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside, on the pavement, Serafina stood looking at the closed door.

“Is she—” she said.

“Yes,” said Raiden.

He’d come down the stairs when he heard the car. He’d come out of the side door in time to see her hit Haozhen and pull the roll-up door down. He stood on the pavement in his apron with a wooden spoon still in his hand and looked at the door. The radio was so loud you could hear it all down the street.

“She does this,” he said. “With the radio. She does it when it’s too much.”

The anchor woman had come out of her shop. Mrs. Tong had come out of hers. They stood in their doorways and looked at the black door and didn’t come any closer.

Serafina looked at him.

“Should you go in?” she said.

“No,” said Raiden.

He put the wooden spoon down on the step. He sat down on the pavement, with his back against the black roll-up door, in his apron, with his knees up.

“She’ll open it when she’s done,” he said. “I’ll be here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina and the quiet man went away, after a while. Serafina said she’d come back tomorrow. She looked at the door, and at Raiden on the pavement against it, and her mouth went tight, and she got back in the grey car with the hole in it and drove away up the street very slowly.

Raiden sat on the pavement.

The radio played. A song about a boat. A song about a girl. A song he knew from the farm, that Auntie used to play in the kitchen. He sat with his back against the door and felt it, through the steel, every time she moved on the other side. He couldn’t hear her. The radio was too loud. But he could feel it in the door, her shoulders against it, shaking.

He put his hand flat on the pavement beside him, palm up, where nobody could see it.

He sat there for over an hour.

Mrs. Tong brought him a bowl of noodles at seven, without saying anything, and he ate them sitting on the pavement. The anchor woman brought him a cushion. He didn’t use it. He put it beside him, on the step, for when she came out.

At ten past seven, the radio went off.

The whole street heard it stop. Then, slowly, with the sound it always made, the roll-up door went up a metre, not all the way.

He didn’t get up. He turned round on the pavement and looked under it.

She was sitting on the concrete on the other side with her knees up, her face white and wet and swollen and her eyes red and her hair everywhere, in her overalls, with grease on her cheeks where she’d wiped them. Looking at him.

In three years he’d never seen her face like that.

He crawled under the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything. He sat down beside her on the concrete, inside, and put his arms round her, and she let him. She turned her face into his neck and stayed there. The door was still up a metre behind them, and the street light came in under it in a long gold stripe across the floor, and the anchor woman’s cushion was on the step outside.

“I didn’t know if she was alive,” said Jinx, into his neck. “Six weeks.”

“I know.”

“I told him not to bring it back with a hole in it.”

“I know. I heard you. In September.”

“He brought it back with one. And one in him.”

“He brought her back,” said Raiden. “That’s what it cost him.”

She was quiet for a while.

“I hit him,” she said.

“You did. On his good arm. He let you.” He kissed her hair. “I think he’ll remember it for the rest of his life as the nicest thing anyone’s ever done for him.”

She made a sound that was half a sob and half a laugh, into his neck.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning she couldn’t sleep.

She got up, and put on a vest and her overalls, tied at the waist, and went down. She didn’t put the big lights on. Just the lamp over her bench, the one by the window, so the rest of the workshop was dark and the bench was a little island of yellow light with the bikes standing round it in the shadows.

She took the black bike’s carb off. There was nothing wrong with it. She took it to pieces on a rag, every jet and screw, in rows, and started cleaning them, one by one, because that was the only way she’d ever known to think.

She heard him on the stairs.

She didn’t look up. She knew he’d sit on the crate. He always sat on the crate. He’d open his sketchbook, and draw the bikes, or her hands, or the back of her neck, and they wouldn’t talk, and that would be all right.

He didn’t sit on the crate.

He pulled it right up to the end of the bench, into the light, close, closer than he’d ever sat. He opened his sketchbook and looked at her.

Not at her hands. At her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked up.

He was looking at her face. The way he’d looked at the warehouse on the shipyard road, kneeling in the middle of a race. As if it were the only thing in the world.

“Don’t move,” he said. “Please.”

She didn’t move.

She sat there at the bench, in the yellow light, with a jet in her fingers and grease on her cheekbones where she’d wiped them at seven o’clock and her eyes still swollen and her hair a mess and the steel ring on its chain lying on her chest over the vest. And he drew.

He drew slowly.

She’d watched him draw a thousand times, buildings, fast and sure. This was nothing like that. He drew slowly, with his whole body still, and his face serious, and his eyes going from her to the paper and back, from her to the paper and back, as if every line cost him something. He didn’t rub anything out. He didn’t turn the page.

It took him two hours.

She didn’t move once. Her neck ached. Her hand, holding the jet, went numb. Outside, the first lorries started on the Docks road. A gull came and sat on the roof and went away again. She sat there in the light at her bench and let him look at her, all of her, her face, the way she’d never let anyone look at her in her life.

At four o’clock he put the pencil down.

He sat there looking at the paper.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Can I see?” she said.

He didn’t answer. He didn’t move. She saw his hands, on either side of the sketchbook, on the bench. They were shaking.

She put the jet down and came round the end of the bench.

She looked over his shoulder.

It was her.

It was her face. All of it. At the bench, in the yellow light, with the shadows of the bikes behind her. The shaved side of her head and the rest of her hair falling over it. The grease on her cheekbones. Her eyes, swollen, red at the edges, looking straight out of the page. Her mouth, which was set hard, the way it always was, except at one corner, where it wasn’t. Where it had gone soft, and he’d caught it. The carp on her forearm. The ring on its chain. Her hands on the rag, with a jet in her fingers, black to the knuckles.

It wasn’t pretty. She wasn’t pretty in it. She was tired and sad and filthy and had been crying for an hour against a roll-up door, and she couldn’t stop looking at it.

She stood behind him and didn’t breathe.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I couldn’t draw you,” he said.

His voice was quiet.

“Three years. Hundreds of times. I tore them all out. I can draw anything, I can draw a building from across the harbour, and I couldn’t get you.” He looked at the drawing. “And tonight I looked under that door and saw you on the floor with your face all—like that. And I got it.”

“Got what?”
