“You never let it do anything,” said Raiden. “Your face. You learned that at the shop. So I kept drawing a face that wasn’t doing anything, and it came out wrong every time, because that’s not you. That’s you with the door shut.” He turned round on the crate and looked up at her. “Tonight you let it. That’s all it was. Three years.”

She looked down at him. She could feel her face going, and she didn’t stop it.

He looked at it.

“There,” he said, barely out loud. “That. That’s what I couldn’t get.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She kissed him.

She bent down and took his face in her black hands and kissed him on the crate at the end of her bench at four in the morning, with the drawing on the bench between them, and she wasn’t careful about the drawing, and he wasn’t either. He stood up off the crate into it and the crate went over and he pulled her against him, and she walked him back, and back, until he hit the black bike on its stand, and it rocked, and held.

“The bike,” he said against her mouth.

“It’s on the stand,” said Jinx, and pulled his shirt over his head.

It was slow, and then it wasn’t. It was the floor of the workshop, on the old blanket she kept for lying under bikes, in the dark beyond the lamp, with the drawing safe on the bench in the yellow light where neither of them could see it and both of them knew it was. It was her grease on his chest, and his hands in her hair, and the ring on its chain swinging between them and catching the light, and him saying her name, Jia, over and over, as if he’d only just learned it. It was laughing, once, when her elbow knocked a socket off the bench and it rolled across the floor and they both stopped to listen to it go, and then not laughing at all. It was her face. She let it do whatever it wanted. All of it. And he watched it, every second, as if he was still drawing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards he drew her again.

Lying on the blanket, on her back, on the workshop floor, with her arm over her eyes and grease all down her side and her hair everywhere. He did it in ten minutes, fast and sure, the way he drew buildings.

“Now it’s easy,” he said, sounding astonished. “Look. Now I can do it. Now I’ve got it, I can do it in ten minutes.”

“Let me see.”

He showed her. It was her. Lying there, laughing, with her arm over her face.

“You can do it every time now,” she said.

“Every time,” said Raiden. “For the rest of my life. You’ll never get rid of me. I’ll draw you every single day. You’ll be the most drawn woman in the history of the city.”

“Idiot,” said Jinx, and pulled him back down.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t show the first one to anyone.

He put it in a frame. A plain one, black, from a shop in the old town. And he hung it in the steel room, behind the tool wall, over the bench with the mattress, beside the warm lamp and the tin of peaches.

“Why there?” she said.

“Because it’s the safest room in the city,” said Raiden. “And it’s the most important thing I’ve ever made.”

He showed it to no one for a month.

Then, in July, he showed it to Elowen.

She came to the garage on a Thursday, for the first time, with Zhao behind her carrying a box of roses she’d brought for no reason, and Raiden took her down to the tool wall and swung it out and opened the steel door, and let her go in, and stood outside.

Elowen was in there.

When she came out, her face was doing nothing at all. The way Lin faces did, when they wanted to. She walked past Raiden. She walked past Zhao, by the bench, with his roses. She walked across the workshop to where Jinx was under a bike on the creeper, with only her boots sticking out, and stood beside the boots.

“He got you,” said Elowen.

Jinx pushed herself out on the creeper and looked up at her.

Elowen’s face was wet, and she hadn’t done anything about it.

“He’s been trying since he was ten,” said Elowen. “To draw something that would stay still long enough. Buildings. Doors. Rooms nobody can get into.” She wiped her face, once, with the back of her hand. “He never got a person before. Not one. Not me, not Ev, not our father. He told me once he couldn’t. That people kept moving.” She looked down at Jinx on the creeper. “You stayed still.”

“I didn’t,” said Jinx. “I moved. He just looked anyway.”

Elowen looked at her.

Then she held out her hand, and Jinx took it, and Elowen pulled her up off the creeper, and held on to her hand a moment longer than she needed to, and let go.

“Zhendong,” she said, without turning round, “you’re still holding her roses.”

Zhao came across the workshop and gave Jinx the box of roses. He looked at her for four seconds.

“Hm,” he said. And then, after a moment: “Good.”

chapters.title: Jinx Opens Her Own Shop
chapters.desc: November 2024. A fortune from a very large man for a house on a hill, an old chandler’s warehouse three doors down, his design, her name. A sign she cuts herself from steel. Then a customer in a good jacket who wants a bike nobody can catch.
chapters.epigraph: “His design. My name. My sign. I cut it myself. Nobody touches it.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
The money came in August.

He came up the stairs on a Tuesday evening with an envelope and put it on the long table beside her plate and sat down across from her and didn’t say anything, which was how she knew it was something.

She opened it. It was a bank letter, for a transfer into the account with her name on it, the one with the code oh-three-one-one.

She looked at the number.

She looked at it again. She counted the zeros with her fingernail on the paper, the way she counted threads on a bolt.

“What is this?”

“Jun Hyuk,” said Raiden. “For the house. The one on Fig Tree Lane. He wanted the safest house in the country, with a garden and a postbox and windows that open, and he didn’t want Ev ever to look at it and see that it was safe. So I drew it. And he asked what I’d charge. And I said a fortune, and that I’d give it to you.” He put his chin on his hand. “He paid twice what I said. He said the first fortune was for the house and the second was because I’m her brother.”

She put the letter down.

“I said I’d give it to Jinx for a new workshop,” said Raiden. “In July. In front of Ev. So I have to. I’m a Lin. We keep our word when there are witnesses.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t sit in the van with the radio this time.

She sat at the long table and looked at the number for a while. Then she looked out of the five tall windows at the rope shops and chandlers and Mrs. Tong’s sign, and three doors down, on the other side, past the anchor woman’s, at the old chandler’s warehouse that had been empty for two years.

It was big. Two storeys, brick, with an arched door you could drive a lorry through, and a row of tall windows along the top that had been boarded up since the chandler died. She’d looked at it every morning for two years from the step of the black door. She’d never said anything.

“That one,” she said.

He looked out of the window where she was looking.

“I know,” said Raiden. “I bought it last week.”

She turned round.

“In your name,” he said. “With my money. Not his. His is for what goes inside it.” He was smiling a little. “You’ve looked at it every morning since 2022. I’ve watched you. You stand on the step with your coffee, all three of them, and you look at it. Every single day.” He reached across the table and took her hand. “I’ve been drawing it for a year.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He showed her the drawings that night.

In the steel room, with the door shut and the warm lamp on, out of the safe. He’d kept his promise. He never left anything by a window any more.

It was the chandler’s warehouse, inside out. The big arched door at the front, with a new steel shutter that rolled up like hers, but twice as wide. The ground floor open, the whole length, with benches down both sides and lifts in the floor for the bikes, so you could work standing up, and a pit for the dyno, which was going to move from the sailmaker’s. A paint booth at the back, sealed, with its own air. A machine room with a lathe, a new one, and a mill, a five-axis one, the kind she’d only ever seen in the brochures in the shop in the north that she’d picked up and put down again.

“I can’t use a five-axis,” she said.

“You can learn. You learned to read from a workshop manual.”

And upstairs, a mezzanine, half the depth of the building, with a glass front, looking down over the whole floor. A drawing office, with two desks, one for her and one for him.

“I’ll be quiet,” said Raiden. “You won’t know I’m there.”

“I’ll always know you’re there.”

He looked very pleased about that.

And along the front of the building, at the bottom, where the chandler’s windows had been, a long low window, the whole width, at the height of a person walking past. So that anyone going down the street would see the bikes, the benches, and her, working.

She looked at that.

“People will look in,” she said.

“Yes,” said Raiden. “That’s the point. You won Best in Show. You built a dead man’s bike in a night. You’re the best in the city and nobody knows where you are because you’ve been hiding behind a black door with a rope company’s name on it.” He put his finger on the long window. “I’ve spent my whole life making places nobody can see into. This is the first one I’ve ever drawn that everybody can.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It took three months.

She kept the black door open the whole time. She kept working. And every evening at six she walked three doors down with him and stood in the chandler’s warehouse in a hard hat and watched it turn into the drawings.

The builders called him Mr. Lin. They called her Boss.

She didn’t know when that started. The foreman said it first, in September, when she came in at six and told him the bench height on the left side was two centimetres out and he got his level and found she was right. Yes, Boss. And after that they all did.

The dyno moved in October, on a lorry, in a cradle, with her walking beside it the whole length of the street.

The lathe came from Germany in October too. It was the size of a car. It took six men and a crane. She stood beside it when they’d bolted it down and put her hand flat on it the way she’d put her hand on the red door in the Walled City, and didn’t say anything, and he stood behind her and didn’t either.

And in November, at night, in the black door’s workshop, she cut the sign.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d drawn it herself.

He’d offered. She’d said no. She’d drawn it on the back of an invoice in biro, in capitals, because her handwriting was bad and capitals were all she trusted. Four letters. Big, square, plain. And she’d taken a sheet of steel, eight millimetres, two metres long, and laid it on the bench in the sailmaker’s under the work lights, and marked it out with a scriber and a ruler, and cut it with the plasma torch.

The marking out took three hours. The cutting took twenty minutes.

The torch screamed. The sparks went down off the bottom of the sheet in an orange fan and bounced across the floor. She worked in her mask and her leather apron with the sweat running down inside them, following the scribed line through the steel at the right speed, not too fast, not too slow, the way you followed a line on a road.

He sat on the crate in the doorway, out of the sparks, and watched.

When she’d finished, she turned the torch off and pushed the mask up. The letters lay in the sheet, still glowing at the edges, dull red, and then grey, as the steel cooled.

JINX.

She knocked them out of the sheet one by one with a mallet. She ground the edges. She drilled the holes for the bolts. She didn’t paint them. She left them steel. Grey and plain, with the cut marks still on the edges, where anyone who knew what they were looking at could see that somebody had done it by hand.

“His design,” she said, to him, in the doorway, with the mask on top of her head. “My name. My sign. I cut it myself. Nobody touches it.”

“Nobody,” agreed Raiden.

He got up off the crate. He came across the sailmaker’s, through the smell of hot steel, and took her face in his hands, mask and all, and kissed her. She tasted of metal. He didn’t care. He kissed her standing over the four letters on the bench, slowly, and she let him, with her gloves still on, and the steel ticked as it cooled.

✦ ✦ ✦

They opened on the sixteenth of November, a Saturday.

She hadn’t wanted a party. He’d said not a party, an opening, and she’d said what’s the difference, and he’d said the difference is that at an opening people come to look at your work instead of each other, and she’d thought about it and said fine.

So people came.

Everyone. The anchor woman, in her best coat, with an anchor. Mrs. Tong, with noodles for fifty. Big Fok from the shipyard road, and half the riders from the Saturday nights, who’d never been inside the black door and walked round the chandler’s warehouse with their mouths open. The old man from the magazines, who’d driven two hours from the north. The foreman and his brother-in-law, who’d got his bike. Xiao Pan, on the small red one, with Elowen on the back.

Serafina, with Haozhen, whose arm was out of the sling, and whose name she knew now. He stood by the dyno for half an hour looking at it and didn’t say anything, and Serafina said that meant he loved it.

Her father, in a new coat, who’d come on the bus from the sea side, and who stood at the long low window looking in for ten minutes before he came through the door. He brought a pigeon in a basket. He said it was for luck. He said it was the fastest one he had and he’d named it after her.

Her family. The other one. Lin Jian, who came in the black car and stood in the street looking at the sign before he came in. Elowen and Zhao. Evangeline, in pale blue, with Jun Hyuk beside her, enormous, who walked round the whole floor asking her questions about the five-axis mill until Evangeline put her hand on his arm and he stopped. Elara, from a night shift, in scrubs. Eliana, who said spreadsheet and put a camera on the ceiling that nobody had asked for.

And the sign.

Up over the arched door, on its bolts, at the height of the old chandler’s name. Four steel letters. JINX. Plain and grey, with the cut marks on the edges.

✦ ✦ ✦

The customer came at four o’clock.

She was at the long low window, with a cup of Mrs. Tong’s tea, watching the street. She saw him before he came in. A young man, late twenties, in a good leather jacket, with clean boots and a watch she could see from across the street. He stood outside the window and looked in, at the bikes, at the benches, at her. Then he came through the arched door.

“Jinx,” he said. “Congratulations. Beautiful place.”

She didn’t say anything.

“I want a bike,” he said. “Something special. Something fast. Something that doesn’t look like much, and can carry a case on the back, and nobody can catch.” He smiled. “I heard you’re bad luck for the police. I heard nothing you build ever gets caught.”

She looked at him.

She didn’t know his name, but she knew him. She’d known men like him since she was twelve. They’d come down the lane under the flyover in good jackets and clean boots and stood in the yard and looked at what was ready. She knew the jacket. She knew the boots. She knew the voice, polite and pleased, as if he were ordering dinner. She knew exactly who he worked for, and who that man worked for, and where the case was going.

Across the floor, by the dyno, Raiden had stopped talking to the old man from the magazines.

He didn’t come over. She saw him not come over. She saw him put his hands in his pockets and stand still by the dyno and watch her, from across the whole length of the floor, and not move.

“No,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

The young man kept smiling.

“I’ll pay,” he said. “Whatever you ask. Double. Cash.”

“No.”

“You haven’t heard what—”

“I know what,” said Jinx. “It’s standing in my shop in a jacket that cost more than a car.” She put down the tea. “I’ll build you a bike to ride. Saturday nights, the shipyard road. I’ll charge you a fortune and it’ll be the best thing you’ve ever sat on.” She looked at him. “I don’t build bikes for cases.”

He looked at her for a moment.

“Nobody says no to—”

“Everybody says no to someone,” said Jinx. “I’m saying it to you. Go and tell whoever sent you that the bad luck’s retired.”

He stood there.

He looked round. The anchor woman was looking at him. So were Mrs. Tong, and Big Fok, and half the riders from Saturday nights, and an old man in a new coat with a pigeon in a basket. A big grey man by the paint booth, who had once been the most frightening man in the Walled City, was looking at him with mild interest. A man in black by the arch, with his hands in his pockets, looked at him for four seconds.

He left.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden came across the floor.

He came through all the people, slowly, with his hands in his pockets, and stopped in front of her at the long low window. He didn’t say anything. He looked at her.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing,” said Raiden. “I’m just looking at you.”

“Stop it.”

“No,” said Raiden. “Never. I’m going to look at you saying no to a man in a good jacket in your own shop for the rest of my life. I’m going to draw it. I’m going to draw it every day.”

She looked at him. Then she put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart, the way she had on the night of the Peak drawings, when she’d said I’m frightened.

“I’m not frightened,” she said.

He put his hand over hers.

“I know,” he said. “I can see.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, when everyone had gone, they sat on the step of the chandler’s warehouse under the sign.

It was cold. November. The street was empty. The cranes were lit up over the roofs and somewhere out in the basin a ship was sounding its horn, long and low, the way it had on the first Sunday, in May 2021, when he’d sat on the crate until six o’clock waiting for her to say Thursday.

She had his jacket round her shoulders. He had his arm round her.

Above them, the four steel letters.

“You built me a window,” she said.

“I did.”

“Everyone looked in. All day.”

“They did,” said Raiden. “They looked at you. And nobody took anything. And you said no to a man in a good jacket, and he went away.” He kissed her temple. “That’s all I ever wanted for you. A room everybody can see into, and nobody can take you out of.”

She turned her head and looked at him.

Then she kissed him, on the step, under the sign, slowly, the way she had on the roof in the Walled City at midnight, with her hand on his face and the ship’s horn still going out in the basin. And he kissed her back with his cold hand on the back of her neck, under the sign with her name on it, until the horn stopped.

Behind them, in the long low window, a light was still on over her bench.

Anybody walking down the street could see it.

chapters.title: The Fire at the Shop
chapters.desc: June 2025. Two in the morning, a camera nobody asked for, and smoke coming out of the long low window. He runs three doors down barefoot. She comes out of the back lane through a stair he drew, black to the eyes. Then six weeks, and every Lin with tools.
chapters.epigraph: “I said the roof would never fall on your head. I didn’t say I’d be calm about it.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
His phone screamed at nine minutes past two in the morning.

Not rang. Screamed. A sound he’d never heard it make, high and flat, over and over, and he was out of the bed before he was awake, in the dark of the long room above the black door, reaching for it on the floor.

The screen was red.

SMOKE — JINX — FLOOR — CAM 3.

Eliana’s camera. The one on the ceiling of the shop that nobody had asked for. He’d laughed at it. Everyone had. Spreadsheet, she’d said, and put it up in November, and wired it into something, and gone home.

He turned round to the bed.

The bed was empty.

Her side was cold. She’d said, at eleven, I’m going to finish the tank. A commission. A collector’s tank, in a candy red that had to go on in nine thin coats with an hour between each one, and she’d said I’ll sleep on the sofa upstairs at the shop, don’t wait up. And he’d said don’t breathe the paint, and kissed her, and gone to sleep.

He didn’t put his shoes on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The street was full of smoke.

He came out of the side door of the black one barefoot, in his shorts and a T-shirt, with his phone in his hand still screaming, and the whole street was grey. It was coming out of the chandler’s warehouse. Three doors down. Out of the long low window, which had cracked, and out of the gap under the big steel shutter, thick, rolling, and inside it, through the window, low down at the back of the floor, a moving orange light.

He ran.

He didn’t remember running. He remembered the cobbles under his bare feet, and the smoke in his mouth, and the sound. A roar. Like the triple under the flyover, but low and enormous and wrong. And the anchor woman’s door opening, and her shouting something, and a siren a long way off, coming.

He got to the shutter. It was hot. He put his hands on it and it burned him and he didn’t take them off.

“Jia,” he said. And then, louder, at the top of his voice, the way he’d yelled in the hangar in the north. “JIA.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t know where she was.

Afterwards, when he tried to tell her about it, that was the only part he could say. He stood in the smoke with his hands on the hot shutter and he didn’t know where she was. On the sofa, upstairs, on the mezzanine, behind the glass, above the floor. Or at the paint booth, at the back. Or at her bench. He didn’t know. He’d drawn every centimetre of that building and he didn’t know where in it she was.

He tried the shutter. It was locked. From inside.

He tried the side door. It was hot. He got it open a crack and smoke came out of it like water out of a pipe and knocked him back into the street, coughing, on his knees.

He got up. He went back to it.

Someone grabbed him.

The anchor woman. She was seventy and she grabbed him round the waist from behind with both arms and held on like a woman holding an anchor chain, and he fought her, and she didn’t let go, and then there were other hands, Mrs. Tong’s, and then the first fire engine came round the corner at the top of the street with its lights going and men got out of it in yellow and one of them took him by the shoulders and said is anyone inside and he said my wife.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went in.

Two of them, with masks, through the side door. They told him to stay back. They told him twice. The anchor woman held his arm. He stood in the street in the smoke in his bare feet with his burned hands and watched the side door where they’d gone in, and didn’t breathe.

Everyone he loves is something someone else can take.

He’d thought it was men. He’d thought it was people. Guo. A man in a good jacket. Someone who’d look at the useless Lin boy for half a second and know. He’d built her a steel room and a stair to the roof and laminated windows and a wall that would take a truck, against men.

He hadn’t thought about fire. Nobody at all, just a building burning with her in it.

The paint, he thought. Nine coats of candy red. Thinners. The booth. Don’t breathe the paint.

He stood there.

And from behind him, from the back lane, round the end of the street, where nobody went, a voice said, in between coughing, flat and exact and furious:

“The battery. It was the battery. The delivery boy’s.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He turned round.

She was standing at the corner of the back lane.

She was in her vest and her overalls tied at the waist, black from her hair to her boots. Her face was black except round her mouth and nose, where she’d had the paint mask on, and her eyes were streaming, and she was coughing so hard she had one hand on the wall. Under her other arm, wrapped in her jacket, was a candy-red motorcycle tank.

“Some boy’s e-bike,” she said, coughing. “Left on charge. In bay two. A cheap charger. I told him. I told him on Tuesday it was cheap. I heard it pop. Through the floor. I was asleep and I heard it pop.” She coughed. “Then the battery went up. They do that. They go up like a bomb. I couldn’t get to it. It was too—so I went out the stair.”

He didn’t move.

“The stair,” said Jinx. “Your stair. Behind the bookshelf on the mezzanine. I went out the stair.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d drawn it in April 2024.

A stair. A narrow one, in a shaft, lined with fire board, two hours’ rating, with its own door at the top, steel, that looked like part of the bookshelf in the mezzanine office. You pushed the third shelf. It went down inside the back wall of the building, behind the paint booth, where nothing else could be, and came out through a steel door at the bottom into the back lane. Nobody knew about it: not the builders, who’d built it in pieces without being told what it was, not the fire inspector, not even her, until he’d shown her, on the night before the opening, with the door shut and the lamp on.

If you ever need it, push the third shelf, he’d said. And go down. And don’t stop. And don’t go back for anything.

She’d gone back for the tank.

He looked at the tank.

“You went back for the tank,” he said.

“It’s a commission,” said Jinx. “Nine coats. I wasn’t leaving it.” She coughed. “It was on the bench by the shelf. It was a metre. I didn’t go back. It was on the way.”

He crossed the street.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t remember crossing it.

He was standing in front of her at the corner of the back lane. He took the tank out from under her arm and put it on the ground, carefully, on the anchor woman’s cushion, which the anchor woman had somehow brought. Then he put his hands on her face, his burned ones, on her black cheeks.

She looked at him. At his hands.

“You’ve burned your hands,” she said.

“The shutter.”

“You touched the shutter.”

“I was trying to get in,” said Raiden. His voice wasn’t working. “I didn’t know where you were. I drew every centimetre of that building and I didn’t know where you were.”

She looked at him in the smoke, with the fire engines going behind him and the water starting, and her eyes streaming.

“I was on the stair,” she said. “Where you put it.”

He kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was smoke. It was ash. It was her black face and the taste of burning and her coughing against his mouth and him not stopping. He kissed her at the corner of the back lane with his burned hands on her face and the whole street watching, Mrs. Tong and the anchor woman and three firemen and the man who sold marine paint in his pyjamas, and she grabbed the front of his T-shirt in both fists and held on, and kissed him back so hard they both nearly went over.

“Breathe,” said a fireman behind them, at last. “Miss. You need oxygen. Both of you. Please. Breathe.”

She pulled back an inch, her forehead on his.

“You said the roof would never fall on my head,” she said. “It didn’t.”

He made a sound that wasn’t a word.

“I didn’t say I’d be calm about it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They spent the rest of the night at the City Hospital.

The same one. Not the sixth floor. The emergency department, on two trolleys, side by side, with masks on their faces and a nurse who kept telling him to lie down. Smoke. They’d both breathed a lot of it. She had a burn on her left forearm, under the carp, from the door handle of the stair. He had burns on both palms, from the shutter, the kind that blister, and a nurse dressed them and wrapped them in white so that his hands looked like two clouds.

He couldn’t draw. He couldn’t hold a pencil.

He lay on the trolley with his white hands on his chest and turned his head and looked at her, on the next trolley, with the mask on her face, looking at the ceiling.

“Last time,” he said, through his mask, “you sat by me all night.”

“I remember.”

“You held my hand.”

She turned her head. She looked at his hands, in their white wrapping.

Then she reached across the gap between the trolleys, and put her hand carefully on his wrist, above the dressing, where it wasn’t burned, and left it there.

At five in the morning, Elara came down from the wards in her scrubs, with her hair everywhere, and looked at both of them, and said, “Again?” in a voice that went right up the corridor.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the battery.

The fire investigator said so on the Monday. A cheap lithium battery in a cheap e-bike, on a cheap charger, left overnight in bay two by a delivery rider who’d brought it in on Tuesday with a broken brake. It had overheated, and gone into what she called thermal runaway, and burned so hot and so fast that it had set light to the bench and the tyres racked above it, and the smoke had done the rest.

Nobody had done it. Nobody had come for her.

He’d thought somebody had. He’d thought it all night, on the trolley, with his hands in clouds. He’d thought Guo. He’d thought the man in the good jacket. On the Saturday, before the investigator came, he’d taken a taxi to Sandpit Lane with his hands still wrapped, because he couldn’t have held the bars, and stood across the street from number forty, where the third floor was propped with steel now and the gold cat waved in the window, and he’d looked at it.

He’d gone home again.

“I thought it was him,” he told her, on the Monday night, after the investigator.

“I know.”

“I went to look.”

“I know,” said Jinx. “Mrs. Tong saw you go.” She put her hand on his face. “It was a battery. Sometimes it’s just a battery.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop was black inside.

The fire had gone up the back wall from bay two and along the ceiling and down the other side. The benches on the left were gone, and the racks and the tyres. The paint booth was scorched but sealed; the fire hadn’t got in. The lathe, the big German one, was black with soot and fine underneath, because a lathe that size didn’t care. The five-axis was damaged, the electronics. The dyno, in its pit, was untouched.

The mezzanine was blackened, the glass front cracked. The bookshelf with the third shelf was charred all down one side.

The stair behind it was clean, as if nothing had happened.

She stood in the middle of the black floor on the Tuesday morning, with her arm in its dressing, and looked at all of it. He stood beside her with his hands in theirs.

“Six months,” she said. “To rebuild. Maybe more.”

“No,” said a voice behind them.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was Elowen.

In the arched doorway, in green, with her sleeves rolled up. And behind her, Zhao, carrying a box of tools that looked like it weighed as much as she did, as if it weighed nothing. And behind him a lorry, in the street, with four men getting out of it in work clothes who didn’t look at anyone and started unloading scaffolding.

“Six weeks,” said Elowen.

Jinx looked at her.

“Zhendong’s men do the walls,” said Elowen. “Aurelia’s sending a glazier. She says she’s paying and if anyone argues she’ll be unbearable about it at New Year.” She came into the black shop and looked round, coolly, at the ceiling. “Eliana’s doing the wiring. All of it. She says the camera worked and she’s never going to let anyone forget it.”

“Elara?”

“Is on nights. She’ll come on her days off. She’s very good at small things.” Elowen looked at her. “And Ev.”

Jinx turned.

Evangeline was in the doorway behind her sister, in grey, with her sleeves rolled up and a paint roller in one hand and a tray in the other. Behind her, filling the whole arched doorway, Jun Hyuk, with a steel beam on his shoulder that four men had been going to carry off the lorry, and that he was carrying on his own, and talking, all the way in, about whether the new one should be heavier.

Evangeline looked at Jinx.

She nodded, once.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took six weeks and two days.

They came every day. All of them. Not all at once, in shifts, the way the Lins did everything, without anyone deciding. Zhao’s men did the walls and the ceiling. Aurelia’s glazier did the long low window, the whole width, and the mezzanine glass, and Aurelia came twice, in gold, and stood in the middle of the floor and pointed at things and was unbearable. Eliana rewired the building in nine days, on her own, in a hoodie, with her laptop open on the floor and the camera blinking above her, and put in two more cameras that nobody asked for. Elara came on her days off and did all the small jobs nobody else wanted, the switches and the fittings and the little brackets, with her surgeon’s hands, fast and neat, humming.

Evangeline painted.

She did every wall and every ceiling on her own, in grey, in silence, with a roller, day after day, while Jun Hyuk carried things and talked. She painted the whole inside of the building white, three coats, and didn’t say a word to anyone, and on the last day, on the back wall, by the stair, low down, where nobody would ever see it unless they knew, she painted a small carp.

Serafina came with a big man called Wu and a girl with two laptops and they fixed the five-axis between them in a weekend. Her father came on the bus from the sea side every Saturday and swept. Lin Jian came once, on a Thursday, in the black car, and stood in the middle of the floor in his good coat and looked at it, and then took off his coat and picked up a broom and swept beside her father for two hours, the two of them, two old men who’d once stood on opposite sides of a desk under a flyover, sweeping the same floor in silence.

Jinx saw it from the mezzanine.

She stood at the new glass front and looked down at them, side by side, with their brooms. She didn’t say anything. She stood there with her hand on the glass until Raiden came and stood beside her and saw what she was looking at, and put his hand, unwrapped now, healing, over hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

They reopened on the twenty-sixth of July.

No party. She’d said no, and meant it, and he hadn’t argued. She just put the big steel shutter up at seven in the morning and turned the lights on and opened the long low window, and went to her bench, the new one, the same height, in the same place, and started work.

At ten o’clock he came down the street with three coffees.

She looked up from the bench. He was standing in the arched door in the morning light, with the tray, and his healed hands, and his sketchbook under his arm, the way he’d stood in the black door that Sunday in May 2021, a lifetime ago.

“Good morning,” he said.

She took the black one. And the one with milk. And the one with condensed milk.

He sat down on a crate at the end of her bench, close, in the light from the long window, and opened his sketchbook, and drew her drinking all three.

Upstairs on the mezzanine, behind the third shelf of the new oak bookshelf, the stair was still there, clean and lined with fire board, in case.

chapters.title: “Is That a Racetrack?”
chapters.desc: October 2025. A drawing left on his desk on purpose: a house on a hill, a workshop on the roof under glass, two workbenches, and something long and curly in the garden. He says it’s a driveway. It is a racetrack.
chapters.epigraph: “Let me be rich at you. Just once. Just this. I’ve been practising for four years.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
Serafina crashed at the Needle on the fourteenth of September, and for a week Jinx didn’t sleep.

They went to the hospital on the second night. Serafina was on the ninth floor with her left arm strapped across her chest, a new plate in her collarbone, the breathing tube only just out of her throat, and her face grey, and Haozhen sat beside the bed in the same chair he hadn’t got out of in forty hours. Jinx stood at the end of the bed and didn’t say anything. She’d been the one who’d said you never bring it back with a hole in it, and now there were holes in Serafina, and Jinx stood at the end of the bed with her hands in her pockets and felt every one of them.

Serafina looked at her.

“Don’t,” said Serafina, in a voice the tube had scraped down to almost nothing. “Don’t look at me like I’m a bike you can’t fix.”

“I can fix bikes,” said Jinx.

“I know,” said Serafina. “That’s why I hate it.”

On the way home in the taxi, Raiden held her hand and didn’t say anything.

That night she lay on her back in the long room above the black door and looked at the ceiling until four. And the next night. And the next. And on the fourth night he got up at two and went down to the workshop, and she heard the light go on, and his pencil, and she lay there and listened to it for two hours, and didn’t go down, and fell asleep at last to the sound of it, the way she used to fall asleep to the cranes.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Saturday in October she found the drawing on his desk.

On the mezzanine at the shop, at seven in the morning, before he came in. He never left anything out, not since the Peak drawings in June 2023. Every drawing he made went into the safe in the steel room before he went to bed.

This one was in the middle of his desk, flat, with nothing on top of it.

She looked at it for a while before she touched it.

He’d left it there on purpose. She knew that. He’d left it there the way he’d left three coffees on her bench every morning for four years. So she’d find it.

She sat down in his chair.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a house.

On a hill. He’d drawn the hill first, from the side, in long soft lines, with the contours marked, and trees. A valley below it. Water at the bottom of the valley, a long thin lake. A road along the edge of the lake that she knew, the reservoir road, the one you took to Fig Tree Lane. Except this hill was on the other side of the valley. Looking across at it.

And on the top of the hill, a house.

Long and low. Concrete and glass and dark timber. Two storeys, built into the slope so the bottom one was half underground at the back. A kitchen, a long one, with a long table and eight chairs, at one end, with windows down to the floor looking out over the valley. A bed at the other end. A bath in a tower, a round one, with a window at the top so you could lie in the bath and see the sky. A drafting room for him. A bench for her, by a window. A shelf over the bench.

And on the roof, a workshop.

Glass and steel. A long shed of it, the whole length of the roof, with benches down both sides, two of them, side by side. And a lift, a big one, a goods lift, going down through the house from the roof to the ground, big enough for a bike. And a balcony round the outside of the workshop on all four sides, so you could walk out of it with a cup of tea and stand over the whole valley.

At the bottom of the sheet, the scale bar. 1:200.

There was no question under it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She turned the sheet over.

On the back, there was a plan of the land. From above. The house on the top of the hill. The road coming up to it from the reservoir road, in long curves, through the trees.

And the driveway.

It didn’t go to the house. It went past the house, and round it, and down the other side of the hill, and back up, in a long loop. She traced it with her finger. Out from the gate in a long straight, and then a tight left, and a fast right, and a long sweeping curve round the shoulder of the hill, and down into a dip, and a hairpin, and up again, and a chicane, two quick bends, left and right, and a straight back to the gate.

It was marked in his capitals at the side: 1.2 KM.

She sat there in his chair with her finger on the hairpin.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in at ten with three coffees.

He came up the stairs to the mezzanine and stopped at the top, and saw her in his chair, with the sheet turned over on the desk in front of her, and her finger still on the hairpin.

He put the coffees down on the desk carefully.

“Ah,” he said.

She looked up at him.

“Is that a racetrack?” she said.

“It’s a driveway.”

“It’s got a hairpin.”

“It’s a hilly site,” said Raiden. “The road has to go round.”

“Raiden,” said Jinx. “It’s one point two kilometres long and it doesn’t go to the house. It goes round the house. Twice.”

“It’s a very long driveway,” said Raiden, and his face didn’t move at all, and then it did, all at once, and he started laughing, and couldn’t stop, and had to sit down on the edge of his own desk.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her.

He’d found the land in the spring. On the other side of the valley from Fig Tree Lane, looking across at Ev’s house, so that on a clear night they’d be able to see each other’s lights across the water. Forty acres. A hill, and woods, and an old farm road nobody used, and a spring at the bottom that came out of the rock. Owned by an old man who’d had it from his father and wanted it to go to someone who wouldn’t put a hundred houses on it.

“I told him I’d put one house on it,” said Raiden. “And a workshop. And a very long driveway. He looked at me and then said yes.”

“You bought it.”

“In June. After the fire.” He looked at her. “In your name. And mine. Both. That’s new. I’ve never put my name on anything I’ve given you before.” He hesitated. “I wanted it to be ours. Not yours that I live in. Ours.”

She looked at the drawing.

“I’ve been drawing it since the fire,” he said. “Every night, while you were asleep. I couldn’t sleep either. I kept thinking about the stair. That you went down it and it held.” He rubbed his face. “And I thought, I want to build you something that isn’t a stair or a steel room. A house on a hill, where you can see anything coming up the road a mile off. Nothing to run from. Nothing to hide in. Just building things and driving round in circles.” He smiled. “On the driveway.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“It’s too much,” she said.

She’d said it about the dyno. She’d said it about the lathe. He’d said I know, I’m a Lin, I’m rich, I like you, that’s what happens, and she’d stopped saying it.

She was saying it now.

“I know,” said Raiden. “It’s far too much. It’s the most I’ve ever done.” He came round the desk and crouched down beside the chair, the way he’d knelt on the floor of the long room with the thirty-first napkin, so his face was below hers. “Let me be rich at you. Just once. Just this. I’ve been practising for four years. The coffees. The building. The dyno. They were all practice. This is what they were for.”

She looked down at him.

At his face, the pencil behind his ear, his hands, healed now, with the new pink skin on the palms where the shutter had been.

“I’m paying half,” she said.

He blinked.

“The house,” said Jinx. “Half. I’ve got money. I’ve got a waiting list two years long. I haven’t been poor since the black door.” She put her finger back on the hairpin. “You pay for the driveway. It’s the most ridiculous thing anyone’s ever drawn and I want you to have paid for it. The house is half mine.”

He stared at her.

“And I build the workshop,” she said. “On the roof. Myself. You draw it. I build it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He started to laugh again, quietly this time, with his forehead down on her knee.

“You’re paying half,” he said into her overalls. “For a house I drew. On a hill I bought.”

“Half of which is mine. You said.”

He lifted his head. His eyes were wet. “Four years ago you wouldn’t let me buy you a mirror.” He took her hand off the drawing and kissed the inside of her wrist, where the carp’s tail was. “Half. Yes. All right. Yes. You can pay half of anything you like for the rest of our lives.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went to see it that afternoon.

In the sidecar, out along the reservoir road, past the turning for Fig Tree Lane, with the lake going blue and silver on their left and the hills going gold. He had the board out over his knees and wasn’t drawing, just holding on, with his face turned up to the sun.

There was an old wooden gate hanging off one hinge. She stopped in front of it, and he got out, and lifted it, and walked it open, and she rode through, slowly, onto an old farm road going up through the trees.

At the top there was nothing.

Just long gold grass going down the hill on every side, a broken stone wall, and a big old tree on its own with its branches out. Below them was the whole valley and the lake, and on the other side of the lake, on its own hill, tiny, a white house with a deep verandah, and a garden going down to a stream.

“That’s Ev’s,” said Raiden.

She stood beside the sidecar and looked at it.

Then she looked at the long gold grass, and the top of the hill, where he’d drawn the house. And down the slope, where he’d drawn the driveway going round the shoulder of the hill, and down into the dip, and up again.

She could see the whole thing, the way she could see an engine before she built it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d brought a blanket.

Of course he had. And a basket, from Mrs. Tong’s, with noodles in tubs and a flask and two bottles of beer. He spread the blanket out under the big old tree on the top of the hill and sat down on it, and held up his hand to her.

She took it. He pulled her down.

She ended up on top of him on the blanket in the long grass, with her knees either side of him and her hands on his chest, and he lay back and looked up at her with the branches over his head and the sky behind them and his whole face shining.

“Is that a yes?” he said.

“You didn’t ask a question.”

“No,” he said. “I didn’t, did I. I left it off the drawing.” He put his hands on her waist. “I’m asking now. Will you build a house with me on a hill, with a workshop on the roof and a bath in a tower and a driveway that’s definitely not a racetrack, and live in it, and drive round it in circles, until we’re very old and very annoying and Eliana has to come and put us in a home?”

She looked down at him.

“Yes,” she said, and bent down and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed up there all afternoon.

Under the old tree on the top of the hill, on his blanket, in the long gold grass, with the noodles going cold in the basket and the beer going warm. It was slow and lazy and full of laughing, the way it had been on the floor of the Meridian with his arm in plaster, the way it had been in the flour. He kissed her and she kissed him and he rolled her over into the grass and she rolled him back, and they argued about whether the bath should be in a tower, she said it would be cold, he said that was what the sky was for, and he kissed her in the middle of the argument and she lost it on purpose.

“I want to,” he said, against her neck. “Here. Under the tree. Can I?”

“There’s nobody for a mile.”

“That’s not an answer,” said Raiden, and lifted his head and looked at her, seriously, with grass in his hair. “Is it yes?”

She had his shirt unbuttoned before he’d finished asking.

“Yes,” she said, against his mouth. “Yes.”

The grass was warm and it prickled, and when she swore at it he laughed and rolled them over so it was under his back instead. He took his time. He kissed the place on her shoulder where the strap of her vest had been, and the carp, and the hollow of her throat, and she pulled him up by the hair to get his mouth back, and they started arguing about the bath again for one breath and then didn’t. The sun came down through the branches in pieces. A long way below them a car went along the reservoir road and didn’t stop. And when it was over they lay on their backs on the blanket with her head on his chest and the whole valley under them going from gold to pink to blue, and across the lake, on the other hill, the lights came on in the white house with the verandah, one by one.

“They can see us,” said Jinx.

“No, they can’t. We’re under a tree.”

“They’ll see our lights. When there are lights.”

“Yes,” said Raiden. “That’s the point. Every night.” He kissed the top of her head. “Ev on her side and you on yours, with a lake in between.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He drew her afterwards.

Lying in the grass, with her arm behind her head, in his shirt, looking across at the lights.

It took him ten minutes.

He’d been able to do it in ten minutes since May 2024. He’d drawn her hundreds of times since then, and the full sketchbooks were in a box under the bed. Her at the bench. Her on the creeper. Her in the bath. Her saying no to a man in a good jacket. Her in the smoke at the corner of the back lane with a candy-red tank under her arm. Her face. Every time, her face.

He showed it to her.

She looked at it. At herself, in the grass, at the top of a hill that was half hers, looking at her sister-in-law’s lights.

“Put that on the house drawing,” she said.

“What?”

“The one from your desk. In the corner, by the scale bar.”

He looked at her.

“So that when they build it,” said Jinx, “whoever builds it knows who it’s for.”

He didn’t say anything. He took the drawing of the house out of his jacket, folded, the one with the racetrack, where he’d put it, against his chest, and unfolded it on the blanket, and in the corner, beside the scale bar, small, he drew her again, in the grass, looking at the lights.

Then he wrote, underneath, in his capitals:

FOR J. (SHE’S PAYING HALF.)

chapters.title: The Roof Never Falls
chapters.desc: October 2026, a mountain hillclimb, sidecar class. She drives. He’s the passenger, hanging off the chair with pace notes he drew himself. They win by 1.4 seconds and kiss at the finish. Then the epilogue: a roof he designed, a spring night, and the lights across the lake.
chapters.epigraph: “I promised you the roof would never fall on your head. I didn’t promise I’d ever stop building you roofs.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
The passenger in a racing sidecar is called the monkey, and for the first two weeks Raiden refused to answer to it.

“I’m the navigator,” he said.

“You’re the monkey.”

“Navigators have maps. I have maps. I’ve drawn every corner of that mountain at one to five hundred. I’ve walked it four times. I know where the drains are.” He was sitting in the chair of the outfit in the shop, on its stand, with his knees up and his pace notes in a plastic sleeve on a board on his lap, looking at her with great dignity. “Monkeys don’t have maps.”

“Monkeys hang off the side,” said Jinx, “and move their weight so the outfit doesn’t flip over. That’s what you’ll be doing. For six kilometres. At a hundred and forty. You’ll be hanging off the side with your head a hand’s width off the road.”

He looked at her.

“With maps,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

It had been her idea, though afterwards nobody believed it, not Elowen or Serafina or the old man from the magazines. She’d built sidecars since 2022, since the first one, the one with the board over the knees and the tray for pencils. She’d built four since. She’d raced none of them. She didn’t race. She tested.

But in the spring, in the new shop, a man had come in with a brochure for the hillclimb on the mountain road in the north, the old pass, which closed for one weekend every October. Six kilometres. Ninety-one corners. Classes for cars, which she didn’t care about, and bikes, which she did, and sidecars, which nobody entered any more, because there were only two outfits left in the country that could do it and their owners were both over sixty.

She’d looked at the brochure for a while.

Then she’d looked up, at the mezzanine, where he was drawing at his desk behind the glass.

“Raiden,” she’d said. Not loud.

He’d heard. He always heard.

✦ ✦ ✦

They practised all summer.

On the driveway.

The house on the hill had been finished in August. Not all of it. The inside was still bare concrete in places and the bath in the tower didn’t have its window yet. But the driveway was done. All one point two kilometres. Tarmac, black and smooth, round the shoulder of the hill and down into the dip and the hairpin and up through the chicane and back to the gate. He’d had it laid in June. He’d stood at the gate in the evening with the men from the tarmac company and watched the last of it go down and said it’s a driveway, and the foreman had looked at him and said yes, Mr. Lin, and not laughed.

They went round it every evening.

They went round in the outfit, with the lights on when it got dark: her on the bike, low and flat, with her hands on the bars and her knee on the pad, and him beside her on the chair’s platform, kneeling, hanging on to the grab rails, moving. Out over the wheel on the right-handers, as far as he could go, with his whole body off the side and his face over the road, so the chair stayed down. Back over the bike on the lefts, half on top of her, with his chest against her back and his arm round her, so the outfit didn’t lift. Shouting the notes in her ear. Left three, tightens. Over crest. Right one, long. In order, all the way round, the way he’d counted in the freezer.

The first time, he was sick in the grass by the hairpin.

The second time, he fell off. At twenty kilometres an hour, in the chicane, gently, into a hedge, and lay there laughing.

The tenth time, they went round without speaking at all except the notes. And when they stopped at the gate, she turned the engine off, and sat there, and he knelt in the chair beside her, breathing hard, with his hair everywhere and grass on his knees and his face still, and she could see he’d been doing what she did: not thinking, listening, the way she listened to engines.

“You felt it,” she said.

“I felt it,” said Raiden. “I felt the chair go light on the crest. Before it went. I moved before you told me.” He looked at her. “Is that what it’s like? For you? All the time?”

“Yes.”

He didn’t say anything. He reached across from the chair and took her face in his hands, with his gloves still on, and kissed her, there at the gate, with the engine ticking as it cooled and the lights coming on in the white house across the lake.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hillclimb was on the first Sunday in October.

The whole family came.

They stood at the finish line, at the top of the pass, in the cold, in a row. Lin Jian in his good coat. Elowen in green with Zhao in black. Evangeline in pale blue with Jun Hyuk, who’d brought a flask and a folding chair for his father-in-law and a bag of pastries for everyone and was telling the marshal beside him, at length, how the sidecar’s steering worked. Elara, with the tall doctor in glasses. Eliana, with a laptop and a camera on a stick and a boy from next door. Her father, with a pigeon in a basket, which he’d been told not to bring, and had brought.

Serafina, on the wall by the timing hut, with her husband, in a red jumper, shouting things.

And the old man from the magazines, at the timing hut, with a stopwatch of his own, because he didn’t trust the electronic one.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were three outfits in the sidecar class.

Two from the north, old ones, beautiful, owned by men who’d been racing them since the eighties. They went first. One did six kilometres in four minutes and nine seconds. The other in four minutes and seven.

The black outfit went last.

She’d built it in the new shop over the spring. Long and low and black, with the carp on the tank, swimming up toward a spark plug, and the chair beside it, a flat platform with grab rails, nothing on it at all except one word, MONKEY, scratched into the steel by his left knee in her bad capitals. No board. No tray for pencils. No seat. He’d asked her, in April, if he could have the board. She’d said no. He’d said what about the pencils. She’d said you can put one behind your ear.

He had one behind his ear. Under the helmet. She’d watched him put it there at the start.

They sat on the line.

The start marshal held up his hand. Five fingers. Four.

She felt Raiden, beside her, kneeling on the platform, still. She felt him breathe out.

“Left four,” he said, in her helmet, through the radio. “Long. Then the bridge.”

The marshal dropped his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember most of it.

She remembered it the way she remembered the shipyard road, in pieces, frozen, like lightning going off. The first left, long, and the bridge, and him coming back over the bike, half on top of her, his chest against her back, his arm round her ribs. The hairpin at the first kilometre, a right, and the engine screaming, and the chair going light, and him out over the wheel before she said anything, all of him, so far she couldn’t see him at the edge of her eye, his voice in her ear saying crest, crest, hold it. The long fast right along the side of the mountain with the drop on the left and nothing between them and the valley but a wall the height of her knee. The trees. The rock. The marshals at the side of the road with their flags, going past in a smear.

And his voice. The whole way. In order. Right two. Left one, tight. Over crest, keep in. Right three, opens. Never once wrong. Never once late. Every corner she came to, he’d already told her what it was.

She’d never driven anything like it, and she’d never done anything like it with someone else. She’d always been alone: under a bike, on the shipyard road, in the yard under the flyover at five in the morning with a widowmaker that wouldn’t start. She’d built her whole life with her own hands, alone, on purpose, because that was the one thing nobody could take.

And she came round the last corner of the pass, the long right before the finish, flat out, with the chair going light and him hanging off the side of it with his whole body out over the road and his voice in her ear saying last one, last one, go, Jia, go, and she wasn’t alone at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Four minutes and five point six seconds.

The old man from the magazines read it off his stopwatch. Then off the electronic one. Then off his stopwatch again.

One point four seconds.

She stopped the outfit past the line, on the gravel, in front of the whole family, and turned the engine off, and sat there with her hands on the bars and her chest going.

He was off the chair before she’d got her helmet off.

He came round the front of the outfit, pulling his own helmet off and throwing it on the gravel, and his hair was flattened to his head with sweat and his face was white and his eyes were enormous, and he didn’t say anything. He took her helmet off for her. She let him. He undid the strap under her chin, the way she’d done his for five years, and lifted it off, and put it down on the tank, carefully, on the carp.

Then he kissed her.

In front of everyone. At the top of the pass, on the gravel, with the engine ticking and the whole family at the finish line and Serafina shouting and Eliana filming and the old man from the magazines still holding up his stopwatch. He kissed her with both hands in her hair and his whole body shaking, still, from six kilometres of hanging off the side of a mountain, and she grabbed the front of his leathers in both fists and kissed him back so hard they both went over against the bike.

Behind them, somebody whistled. Somebody else said hm. Lin Jian laughed, the big rusty one, right across the top of the mountain.

“One point four,” said Raiden against her mouth. “We beat a man who’s been doing this since 1983.”

“I know.”

“You didn’t flip it. Not once. I thought we’d flip it on the bridge.”

“You didn’t let it,” said Jinx.

He went still.

“You didn’t let it,” she said again. She put her hands on his face. “You were out over the wheel. The whole time. I didn’t have to tell you. I’ve never—” She stopped, looking for the word. “I’ve never done anything with anyone. Not once. I’ve always done it alone.”

He looked at her.

“Not any more,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

The old man from the magazines came over afterwards.

He looked at the outfit: the carp on the tank, the bare chair with its grab rails, the pencil that had fallen out of Raiden’s helmet and was lying on the platform.

He looked at Raiden.

“You’re the monkey,” he said.

“I’m the navigator,” said Raiden.

The old man looked at him a moment longer. Then at Jinx.

“Not bad,” he said, and went away.

✦ ✦ ✦

They moved into the house on the hill in March 2027.

The window went into the tower in February. The bath under it. The long table went into the kitchen with its eight chairs, and the shelf over her bench, with the glass prize and the Best in Show and the hillclimb trophy and the tin of washers, and the little brass anchor, and Guo’s brother’s old ignition key, which Guo had sent her in a box in the post in 2024 with no note.

The workshop on the roof she built herself.

All spring. With his drawings, which she followed exactly, except twice, where she was right. Steel and glass. Two benches, side by side, his and hers, in the light that came in from all four sides and from the sky. The goods lift down through the house, big enough for a bike. The balcony all round the outside.

And at the back of the workshop, behind a steel cabinet that looked like it had been there forever, a door.

She’d watched him build it. He hadn’t hidden it from her this time. He’d shown her the drawings first. Behind the door was a stair, down through the back wall of the house to the ground and out into the woods, lined with fire board like the last one.

“Just in case,” he’d said, and she hadn’t argued.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eighth of April they went to Fig Tree Lane for the party.

The one on the day in between. Raiden’s birthday and Evangeline’s, which weren’t the same day and never had been, so they had it on the eighth, which was neutral, like Switzerland, and there were two cakes, and they blew the candles out together, both of them, side by side, at the end of the long dark table, and nobody went first. Jun Hyuk carved a duck. Lin Jian had to go out onto the verandah for a minute. Eliana filmed it and posted DRAW (OFFICIAL) and Raiden contested it.

They came home at midnight in the sidecar outfit, the old one, the first one, the one with the board, round the head of the lake and up the long drive that wasn’t a racetrack, slowly, with the lights on.

She didn’t stop at the house.

She went up in the goods lift with the outfit and rode it out onto the roof, into the workshop, in the dark, and turned it off between the two benches, and got off, and went out onto the balcony.

He followed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The valley was black.

The lake was black, with stars in it. The hills on the other side were black. And on the far hill, across the water, there were lights in a white house with a deep verandah: one, two, a third in the window over the garden.

And behind them, on their side, in their own house, every light they had.

She stood at the rail with her hands on it.

He came and stood behind her and put his arms round her waist, with his chin on her shoulder, the way he had on the roof of the noodle factory, and on his father’s roof at New Year.

Below them, on the driveway, nothing moved. Nothing could come up that road without them seeing it a mile off.

“Six years,” he said, into her ear.

“Five years and eleven months,” said Jinx.

He laughed against her neck.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I promised you,” he said, after a while. “On the day I bought you the building. That the roof would never fall on your head.”

“I remember.”

“It didn’t,” said Raiden. “Not once. Not the building. Not the shop. Not in the fire.” He tightened his arms. “I want to promise you something else now. I’m not going to stop. I’m never going to stop building you roofs. Every year. Something. A shelf. A room. A stair. A driveway. Until we’re very old. Until Eliana has to put us in a home, and I’ll build that too, and it’ll have a workshop on the roof.”

She turned round in his arms.

She looked at his face in the dark, with the lights from the workshop behind him, and the pencil behind his ear, the one that had fallen out on the mountain, which he’d picked up off the platform and kept.

She’d never been good with words. She’d never had them. She’d learned to read from workshop manuals at nine, and the first words she’d ever read were torque, and clearance, and do not overtighten.

“I love you,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t move.

She’d never said it. Not once. In six years. Not on the creeper, or in the bath, or in the yard under the flyover, or on the step of the registry office, or at the top of the pass. She’d said I know. She’d said yes. She’d said idiot, which he said was the same thing. She’d never said it.

She watched it go into him, the way she’d watched not yet and yes go into him, all the way down.

“Say it again,” he said. His voice had gone. “I’m sorry. Say it again.”

“I love you, Raiden.”

He put his face in her neck.

He held on, on the balcony of the roof he’d drawn, over the valley, with the lights across the lake. He held on so hard she couldn’t breathe, and she didn’t want to, and she put her hands in his hair and held on back, and somewhere below them in the woods an owl started up, and across the water the light in the window over the garden at Fig Tree Lane went out.

When he lifted his head, she kissed him slowly, with her hands on his face, the way she’d wanted to since a man knelt in the middle of a race and looked up and said oh, hello. And he kissed her back with his hands shaking in her hair, and didn’t let her go until the owl stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, in the workshop, between the two benches, by the light of the outfit’s headlamp, he drew her.

She was at her bench, in her red dress, the one from the flower shop and the registry, with her boots on and the steel ring on its chain and her face doing whatever it wanted, which was smiling.

It took him ten minutes. It always did now.

He wrote something underneath in his capitals, and held it up.

J., AS SHE REALLY IS. R. 2027.

She took it. She went to the back wall of the workshop, where she’d strung a line of string between two nails, with clothes pegs on it. There were drawings already hanging there. The first one, from 2021. J’s bike, as it really is. A crayon motorbike with backwards letters and every fin on every cylinder. And a napkin, the thirty-first, two creepers under a bike, to scale.

She pegged the new one up beside them.

Then she stood back, and he came and stood beside her, and they looked at it together in the light of the headlamp.

chapters.title: Oil on His Cheek
chapters.desc: July 2022. He hovers. He shows her memes. He reads her the safety notices off the welder. She’s been under a gearbox for six hours. She started it.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve had my hands on engines all day. You’re the only thing in here I actually want to get my hands on.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
He’d been hovering for an hour.

She knew he had. She could feel him. He did it on Saturdays, when the firm in the south was shut and he’d drawn everything he wanted to draw and the pale green bike had a flat. He came down to the workshop with his sketchbook and his phone and didn’t sit on the crate. He walked round. He stood behind her. He leaned on things.

She was under the gearbox of a big old touring bike, on the lift, with her arms up inside the casing to the elbow, and he was leaning on the lift.

“Look,” he said.

She didn’t look.

“It’s a dog,” he said, holding the phone down where she could see it, under the bike, upside down. “It’s a dog in a bucket. It’s stuck. Look at its face. It’s not even upset. It’s just living there now.”

“Raiden.”

“That’s you,” he said. “When you’re under a bike. You’re the dog. You’ve just accepted the bucket.”

She got a bolt out. She put it in the tray. She didn’t laugh.

He went away. He came back. He read her the safety notice off the side of the welder, out loud, in the voice of a news announcer. He showed her a video of a goat on a trampoline. He showed her a photograph of a bridge that didn’t meet in the middle. He stood beside the lift and talked about the gearbox, which he knew nothing about, and asked what every part was, and when she told him he said beautiful about each one in a different voice.

It was a hot day. The roll-up door was all the way up. The street outside was white with sun and empty. Mrs. Tong’s radio was going across the road. A fly went round and round the work light.

She’d been under the gearbox for six hours.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four o’clock he asked if she wanted a drink. She said no. He asked if she wanted him to stop talking.

She came out from under the bike.

She didn’t decide to. Her arms just came out of the gearbox casing, black to the elbow, and she ducked out from under the lift, and stood up, and put down the spanner on the bench. She turned round. He was leaning on the lift with his phone in his hand and his sleeves rolled up and his hair falling in his eyes and the pencil behind his ear, looking at her, pleased, the way he always looked when he’d finally got her out from under something.

She walked up to him.

She put her right hand flat on his face, black all over from six hours inside a gearbox, and drew it down his cheek, slowly, from his cheekbone to his jaw, so there was a long black stripe of oil all down one side of his face.

He stood still.

“Oh,” he said.

She took the front of his shirt in the same hand. The white one. And pulled him off the lift, toward her, by the collar, so his face was right in front of hers.

“I’ve had my hands on engines all day,” she said. “You’re the only thing in here I actually want to get my hands on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

For about a second he didn’t say anything. She watched it land. She watched his face go red under the oil, all the way to his hair, the way it had gone at the top of the stairs in the black dress. He opened his mouth. He shut it.

Then he grinned, slowly, the grin that started in his eyes.

“You started it,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I want that on record. I’m going to tell Mrs. Tong. She started it.”

“Tell her,” said Jinx, and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kissed her back like he’d been waiting all day, which he told her afterwards he had. Since about eleven. Since she’d gone under the gearbox in the vest with the strap that kept falling off her shoulder, and he’d stood there with his phone and thought I’m going to show her a dog in a bucket until she comes out.

She told him, against his mouth, that he’d planned it. He said he was an architect, he always planned it, and the dog had been load-bearing.

She laughed into his mouth, and he took the chance and walked her backwards, the four steps to the bench, and lifted her onto it, onto the clean rag she’d laid out for the gearbox parts. The parts went everywhere. A washer rolled off the end and pinged across the floor.

“The parts,” she said.

“I’ll find them,” he said into her neck. “All of them. I’ll put them back in order. Smallest at the top.” He lifted his head. He had oil on his face, and on his neck now too, and on his shirt, in the shape of her hand. “The door’s open. The whole street can see.”

“Mrs. Tong’s asleep. The anchor woman’s at her sister’s. I checked at three.”

He stared at her.

“You planned it too,” he said.

“I’m an engineer,” said Jinx, and pulled his shirt off over his head.

The bench was hard and the rag was oily and neither of them cared. She kept her black hand flat on his chest, over his heart, and watched the print of it spread as he leaned into her, and he laughed into her mouth when he saw what she was doing and let her. The fly went round the work light. Across the road Mrs. Tong’s radio played something with a lot of violins. He kissed her throat, and the strap that kept falling off her shoulder, and took it the rest of the way off, and she stopped watching anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did put the parts back afterwards, in order on the rag, smallest at the top. He went round the whole floor on his hands and knees with no shirt on and oil all down one side of his face, finding them, while she sat on the bench in his shirt and watched him and didn’t help.

He found the washer under the lathe. He held it up.

“Last one,” he said.

She held out her hand. He put it in her palm. He closed her fingers over it with his, and held them.

“Can I draw you?” he said. “Like that. On the bench. In my shirt.”

She looked at him. On his knees on the concrete, with oil on his face and her hand in his.

“You can’t do faces.”

“I know,” said Raiden. “I’ll do the shirt.”

He did the shirt. And her hands, round the washer. And her boots, hanging off the end of the bench, and the gearbox on the lift behind her, and the long white street outside the open door. And when he’d finished he wrote underneath it, in his capitals:

SHE STARTED IT. R. 2022.

She put it on the string with the others. Mrs. Tong saw it there on the Monday and laughed for ten minutes.

chapters.title: Jinx Tries to Cook
chapters.desc: April 2023. The day after his birthday, which he always spends at the Walled City without her. She decides to cook him fish, the way he cooks it. The fire extinguisher is very efficient.
chapters.epigraph: “It was going very well until the oil.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
He always spent his birthday at the Walled City.

The ninth of April. His real one, and Evangeline’s paper one, which wasn’t the same thing, though nobody but the two of them and their father knew that. Two cakes or one cake at the long kitchen table, and the whole family, and Ah Sim, and candles. He’d gone every year since he was ten. He’d gone in 2021 and 2022, when she was still a secret, and come home at midnight with a slice of cake in a napkin for her, and told her what was wrong with everyone.

In 2023 she decided to give him a birthday of his own.

The day after, the tenth, a Monday. Dinner at home above the black door, and she’d cook it.

She’d never cooked anything in her life.

✦ ✦ ✦

She planned it like an engine.

She watched him all March. Every time he made fish, she sat at the long table and watched his hands, and didn’t say why, and he thought she was just watching him, which she was. She learned the order. The ginger first, sliced thin, in matchsticks. The spring onions. The fish, a whole one, scored three times on each side, on a plate, in the steamer, for exactly as long as it took. The soy sauce, warmed. And then, at the end, the oil. Hot. Very hot. Poured over the top so it hissed and the ginger and the onions went bright and the whole room smelled of it.

She wrote it down on the back of an invoice, in capitals.

GINGER. ONION. FISH. 8 MIN. SOY. OIL — HOT — LAST.

She bought the fish on Monday morning from the market at the end of the Docks, at six, before work. A big one, a grouper, that the man said was the best he had. She bought the ginger and the onions. She bought a cake from the shop on Harbour Road, because she wasn’t stupid, and hid it in the steel room behind the tool wall, behind the tin of peaches.

She told him to stay at the firm until seven.

He looked at her for a while over his coffee, all three of hers. Then he said seven, seriously, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was going very well until the oil.

The ginger was fine. She cut it into matchsticks with her good knife from the bench, the one she used for gaskets, neatly, each one exactly the same. The onions were fine. The fish was fine. She scored it three times on each side, measuring with a rule. She put it in the steamer and set her phone for eight minutes and stood over it with her arms folded the whole time, listening to it, the way she listened to a bike on the dyno.

At eight minutes she took it out. It was perfect. She knew it was perfect. It looked exactly like his.

She put the soy on. Warm.

She put the oil in the little pan on the hot plate, to get hot.

She’d written HOT. In capitals. She’d underlined it. And she stood beside the hot plate with the little pan and waited for it to get hot, and it didn’t seem to be doing anything, so she turned the hot plate up. All the way. And waited. And it still didn’t seem to be doing anything, so she went to check the cake was still behind the peaches.

She was gone four minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she came back up the stairs the long room was full of smoke and the little pan was on fire.

Not a bit on fire. On fire. A column of flame, yellow and orange, half a metre high, coming out of it, licking up the wall toward the shelf over the hot plate where he kept the spices.

She didn’t panic. She’d been around fire her whole life. Fuel fires, oil fires, a carburettor that went up in the yard under the flyover when she was eleven and took her eyebrows. You didn’t put water on an oil fire. Water made it worse. You smothered it.

She went to the wall by the door and took down the fire extinguisher he’d hung there in 2022, a big red one, the powder kind, and pulled the pin, and pointed it at the pan, and squeezed.

It was very efficient.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came up the stairs at seven.

He stopped at the top.

The long room was white. All of it. The hot plate. The wall behind it. The shelf with the spices. The long table, and the fish on its plate in the middle of the table, with its ginger and its onions, perfect, under a thick layer of white powder, like snow on a mountain. The floor. The window. The ceiling, in a big white fan above the hot plate.

And her. Standing in the middle of it, in her overalls, white from her hair to her boots, with the extinguisher in her hands, and her face perfectly still.

He looked at the fish.

“It was going very well,” said Jinx, “until the oil.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t laugh.

She saw him not laugh. She saw him try. She saw it start, at the corners of his mouth, and his whole face fight it, and his eyes go wet, and his shoulders start to shake, and him press his lips together so hard they went white. He stood at the top of the stairs with his shoulders going and his eyes streaming and not one sound coming out of him.

“Don’t,” she said.

He made a sound like a kettle.

“Raiden.”

“I’m not,” he said, in a very high voice. “I’m not. I’m not laughing. Jia. I’m not laughing. It’s—you made—you made me the fish.” He looked at it, under its snow. “You made the fish. It looks perfect. You scored it three times. I can see. Under the—” He stopped. He put his hand over his face. “Under the powder.”

“It was perfect,” said Jinx.

“I know it was. I can see it was. I’m so—” His voice went. “I’m so proud of you.”

And then he did laugh.

He laughed so hard he had to sit down on the top stair. He laughed until he couldn’t breathe, with his face in his hands and his whole body going, and she stood in the middle of the white room with the extinguisher and watched him, and felt something happen at the corner of her own mouth, and pressed it flat, and it wouldn’t stay flat, and she started laughing too, out loud, with the extinguisher still in her hands, standing in the snow.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate Mrs. Tong’s noodles on the floor.

On the stairs, actually, because the floor was white. Side by side, on the top step, out of the cartons, with the long room behind them like a ski slope. Mrs. Tong had taken one look at her when she came across the road white to the eyebrows and asked for two beef and hadn’t said a word, and had put in extra beef, and a pair of spring rolls nobody had ordered.

He ate her greens.

When he’d finished, he put the carton down on the step, and turned to her, and looked at the powder in her hair and her eyelashes and on her mouth.

“You’ve got extinguisher on your face,” he said. “All over.”

“I was there,” said Jinx.

He brushed it off her cheek with his thumb, then off the other one, then off her mouth, slowly, his thumb on her bottom lip.

“Happy birthday,” she said.

“It was yesterday.”

“I know. This one’s yours. Not theirs.”

He went still.

Then he leaned in and kissed her. On the top step, in the snow. She tasted of powder and chilli oil and he didn’t care. He kissed her slowly, with his hand on her face, and then not slowly, and pulled her into his lap on the stairs, and they both went sideways onto the step and down two more, and he said ow against her mouth and she laughed again, and he kissed her through it.

“The cake,” she said, at last, against his neck. “There’s a cake.”

“Where?”

“Behind the peaches.”

He lifted his head and looked at her.

“In the safe room,” he said slowly. “You hid my birthday cake in the safest room in the city.”

“It was the only place you’d never look.”

He looked at her a moment longer. Then he put his forehead down on her shoulder, and started laughing again, helplessly, and couldn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate the cake in the steel room, on the bench with the mattress, with the warm lamp on and the door open. It said RAIDEN on it in blue, in the shop’s handwriting. She’d asked them not to put happy birthday. She’d asked them to put his name and nothing else.
