He ate two slices and then sat with his back against the concrete wall and the plate on his knee and looked at her.

“Every year,” he said. “On the tenth. Will you burn something? Promise me you’ll at least try.”

She looked at him. At the cake on his knee, with his name on it and nothing else.

“Every year,” said Jinx.

She did. Every year. Something. In 2024 it was rice. In 2025, a cake of her own, which didn’t rise and which he said was the best biscuit he’d ever eaten. In 2026 it was dumplings, and they went soggy, and stuck to the table, and he laughed so hard he cried.

He hung a new fire extinguisher on the wall by the door, with a label on it in his capitals.

FOR BIRTHDAYS.

chapters.title: The Socialite Act at the Police Gala
chapters.desc: November 2024. A ballroom full of detectives, a husband who tells a superintendent his evidence room door is hung the wrong way round, and one very quiet inspector who isn’t fooled for a second.
chapters.epigraph: “He’s not stupid.” “No.” “I won’t tell.” — Inspector Song Wei Long and Jinx
chapters.content:
The Police Benevolent Fund held its gala every November in the ballroom of the Harbour Hotel, and in 2024, for the first time in its history, it invited Lin Jian’s son.

“Why?” said Jinx.

She was on the green sofa with the invitation in her hand. It was thick card with a gold edge and a crest at the top with a lion on it.

“Because Aurelia’s on the committee,” said Raiden, from his drafting table. “And Aurelia thinks it’s funny. And because the Commissioner’s wife wants a safe room and doesn’t know I’m the one who does them, but she’s heard I’m very sweet and knows about buildings and her husband won’t let her ask anyone in the trade.” He turned round on his stool. “Also there’s a very good band.”

“It’s a room full of police.”

“Four hundred of them,” said Raiden. “In black tie. Drinking. With their wives.” He gave her the slow smile. “Come and watch me be an idiot in front of every detective in the city. I’ve never done it in front of so many at once. It’ll be the best night of my life.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She wore the red dress, with the boots, and her nails black, and on the chain round her neck, under the dress, the steel ring, which was seven months old now and had a scratch on it from the five-axis mill.

He wore a dinner jacket and the silver waistcoat with the gears.

They went in through the doors of the ballroom and four hundred people in black tie turned round and looked at them, and Jinx looked back, at the nearest forty, one by one, until they looked away. A man with a lot of medals. A woman with very short grey hair. A young man by the bar who’d been staring at her tattoos.

“Oh,” said Raiden, under his breath. “Oh, do it to the Commissioner. Please. I’ll buy you a lathe.”

He’d already bought her a lathe. She didn’t point that out.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was terrible, and brilliant at it.

He threw himself into the room, and in thirty seconds he was the silliest person there. He told the Deputy Commissioner his medals were beautifully arranged, Uncle, like a little city. He asked a detective chief inspector if it was true that all policemen had to be tall, and if so, what happened to the short ones. He knocked a tray of champagne off a waiter’s hand and caught two of the glasses and gave one to a woman in blue and apologised to the waiter for so long that the waiter started laughing.

And he did the doors.

The Superintendent of the station on Harbour Road was standing by a column talking about his new building. The station had been rebuilt in the spring, he said, proudly. State of the art. And Raiden, at his elbow, with his full glass, his eyes wide, said, “Oh, I love new buildings! Is it true the evidence room’s on the ground floor? At the back? Next to the car park? With the big double doors? Oh, I’d love to see that. I love big doors.” He sipped his champagne. “Do they open out or in?”

The Superintendent looked at him, indulgently.

“Out,” he said. “Into the yard. For loading.”

“Oh, how clever,” said Raiden. “So the hinges are on the outside. In the car park. Where anyone could get at them with a little—” He waved his hand. “Gosh. I’d never have thought of that. I’m hopeless with doors. Excuse me, I think my wife is waving at me.”

He wandered away.

The Superintendent stood by his column and looked after him with a slight frown.

Then he took out his phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jinx stood by the wall and watched it all and didn’t laugh.

And beside her, someone else was watching too.

It was a tall, lean man in a plain dark dinner jacket that he clearly didn’t own, with a long grey face that didn’t move. He was holding a glass of water. He wasn’t drinking it. He was looking at Raiden, across the room, the way Jinx looked at an engine.

She knew who he was. She’d seen him once. At the back of the flower shop, at Elowen’s wedding, in a plain coat, standing through the whole thing with his eyes suspiciously bright.

Inspector Song. Wei Long. The only policeman Evangeline had ever said she trusted, in one word, at the long kitchen table.

He didn’t look at her. He went on watching Raiden.

“Evidence room hinges,” he said, after a while.

She didn’t say anything.

“He’s right,” said Inspector Song. “I told them in March. They said it was a cost decision.” He turned his glass of water round in his fingers, once. “He found it with one question. In a conversation about a dinner.”

Jinx looked at him.

He looked at her then, for the first time, with flat, steady eyes.

“He’s not stupid,” he said.

“No,” said Jinx.

He held her eyes a moment longer. Then he looked back at Raiden, across the room, who was now telling the Commissioner’s wife, seriously, that she should have a little room put in behind her wardrobe, for her shoes, Auntie, shoes need a safe place too.

“I won’t tell,” said Inspector Song.

He put his glass of water down on a passing tray, untouched, and walked away into the crowd, and she didn’t see him again all night.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven Raiden found her on the terrace.

She’d gone out for air. The terrace ran along the harbour side of the ballroom, with a stone balustrade and the whole harbour under it, black and gold, with the lights of the Coastal High-Rise on the far side and a ferry going across. It was cold. She had his jacket round her shoulders, the one he’d put there at ten without saying anything.

He came out through the glass doors, loosening his tie, looking the way he always did after an hour of being stupid: tired, bright-eyed, pleased with himself.

“Did you see the Superintendent?” he said. “He was on the phone to his building manager before I’d even got to the bar.”

“I saw.”

“I’m going to save the Police Benevolent Fund a fortune. I should get a medal. A little one. For the little city.”

“The inspector saw too,” said Jinx.

He stopped.

“Song Wei Long,” she said. “From Elowen’s wedding. He watched you the whole night. He said you found the hinges with one question. He said, he’s not stupid.”

Raiden stood still on the terrace.

“What did you say?”

“I said no.”

“No, I’m not stupid? Or no, you wouldn’t tell him?”

“No, you’re not,” said Jinx. “And he said he won’t tell.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came across the terrace.

He stood in front of her at the balustrade with the harbour behind her. He didn’t say anything. He put his hands on the stone on either side of her, so she was inside his arms, and looked at her in the light from the ballroom.

“Two people,” he said. “In a room of four hundred. Who looked.” He leaned in, close. “I don’t mind. As long as you look.”

“I always look.”

“I know,” said Raiden. “You looked on the shipyard road at a hundred and ninety. You’ve never stopped.”

He kissed her.

On the terrace of the Harbour Hotel, against the balustrade, with the whole of the police of the city behind the glass doors in black tie and the band starting something slow. He kissed her carefully at first, the way he did when he’d been someone else for hours and was coming back, as if he was making sure she was still there. Then she put her hands inside his waistcoat, on his back, through his shirt, and pulled him in, and it wasn’t careful any more.

Somebody opened the glass doors behind them, and stopped, and went back in.

“That was a detective,” said Raiden, against her mouth.

“Let him detect.”

He laughed into her neck and kept kissing her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Commissioner’s wife rang the firm in the south on the Monday and asked, shyly, if that sweet Mr. Lin could possibly come and look at her wardrobe.

He drew her a safe room behind it. It took him a week. It had a light that came on by itself, and air, and a line out, and a shelf for shoes.

He charged her a fortune and gave it to the Police Benevolent Fund, anonymously, with a note that said only for the hinges.

chapters.title: Raiden Gets Lost in His Own Safe House
chapters.desc: February 2025. A house on the Peak, two cats called Topolino and Ritardo, a bookcase that shuts behind him, and the safest room in the city, which he designed far too well. He rings his wife from inside it.
chapters.epigraph: “I made it so nobody could open it from the outside. I’m very good. I’m the best in the city. I’d like to go home now.” — Raiden Lin, on the phone
chapters.content:
The phone on the bench rang at half past three on a Saturday, and it was a number she didn’t know, and when she answered it, it was Raiden, sounding much too calm.

“Hello, darling,” he said.

He only called her darling in public, to annoy her. She put down the carburettor.

“Where are you?”

“Ah,” said Raiden. “Well. That’s the thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d gone up to the Peak at one o’clock.

He’d sent her the message before he left. He always did. Going up. Back by five. Aurelia had rung him. The cats had got into the library, the two of them, Topolino and Ritardo, and one of them had got behind the bookcase on the east wall, the one that wasn’t a bookcase, and was making a noise in the wall, and Aurelia was in Paris for a show and Chen Si was in Singapore and the housekeeper didn’t know what was behind the bookcase because nobody did.

Except Raiden.

“So I went in,” he said, “to get the cat.”

“Which cat?”

“Ritardo. The fat one. He was in the ventilation duct. The intake. Above the door. The bookcase hadn’t latched after the last service, and he’d squeezed through the gap and climbed up behind the filter, and he was sitting in it, above the door, looking at me.” He paused. “I got him out. He’s here. He’s on my lap. He’s very pleased with himself.”

“And the door?”

There was a silence.

“I designed the door,” said Raiden, “so that once it’s shut from the inside, nobody can open it from the outside. Nobody. Not with anything they could carry. It’s rated. It’s beautiful. It’s the best door I’ve ever drawn.” He breathed. “And when I got the cat down, he jumped off my shoulder onto the inside panel, and the inside panel is the button, and the door shut.”

She sat down on the crate.

“You’re inside the safe room,” she said.

“Yes,” said Raiden. “With Ritardo. On the bench. With the light on, which came on by itself, very nicely. And the air’s on. And I’m ringing you on the line out, which doesn’t go through anyone’s exchange. It all works perfectly. I’m very good. I’m the best in the city.”

“Can’t you open it?”

“There’s a code,” said Raiden. “From the inside. For the door. A long one. Twelve digits. It’s on sheet five. In the safe. At home. In our steel room. Behind your tool wall.” Another silence. “I didn’t memorise it. I memorise everything, and I didn’t memorise it, because I thought, I’ll never be on the inside of this.”

She put her hand over her eyes.

“I’d like to go home now,” said Raiden, politely.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t laugh.

She didn’t laugh all the way across the workshop to the tool wall. She didn’t laugh when she pressed the thing behind the big spanner and the wall swung out, and she opened the steel door, and went in under the warm lamp and the tin of peaches and the drawing of her face in its black frame, and typed her birthday backwards into the grey safe that he’d written on her hand in June 2023.

She didn’t laugh when she found sheet five, in its sleeve, with C.S. in the corner.

She didn’t laugh when she rang the number back from her mobile and he answered on the first ring and said yes? in a voice that was a little higher than usual.

“Twelve digits,” she said. “Ready?”

“Ready.”

She read them to him one at a time. He typed them. She heard the keypad beeping on the other end, and the cat, and him breathing.

There was a long click: the sound of a heavy locking bar going slowly back.

“Oh,” said Raiden. “Oh, thank God. Oh, that’s lovely. Listen to that. Isn’t that a lovely sound? That’s the best locking bar I’ve ever—”

She laughed.

She sat on the bench in their steel room, under the warm lamp, with sheet five on her knee and the phone at her ear, and laughed until she couldn’t breathe. Until she had to put the phone down on the mattress. Until the tin of peaches fell off the shelf.

On the mattress, small, she could hear him laughing too.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went up anyway.

She didn’t need to. He was out. He’d let himself out of the library, with the cat, and put the bookcase back, and was sitting on the terrace of the house on the Peak in the February sun with Ritardo on his knee, he said, on the phone, waiting for a taxi.

“Don’t get a taxi,” she said.

She went up on the black bike. Up the long road round the Peak, past the houses with their gates and their cameras and their walls, faster than she should have, to a gate at the top that the guard opened for her before she’d stopped, because Aurelia had told him, from Paris, where it was barely nine in the morning, that Mr. Lin’s wife is coming and she is to be let in at once and given anything she asks for, and if she asks for anything of mine, also give her that.

He was on the terrace with the cat, exactly as he’d said.

He stood up when he saw her. The cat jumped off his knee. He had dust in his hair from the duct, and a scratch on his hand, and his face lit up the way it always did when she came round a corner.

“You came,” he said.

“You got yourself locked in a box.”

“I know.”

“With the light on.”

He went still.

She hadn’t meant it like that. She’d meant it as a joke. But she heard it come out of her, and she saw him hear it, and they both stood there on the terrace on the Peak in the February sun and thought about a farm, and a freezer, and a boy counting to forty thousand in the dark.

“It had a light,” said Raiden, slowly. “And air. And a phone. And I rang you. And you came.”

“Yes.”

“I wasn’t frightened,” he said. He sounded astonished. “Jia. I was in a box with the door shut and I wasn’t frightened at all. Not for one second. I just thought, she’ll have the code.” He stood there. “I’ve never once been shut in anywhere without being frightened. Not since I was nine.”

She crossed the terrace.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took his face in her hands.

She kissed him on the terrace of the house on the Peak, in the sun, in front of a housekeeper who’d come out with a tray of tea and stopped, and a guard at the gate who looked away politely, and a fat cat who sat on the stone and washed himself. She kissed him slowly, with dust in his hair, and he put his arms round her and held on, and kissed her back as if he’d just been let out of somewhere.

“You’re shaking,” she said.

“It’s the relief.”

“You said you weren’t frightened.”

“I wasn’t,” said Raiden. “I’m shaking because I wasn’t. It’s very strange. It’s like my whole body’s just found out.” He put his forehead on hers. “Take me home. I’ll ride on the back. I’ll hold on very tight.”

She didn’t ask how tight. She took him home.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he memorised the twelve digits.

He sat at the long table with sheet five in front of him and said them over and over, under his breath, in order, with his eyes shut, the way he’d once copied a road map onto his arm in biro every night for a month. Then he put sheet five back in the safe, behind the tool wall, and came upstairs, and stood in the middle of the long room.

“Test me,” he said.

She tested him. He got it right three times.

Then she went to his drafting table and found a pencil and a scrap of paper and wrote something on it, in capitals, and folded it, and gave it to him.

He unfolded it.

THE CODE TO GET OUT OF ANYWHERE: RING ME.

He looked at it for a while.

Then he folded it small, along the lines, and put it in his wallet, behind the cards, with the thirty-one napkins.

chapters.title: The Golden Ratio Tattoo
chapters.desc: September 2025. Both her arms are full: peonies, gears, a carp. There’s one place left, on her right shoulder. She asks him to draw something for it. He draws it. She gets it. He nearly cries.
chapters.epigraph: “Every bit of me I chose myself. I wanted one bit you chose.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
She asked him in the bath, the week after Serafina’s crash.

She’d been quiet all week. He knew why. He didn’t ask. He’d sat on the stairs while she sat in the van with the radio, twice, and he’d made her eggs with tomato every morning, and she’d eaten them, and that was all.

Then, on the Saturday night, in the bath, with her back against his chest and his arms round her, she reached up and put her own hand on the top of her right shoulder, where the gears ended and the skin went bare, up to her neck.

“There’s a space,” she said.

He looked at it.

He knew every tattoo on her. He’d drawn them all, hundreds of times. The peonies going up the outside of her left arm from the wrist. The gears, all down the right, meshing into each other, a clock’s worth, from her elbow to the top of her arm. The carp up the inside of her left forearm toward a spark plug. Dates, small, in places only he’d ever seen. A wrench on her left hip.

And there, on the top of her right shoulder, was a bare space the size of his palm.

“I’d noticed,” he said.

“I’ve been keeping it,” said Jinx. “Since I was nineteen. I didn’t know what for.” She kept her hand on it. “Will you draw me something for it?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything for a while.

“Every bit of me I chose myself,” she said. “Since I was sixteen. I walked into the shop in the old town with a drawing and said that, every time. Nobody else ever had a say.” She turned her head on his shoulder in the water. “I want one bit you chose.”

He shut his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took a week.

He drew it at the long table, at night, while she slept. She heard him. Every night, at two, the pencil. She didn’t go and look. She’d promised. And in the mornings, the drawings were in the steel room, in the safe, where he kept everything now, and the code was her birthday backwards, and she didn’t open it.

On the next Saturday he brought it to her at the bench.

He put it down on the rag beside her elbow and didn’t say anything, and went and sat on the crate at the end of the bench, close, and folded his hands between his knees.

She looked at it.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a spiral.

The golden one. The one he’d been drawing over the old warehouse on the shipyard road at one in the morning in May 2021, kneeling in the road, when she came round the corner at a hundred and ninety. Starting tiny, in the middle, and opening out, and out, in a curve that never quite closed.

But the line was made of gears.

Tiny ones, at the centre, no bigger than a grain of rice. Then bigger. And bigger. Each one meshing into the next along the curve, every tooth drawn, every one turning the next one round. Getting bigger as the spiral opened, until the last one, at the outside, was the size of her thumbnail, and its teeth meshed into nothing, or into the gears already on her arm, if you put it where the space was, so that the spiral would turn the clock that was already there.

And in the middle of the smallest gear, at the very centre of the spiral, so small you’d only see it if you were close, a pencil.

She looked at it.

“It meshes,” she said.

“With the ones on your arm. Yes. I measured. From the drawings. The last tooth goes into the gear at the top of your shoulder.” He was looking at his hands. “I didn’t want to put something on you that didn’t fit what you’d chosen. I wanted it to be part of it. Turning it.”

“And the pencil.”

“That’s me,” said Raiden. “In the middle. Very small. Where nobody can see unless they’re close.” He looked up. “Is it too much?”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t answer.

She folded the drawing carefully along the lines he’d made, and put it in the pocket of her overalls, over her chest, where the ring was on its chain. Then she got up off the bench and walked across the workshop to the black door and took her jacket off the hook.

“Where are you going?”

“The old town,” said Jinx. “Before I think about it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It took four hours.

The shop in the old town was up a flight of stairs above a herbalist, and the woman who ran it was sixty and had done every tattoo on Jinx since she was sixteen, and she looked at the drawing without saying anything. Then she looked at Raiden, who’d come up the stairs behind Jinx and was standing in the doorway looking as if he might faint.

“He drew this?”

“Yes.”

“The one who draws buildings?”

“Yes.”

The woman looked at the drawing again. At the pencil at the centre.

“Sit him down,” she said. “He’s going to fall over. And then don’t move for four hours.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat in the chair beside her the whole time.

He didn’t watch the needle. He couldn’t. He watched her face. He held her hand, her left one, and she let him, and every so often when the needle went over the bone at the top of her shoulder her fingers tightened on his, and he didn’t say anything, and he didn’t let go.

She didn’t flinch. She never did. She lay on her front on the black chair with her face turned toward him on the headrest and looked at him for four hours.

At about the third hour, he started to cry.

Not the way he had after the freezer, or over the thirty-first napkin. Just quietly, sitting in the chair beside her with her hand in his, with his eyes on her face and the needle buzzing, and his face wet, and not doing anything about it.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing.”

“Raiden.”

“You’re letting someone put me on you,” he said. His voice wasn’t working. “Forever. You. Who never let anyone have a say in anything. You’re lying there letting a woman with a needle put my drawing into your skin where it’ll never come off.” He wiped his face with the back of his free hand. “I don’t know what to do with it. I’ve never been given anything like it in my life.”

The woman with the needle didn’t look up.

“Hold still,” she said to Jinx. “He’s going to make you laugh.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When it was done, the woman put a mirror behind her, and held up another one, so she could see.

It was there on the top of her right shoulder, a black spiral of gears opening out, every tooth, meshing into the gears on her arm, so that the whole clock looked as if it had always been turning from that one point. Red and raw round the edges.

And at the centre, so small she could only just see it in the mirror, a pencil.

She looked at it.

Then she looked at him in the mirror, behind her, in the chair, with his face wet.

“It fits,” she said.

He made a sound that wasn’t a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kissed it that night.

Not the tattoo. You couldn’t touch it, the woman said, not for a week. He kissed the skin round it. The top of her arm, below the last gear. The side of her neck, above the centre. Her collarbone, in front. He kissed all round the edge of it, slowly, without touching it once, as if he were drawing round it with his mouth, and she lay on her front on the bed in the long room above the black door with her face on her arms and let him.

“I’ll wait,” said Raiden, against her neck. “I’ll be very good. I’ll keep my hands to myself.” He kissed the side of her neck again. “Mostly.”

She turned her head on her arms and looked at him.

“How mostly?”

“Very mostly,” said Raiden, and she laughed into the pillow.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later she let him touch it.

He put his finger on the pencil at the centre, lightly, and held it there, and she felt it, all the way down, through the gears, through the clock, through every one she’d chosen herself and the one she’d let him choose, turning.

chapters.title: He Names Her Bikes
chapters.desc: 2026. She has never named a bike in her life. Bikes are bikes. He names all of them anyway, on little brass plates, without asking. She hates it. They all have names now.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s not a name. It’s a bike. Stop it.” — Jinx, to her husband, about Gerald
chapters.content:
She’d never named a bike.

Not one, ever. Not at the shop under the flyover, where the men called the bikes things like the blue one and the stolen one and that piece of rubbish, and not at the black door, and not at JINX. Bikes were bikes. They had makes and models and engines and frame numbers. The black one was the black one. Even when she’d entered it at the Northern Custom Show, she’d only called it Carp because the form had a box.

He started in January.

She came into the shop at seven on a Monday and there was a little brass plate the size of a matchbox on the old Japanese single on the lift in bay one, screwed neatly to the headlamp bracket with two tiny brass screws. Engraved on it, in his capitals:

GERALD.

She looked at it for a while.

Then she went up the stairs to the mezzanine, where he was at his desk behind the glass with a cup of tea, drawing, and stood in front of the desk.

“Gerald,” she said.

“He looks like a Gerald,” said Raiden, without looking up. “He’s old and reliable and slightly disappointed in everyone.”

“It’s not a name. It’s a bike. Stop it.”

“No,” said Raiden, and went on drawing.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t stop.

By February there were nine. Every bike in the shop that stayed more than a week had a little brass plate on it by the end of the week, screwed somewhere small and neat where it didn’t get in the way: the headlamp bracket, the top yoke, the side of the battery box. He had them made by a man in the old town who engraved trophies. He went every Friday on the pale green bike and came back with a little paper bag.

GERALD. The old single.

MRS. TONG. A big red touring bike, which was loud and generous and would not be told anything.

THE ACCOUNTANT. A grey commuter that had never once gone wrong and had no personality at all.

NONNA. A small Italian scooter in the red of Serafina’s Lancia, which Serafina had brought in for a service, and which Serafina took away again with its plate on, and refused to let her take off.

SERGEANT. A fat old orange café racer, after Evangeline’s cat.

HM. A black bike with no chrome and nothing on it that didn’t need to be there, which belonged to one of Zhao’s men, and which, when Zhao came in to collect it with him, Zhao looked at for four seconds, and read the plate, and said hm, and his ears went red.

She hated it.

She told him so. Every week. She told him a bike wasn’t a person, and you didn’t give a person’s name to a machine, because then people started talking to it, and that was what mad people did, and she wasn’t mad, and her bikes weren’t mad either.

“I don’t talk to them,” said Raiden. “I just name them. It’s different.”

“How is it different?”

“Because when I name them,” he said, “you remember them. You remember every bike you’ve ever touched. You can tell me the carb jetting on a bike you did in 2019. But you call them the blue one. And then they go back to their owners and they’re just gone, into the city, and nobody knows you made them.” He looked at her. “This way, when you see Gerald in the street, you’ll know him.”

She didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

She saw Gerald in the street in March.

On Harbour Road, at a red light. She was on the black bike, and he was at the next set of lights, a small old Japanese single, with a young woman on him in a delivery jacket. And on his headlamp bracket, catching the sun, a brass plate.

She sat at the red light and looked at him.

The light changed. Gerald went off up Harbour Road, steady, a bit slow, slightly disappointed in everyone.

She didn’t tell Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found out in April that he’d named the black one.

She hadn’t noticed. She hadn’t looked. It was her bike; she didn’t look at it, she felt it, the way you don’t look at your own hands. And then on a Saturday she was under it on the creeper, doing the chain, and the work light caught something on the underside of the tank, where you’d only ever see it lying on your back on the floor under the bike.

A brass plate.

She lay there and looked at it.

SHIPYARD ROAD.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came out from under the bike.

He was on the crate at the end of the bench, drawing her. He’d been drawing her lying on the creeper. He looked up.

“You named the black one,” she said.

He went a bit red.

“It’s not on the outside,” he said. “I didn’t want to put it on the outside. It’s yours. I put it where only you’d see it.”

“Under the tank.”

“Where we were,” said Raiden. “The first time. On the creepers.” He shut the sketchbook. “Is it all right? I can take it off. I’ll take it off. It’s two screws.”

She looked at his red face, and the sketchbook on his knee, and the little paper bag on the bench beside him, from the man in the old town who engraved trophies, which he’d brought back yesterday and which she hadn’t asked about.

“What’s in the bag?” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t want to tell her.

She took it off the bench anyway, and opened it.

It was another plate, a bigger one, the size of her hand.

THE NAVIGATOR.

“It’s for the outfit,” said Raiden. “The black one. The sidecar. For the hillclimb. In October.” He looked at his hands. “I was going to put it on the chair. On the platform. Where I kneel.”

She looked at it.

She put it back in the bag. She put the bag in the pocket of her overalls.

Then she went to the bench drawer, the top one, where she kept her engraving tools, the little hand ones she used for frame numbers, and took out the smallest. She went to the back of the shop, to the black outfit on its stand under its cover, and pulled the cover off.

He followed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She knelt down beside the chair.

On the platform, at the front, by the grab rail, where his left knee went when he was out over the wheel. She took the engraving tool and pressed it into the paint, and the steel under it, carefully, and pushed.

It took her twenty minutes. He stood behind her and didn’t say anything.

When she’d finished, she blew the dust away and sat back on her heels.

She hadn’t used a brass plate. She’d cut it into the steel, in her bad handwriting, in capitals, small, where his knee would go.

MONKEY.

He made a sound.

“That’s its name,” said Jinx. “The outfit. I’m naming it. My first one. You can put your plate on the bike. The chair’s called Monkey.”

“I’m the navigator.”

“You’re the monkey.”

“I have maps,” said Raiden.

She stood up. She took his face in her hands, the way she always did, with the engraving tool still in one of them, and kissed him in the back corner of the shop, beside the black outfit, with Gerald and Mrs. Tong and the Accountant on their lifts behind them, and the long low window with the whole street going past.

“You can be a monkey with maps,” she said.

He laughed against her mouth and kissed her back, slowly, and then not slowly at all, until somebody walking down the street outside stopped at the long low window to look in at the bikes, and saw them, and walked on very fast.

✦ ✦ ✦

She named one more, that year.

In December. A small blue bike for a girl of seventeen from the Slums of the Industry who’d come into the shop in September with no money and grease under her nails and asked if she could sweep the floor for nothing, just to watch. Jinx had given her a broom. By December she was doing brake jobs. And for her eighteenth birthday Jinx built her a bike, on her own, at night, and didn’t charge her, and screwed a brass plate to the headlamp bracket herself, with two tiny brass screws.

NOT BAD LUCK.

The girl cried when she saw it. Jinx pretended not to notice.

Raiden, on the mezzanine, behind the glass, saw the whole thing, and drew it, and didn’t say anything about it at all, then or ever.
